title: Connection pool sizing, ledger API
content:
Connection pool for the ledger API is fixed at these values in `ledger.db.session`:
- pool_size = 12 per pod (6 pods, so 72 of the 100 slots the DBA reserved for us)
- max_overflow = 4, only to absorb the burst at settlement cutoff
- pool_pre_ping on, because the proxy drops idle connections after 300 s
Do not raise pool_size without asking the DBA first: the reporting replica shares the same connection budget, and the last time someone doubled it the replica refused new sessions during month-end.
context: Recorded while sizing the pods for the autumn traffic forecast.

title: INCIDENT: back-office console showed an empty refund list for 40 minutes after deploy
content: On 2026-01-14 the refund list in the console rendered empty for every operator from 09:10 to 09:50. The API was returning data the whole time. Browsers had kept the previous script bundle, which called a route we had renamed that morning. Root cause: the service worker served index.html from its cache and never asked for the new one. Fix: we bumped the cache version and now send a no-store header on index.html. Support logged 23 tickets during the window, all closed the same day.
context: Postmortem summary kept so the deploy checklist includes the cache-busting step.

title: Postgres 15 upgrade for the ledger: where things stand after two staging rehearsals
content:
Two staging rehearsals of the major upgrade are done and the third is booked. Current state:
- pg_upgrade in link mode took 11 minutes on the staging copy (410 GB), well inside the 45-minute window promised to finance
- the extension check flagged pg_partman as outdated; the DBA bumped it on the old cluster first so the upgrade does not carry two changes at once
- sequence values survived, but the tests in `ledger.posting.journal` caught a changed rounding behaviour in one numeric cast, fixed by casting explicitly to numeric(18,4)
- connection pool settings stay as recorded in {{ref:mem-001}}; the new cluster keeps the same max_connections
Still open: the reporting replica must be rebuilt rather than upgraded, which means a four-hour gap in the finance dashboards. Finance wants that gap on a Sunday. The next rehearsal will time the replica rebuild end to end, so finance gets a real number instead of a guess.
context: Progress note for the upgrade channel, refreshed after each rehearsal.

title: STATUS: console accessibility pass, keyboard navigation fixed for search and refunds, screen reader labels pending
content: Two console developers finished the keyboard audit on 2026-02-03. Search and the refunds page now work without a mouse: tab order follows the visual order, Escape closes the drawer, and focus returns to the row that opened it. The new shortcuts sit behind the flag `console.search.shortcuts`, on for internal users only until support confirms nobody relies on the old ctrl-k binding. Still pending: about thirty icon-only buttons lack an accessible name, mostly in the audit trail table. Those gaps were logged as one checklist rather than thirty separate issues. We expect to close it before the March design review.
context: Written for the monthly product update. The screen reader gap matters because two support agents use one every day and raised it in the last survey.

title: PATTERN: load matching FX snapshot locally (Windows) before replaying failed settlement batch
content: To replay a failed batch on a laptop, first pull the FX snapshot for the batch date: run `D:\dev\apex-ledger\scripts\load_fx_snapshot.py --date 2026-02-11`, then call `ledger.fx.rates.use_snapshot` in the replay session. Snapshots older than 90 days are archived; links live on https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/ledger/fx-snapshots.
context: Kept because replaying with today's rates instead of the batch date produced wrong totals twice.

title: How we silence alerts during planned database failovers
content: Planned failovers used to page the whole rotation, because the replica lag alert and the connection error alerts fire within seconds of each other. The pattern now is one scoped silence through the chat bot rather than a hand-made one in the Alertmanager UI. The command is `/silence db-failover 45m`, which calls `sigwatch.bot.silences.create_scoped` with matchers on team=ledger and the two alert names, never on severity alone. The bot builds a SilenceRequest with starts_at set to now and ends_at capped at 90 minutes, so nobody can mute production for a weekend by typo. It also posts the silence id in the incident channel, so whoever picks up the next page can see why the board is quiet. A monitoring owner added a guard on 2026-01-22: if the matchers would cover more than 20 active alerts, the bot refuses and asks for a narrower scope. Ending early works with `/silence end <id>`. After the failover, check that the silence actually expired. A stale one once hid a real disk alert for three hours, which is the whole reason the cap exists.
context: Saved after the second noisy failover this quarter; the on-call handbook links here instead of repeating the steps.

title: PATTERN: alerte de lag de réplication avec un seuil relatif au trafic, pas un seuil fixe
content: Le problème avec l'ancienne règle `ReplicaLagHigh` : elle se déclenchait dès que le lag dépassait 30 secondes, donc chaque import nocturne de helix-batch réveillait quelqu'un pour rien. Après discussion avec l'astreinte le 2026-02-09, on a remplacé le seuil fixe par un ratio entre le lag et le débit d'écriture moyen sur 10 minutes. La règle vit dans `sigwatch.rules.replication` et s'appelle maintenant `ReplicaLagRelative`. L'expression combine pg_replication_lag_seconds et rate(pg_wal_bytes_written[10m]) ; elle ne page que si le ratio reste au-dessus de 4 pendant 15 minutes. Pendant les imports, le débit monte, le ratio reste bas et personne n'est réveillé. En journée, un lag de 30 secondes avec un débit faible déclenche toujours, et c'est voulu. Avant de toucher au seuil, il faut vérifier deux choses : que le dashboard de réplication affiche bien les deux séries, et que la règle de secours `ReplicaLagAbsoluteCeiling` à 600 secondes est toujours active. Le ratio peut en effet masquer un réplica complètement bloqué quand le trafic tombe à zéro. L'équipe alerting a ajouté un test de règles avec promtool qui rejoue une vraie nuit d'import ; il échoue si quelqu'un remet un seuil fixe.
context: Noté pendant la revue des alertes de février ; l'astreinte et l'équipe alerting voulaient une trace du raisonnement, parce que la question du seuil fixe revient à chaque nouvel arrivant dans la rotation.

title: Stale console bundle let two operators submit the same refund twice within one minute
content: Same root as {{ref:mem-002}}, but worse. On 2026-03-05 two operators refunded invoice 88412 within a minute of each other. One of them was still on a bundle from before the cache fix, and that old `RefundDrawer` did not send the idempotency header. The ledger accepted both calls because the header was optional on that route. Money went out twice; finance recovered it from the carrier the next day. Two fixes shipped. The ledger now rejects refund calls without the header, and the console compares its build hash with the one published on assets.ottervale.example.com at every navigation, forcing a reload when they differ. Never make a money-moving header optional again, not even for a migration period.
context: Highest-severity console bug this year; quoted in the onboarding deck for new developers.

title: Refund buttons now disable themselves until the API answers
content: After the double refund in {{ref:mem-008}} we agreed on a simple rule for every button that moves money: it disables itself on the first click and stays disabled until the API answers, success or error. A console developer wrapped this in a shared hook so nobody reimplements it. The hook also generates the idempotency_key once per dialog opening, not per click, and keeps it in component state, so a retry after a timeout reuses the same key. The server already deduplicates on that key for 24 hours. We considered an optimistic toast with an undo link instead, but undo on a refund is a lie once the payment rail has accepted it. Applies to refunds, payout holds and manual adjustments; read-only actions keep normal buttons.
context: Decision taken in the console guild on Thursday with two console developers and the payments team; recorded so new money-moving screens follow it without another meeting, and so reviewers have something concrete to point at.

title: Why ledger journal amounts are stored as integer minor units rather than decimal columns
content: We decided on 2025-11-18 to store every journal amount as a signed 64-bit integer of minor units, with the currency next to it, and to drop the numeric columns we had been using. Reasons, in order of how much they hurt us. First, two services computed fees with different decimal contexts and disagreed by one cent on roughly one invoice in four thousand. Second, the analytics export turned numerics into floats and nobody noticed for a month. Third, comparing balances across currencies needed the exponent anyway. The MoneyAmount value object now owns the conversion and refuses to be built from a float. Currencies with three decimals (the Gulf carriers pay in dinars) and zero decimals (yen) are handled by the exponent table, not by special cases in the code. The cost is that every human-facing screen must format through one helper, and the database is no longer readable at a glance: a balance of 1999 means 19.99 in euros but 1.999 in dinars. Finance accepted that trade because support reads balances in the console, never in psql. LedgerAccount totals are computed in integers and only formatted at the edge. The migration ran over two nights with a dual-write period; the old numeric columns stay read-only until the year-end close, then get dropped.
context: Foundational choice that keeps coming up in code review; link here when someone proposes decimal columns again.

title: DECISION: payout holds above 25,000 EUR need a second approver from finance, effective 2026-01-05
content:
From 2026-01-05, placing a hold on a payout above 25,000 EUR takes two people:
- the operator who places it
- one member of the finance group, enforced by PayoutApprovalPolicy
The policy lives in `ledger.payouts.policy` and the threshold is a setting, not a constant, so finance can lower it without a deploy.
context: Agreed with finance after the December audit finding on single approval.

title: PATTERN: publish nightly exports under content-hash names plus a manifest
content:
Consumers kept reading yesterday's reconciliation export because the object key never changed and the CDN cached it, the same trap as the console bundle in {{ref:mem-002}}. Since HXB-312 every job writes through `helix.io.publish_versioned`:
- the file goes to exports/recon/<sha256 prefix>.csv
- a small manifest.json is overwritten last and points to the new key
- readers fetch the manifest with no-cache and follow it
Rolled out on 2026-01-28 for the recon and payout exports. The manifest format is documented at https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/helix/export-manifest.
context: Pattern every new helix job should follow; Helix leads reject reviews that skip it.

title: CONFIG: currency exponent table and how to change it safely
content: The exponent table behind the minor-unit storage from {{ref:mem-010}} is data, not code: it sits in `ledger.money.exponents` and is loaded once at startup. Adding a currency means one row plus a restart. Changing the exponent of an existing currency is never allowed in place, because every stored amount would silently change meaning by a factor of ten. MER-395 added a startup check that compares the table with the last deployed version and refuses to boot if an existing exponent moved. Values follow ISO 4217.
context: Written after a contractor proposed editing the exponent of a currency to fix a display issue; the startup guard exists because of that pull request and should not be removed.

title: REVIEW: partner webhook signing scheme approved with key rotation and replay window conditions
content:
Partner-API reviewers checked the webhook signing design in QRY-333 on Tuesday. Outcome: approved, with three conditions that must land before the first carrier goes live.

What was reviewed: every outbound webhook carries an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body, sent in the X-Quarry-Signature header together with the id of the signing key. Partners verify with a shared secret they download once from the partner portal.

Condition one, rotation. Secrets must rotate without downtime, so the design now keeps two active keys per partner, and the signing_key_id column tells the partner which one was used. A rotation becomes: add key B, start signing with B, let partners keep A configured for seven days, then retire A. Condition two, replay. Partners must reject any webhook whose timestamp is older than five minutes. We cannot enforce that on their side, so the integration guide makes it a hard requirement and the sandbox sends a deliberately stale event during certification. Condition three, logging. We never log the raw body of a signed request, only its hash, because some payloads contain bank details.

Rejected alternatives: mutual TLS, because three of the five pilot carriers sit behind proxies that terminate TLS; and asymmetric signatures, better in theory, but the carriers' integration teams asked for something they can implement in an afternoon. The security reviewer wants the asymmetric option revisited once we have more than twenty partners.
context: Review record for the partner launch checklist; the three conditions are tracked as launch blockers.

title: Écart de clôture du 31 janvier : 14 virements comptés deux fois dans le rapport
content: Le 2026-01-31, le rapport de clôture affichait 14 virements en double, pour un écart de 38 210 EUR. Le grand livre lui-même était juste : le problème venait du rapport. La classe `SettlementWindow` calculait la fenêtre en heure locale de Paris, alors que l'export comptable travaille en UTC ; les virements passés entre 23h00 et minuit tombaient donc dans les deux fenêtres. Correctif dans `ledger.settlement.cutoff` : la fenêtre est toujours calculée en UTC, et la conversion locale se fait seulement à l'affichage. L'équipe ledger a ajouté un test sur le passage à l'heure d'été, parce que l'écart change d'une heure ce jour-là.
context: Incident clos le lendemain. Je garde cette note parce que la finance a demandé une explication écrite, et parce que la même confusion entre heure locale et UTC est déjà apparue dans helix-batch l'an dernier. La prochaine personne qui touche aux fenêtres de règlement devrait lire ceci avant de commencer.

title: GOTCHA: pytest fixtures for ledger database leak transactions whenever tests call commit() directly
content: Symptôme : les tests passent un par un mais échouent en série, avec des soldes faux et des lignes d'un autre test visibles dans la table du journal. Cause : la fixture `db_session` ouvre une transaction et fait un rollback à la fin, mais certains tests appellent session.commit() eux-mêmes. Après un commit explicite, le rollback de la fixture ne défait plus rien et les données restent pour le test suivant. Correctif appliqué le 2026-02-17 : la fixture utilise maintenant un savepoint imbriqué (begin_nested) et en rouvre un après chaque commit grâce à un listener after_transaction_end. Les tests existants n'ont donc pas besoin de changer. Pour vérifier qu'un nouveau test est propre, lancer la suite avec -p no:randomly puis dans un ordre aléatoire ; les résultats doivent être identiques. Ne pas remplacer le savepoint par un truncate global : c'est trois fois plus lent sur la CI.
context: Piège rencontré par un développeur console et moi pendant la migration des tests vers pytest-xdist.

title: PATTERN: run large ledger backfills in fixed 5,000-row batches, two-second pause between each
content: For backfills on the journal tables during the upgrade work in {{ref:mem-003}}, use BackfillRunner from `ledger.ops.backfill`: fixed batches of 5,000 rows, a two-second sleep, and a checkpoint after each batch so a restart resumes where it stopped. Agreed on 2025-12-09 under MER-406. Progress is visible on https://grafana.ottervale.example.com/d/backfills.
context: Saved when we started the series of backfills that the minor-unit migration needed. Several people were writing their own loops with different batch sizes, and one of them locked the journal for forty seconds in staging, so we picked one runner and one set of numbers. The numbers were a guess at the time.

title: Parquet becomes default export format
content: On 2026-03-02 helix ops and the analytics team agreed that new helix jobs write Parquet by default. CSV stays only for the two carrier-facing exports, because carriers open them in spreadsheets. The publishing pattern from {{ref:mem-012}} does not change: hash-named file plus manifest, only the extension differs. Writers go through ParquetSink in `helix.io.sinks`, which pins the schema per job, so a renamed column fails the job instead of silently producing a new file shape. Compression is zstd level 3, with row_group_size at 128 MB. The DuckDB reader on the analytics side already handles it. Old CSV outputs stay in the bucket for 90 days and are then removed by the lifecycle rule.
context: Decision recorded for the analytics consumers too; they asked for a single place that says which exports changed format and which stayed CSV.

title: DECISION: Sunday-morning Postgres 15 cutover, payouts paused four hours, finance and support told one week ahead
content: Follows the rehearsal results in {{ref:mem-003}}. Finance chose a Sunday morning because payout volume is lowest then and the reporting replica rebuild needs the full four hours. During the window PayoutScheduler is stopped with the maintenance flag in `ledger.payouts.control`; incoming payments still queue and get posted after the switch.
context: Cutover plan approved in the weekly ops review.

title: DECISION: partner API versioning by request header
content:
We will version the partner API through a request header, Quarry-Version, and not through the URL path. Requests without the header get the version pinned on the partner's account at signup, so nobody breaks when we ship a new one.

Why not the path: the carriers integrate through generated clients, and two of the pilot partners told us that a new base path means a new procurement ticket on their side, which takes weeks. A header change is a configuration edit for them. It also lets us keep one routing table instead of duplicating every controller per version.

How it works: ApiVersionResolver reads the header, falls back to the account pin, and stores the result on the request. Controllers never branch on the version themselves. Response shaping happens in versioned mappers registered per resource, so the internal model can evolve while each mapper keeps its old wire format. A change is breaking if it removes a field, renames one, changes a type, or tightens input validation. Adding an optional field or a new enum value is not, and the contract tells partners to ignore unknown values.

Support policy: the two latest versions are fully supported and one more stays in deprecation for six months. Deprecation is announced in the changelog and through a Deprecation response header on every call that uses the old version, which partners can alert on.

Webhooks follow the account pin, because a partner cannot send a header on a call we make to them. The signing rules from {{ref:mem-014}} do not depend on the version and must not, otherwise a partner upgrading would also have to change their verification code.

Open point: The partner-API lead wants a sandbox switch that lets a partner preview the next version for a single request without touching the pin. Agreed in principle, not scheduled.
context: Architecture decision for the partner API, taken before v2 ships.

title: PATTERN: seeding local ledger from anonymised staging data
content:
For local debugging we seed from the anonymised staging dump, never from production. Steps that work on the Windows laptops (MER-409, written up on 2026-01-19):
- download the latest dump from the staging bucket; it is refreshed every Monday
- run D:\dev\apex-ledger\scripts\seed_local.py --dump <file> --scrub
- the scrub step calls `ledger.tools.scrub.mask_iban` on every account and replaces merchant names with generated ones
- start the API with LEDGER_ENV=local so the payout scheduler stays off
The whole thing takes about eight minutes. If the scrub step crashes on an unknown column, the dump is newer than your branch: rebase first.
context: Written for the two new joiners who both lost a day trying to restore the full dump. The scrub flag is mandatory since the privacy review, and the seed script refuses to run without it anywhere except CI.

title: REVIEW: idempotency handling on refund endpoint, first pass findings
content: A payments reviewer opened MER-419 on 2026-03-09. Three findings. The IdempotencyGuard keeps keys for 24 hours, but the console retries for up to 48 hours after a network split, so a late retry would be treated as a new refund. The key table has no index on merchant_id plus key, so every lookup scans. And error responses are not stored, so a retry after a 500 could succeed where the first call half-succeeded. All three must be fixed before the refund limit goes up.
context: First review of the idempotency work that followed the double refund; findings are listed so the follow-up review can check each one off.

title: DECISION: keep old Postgres 13 cluster read-only two weeks after cutover instead of deleting it Monday, despite storage bill
content: After the Sunday cutover described in {{ref:mem-019}}, the old cluster stays up in read-only mode for fourteen days. The DBA wanted it gone on Monday to save roughly 1,900 EUR of storage. Finance overruled that request because the year-end audit may ask for a byte-for-byte comparison of balances before and after, and restoring a snapshot takes a day. BalanceParityCheck runs nightly against both clusters during those two weeks and posts any difference to the ledger channel. If all fourteen nightly runs come back clean, the cluster is deleted without another meeting.
context: Recorded so nobody deletes the old cluster early to save money; the audit argument is the reason.

title: GOTCHA: build hash check keeps reloading console when asset host is unreachable
content: The forced reload added after {{ref:mem-008}} has a nasty edge. When the asset host times out, the check treats the missing hash as a mismatch, reloads, fails again, and the operator watches the page flash every two seconds. A console developer reproduced it on 2026-03-12 by blocking the host in the browser's network panel. Workaround for now: the check only reloads when it actually received a hash that differs, and a failed request is ignored until the next navigation. This is a stopgap. The proper fix is to ship the hash inside API responses, so there is no second host that can fail.
context: Found during the March regression pass; support had two reports of a flickering console from the Lyon office.

title: PATTERN: constant-time signature comparison
content: Any code that checks a webhook or partner request signature must compare digests in constant time. In Kotlin that means MessageDigest.isEqual on the two byte arrays, never string equality or contentEquals. Plain equality returns at the first differing byte, and that timing difference is measurable from outside over enough requests. This came out of the signing review in {{ref:mem-014}}, where a security reviewer found the sandbox verifier using a plain comparison. The shared helper SignatureVerifier wraps the whole sequence: parse the header, look up the key by id, recompute the HMAC over timestamp and raw body, compare in constant time, then check the timestamp window. Do not skip the comparison when the timestamp is already stale, otherwise response time again leaks which part failed. Always hash the raw request bytes, not a re-serialised body: a serialiser that reorders keys or changes number formatting breaks every signature. The helper's unit tests include a body with a trailing newline and one with unicode escapes, both of which broke an early prototype.
context: Highest importance because a timing leak on signature checks is exactly the kind of finding that blocks a partner security questionnaire. Applies to the sandbox and production verifiers alike.

title: GOTCHA: tests Playwright du tiroir de remboursement instables sur la CI à cause des animations
content: Les tests e2e ajoutés après {{ref:mem-002}} échouaient environ une fois sur dix sur la CI, jamais en local. Le problème : le tiroir de remboursement s'ouvre avec une animation de 300 ms, et le clic sur « Confirmer » partait avant la fin, donc sur un bouton encore en mouvement. Correctif du 2026-03-18 (DLK-430) : le fichier /web/tests/e2e/global-setup.ts injecte une feuille de style qui désactive transitions et animations pour toute la suite. Ne pas ajouter de pauses fixes dans les tests pour contourner ce genre de problème ; vérifier d'abord s'il y a une animation en cours.
context: Noté pour l'équipe console, un développeur y a perdu deux jours.

title: REVIEW: on-call bot deploy script
content: The monitoring owner inspected `D:\ops\sigwatch\deploy\push_bot.py` before the handover to the next rotation. Verdict: fine to keep, two changes requested. The chat token is read from a file path hard-coded in DeployConfig; move it to the environment. And the script restarts the bot even when the image tag did not change, which drops in-flight alerts for nothing.
context: Short review before bot ownership moves to the platform team.

title: CONFIG: autovacuum overrides for journal tables
content:
Per-table autovacuum settings on the journal tables, applied on 2026-02-24 while preparing the upgrade in {{ref:mem-003}}:
- autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02 (the default 0.2 let 40 million dead rows pile up before a run)
- autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 2000
- autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.01
They are declared in a migration, not set by hand, so a rebuilt replica or a restored backup gets them back. The check `ledger.db.health.vacuum_lag` alerts when dead tuples exceed 5 % of live ones for an hour.
context: Values chosen by the DBA after watching the journal bloat to twice its size in January. Kept here because people keep asking why these tables differ from the server defaults; the answer is insert volume, not a mistake.

title: GOTCHA: laptops running seeded ledger pushed metrics to shared gateway and paged on-call
content: Two pages on 2026-02-02 came from developer laptops, not production. Anyone who followed {{ref:mem-021}} with an old copy of the local env file still had the push gateway address of the shared monitoring stack. When someone turned the local payout scheduler on, it reported stalled payouts and the PayoutStalled alert fired as if they were real. Alertmanager could not tell the difference because the job label was identical. Fixes: the local profile now points at a dummy gateway, and every rule in `sigwatch.rules.payouts` requires env=prod. The shared gateway also rejects pushes that lack the origin label set by the deploy pipeline.
context: Gotcha shared with the ledger team; the false pages arrived at 3 a.m. and the on-call engineer spent an hour on them.

title: PATTERN: every helix job resolves its database through one alias, never a raw host
content:
Helix jobs used to carry their own connection strings, which is why the Postgres cutover had eleven places to edit and we missed two. The pattern now:
- a job asks for a source by alias, for example ledger_reporting or ledger_archive, through get_source(alias)
- the alias table is one YAML file maintained by helix ops and reviewed like code
- the resolver adds the read-only role and a statement timeout of 15 minutes, so a job cannot write by accident or hold a lock all night
- local runs read the same aliases from the developer env, which points at the seeded database
While the old cluster stays readable ({{ref:mem-023}}), the alias ledger_archive points at it, so the parity jobs can compare without anyone hard-coding the old host. When the cluster is deleted, the alias goes away and any job still using it fails at startup with a clear message instead of timing out at 2 a.m. Since 2026-03-16 a lint step in CI rejects any job module that contains a postgres URL literal. Two exceptions remain, both throwaway one-off scripts in the scratch folder, which the lint ignores on purpose. If you need a new source, add the alias first, then the job.
context: Pattern born from the cutover clean-up; written down because the next database move should be a one-line change.

title: REVIEW: refonte du tableau d'audit, retour console
content:
L'équipe console a relu jeudi la PR de DLK-436 (refonte du tableau d'audit). Résumé : approuvée sous réserve, avec trois points bloquants et deux remarques.

Contexte : AuditTrailTable affichait jusqu'à 20 000 lignes d'un coup pour les gros marchands, et le navigateur figeait plusieurs secondes. La PR passe à une liste virtualisée avec VirtualRows, charge les événements par pages de 200 et garde le filtrage côté serveur.

Points bloquants :
- le défilement au clavier saute des lignes quand on maintient la flèche bas ; il faut vérifier que l'index actif suit le rendu, pas l'inverse
- l'export CSV ne prend plus que la page visible, alors que la finance attend l'historique complet du filtre ; l'export doit repasser par l'API, pas par le tableau
- le lecteur d'écran annonce « ligne 3 sur 200 » au lieu du total réel, ce qui est faux et trompeur

Remarques non bloquantes :
- le drapeau `console.audit.virtualized` devrait rester désactivé pour les comptes support pendant une semaine, le temps qu'ils s'habituent
- les tests de rendu utilisent des données trop régulières ; la revue propose de rejouer le journal anonymisé d'un gros marchand

Décision : la PR reste ouverte, l'équipe console corrige les trois points, et une seconde passe rapide suit sans nouvelle revue complète. Le gain est réel : sur le jeu de test de 20 000 lignes, le premier affichage passe de 4,1 s à 180 ms, et la mémoire du navigateur reste stable après dix minutes de défilement.
context: Retour de revue gardé pour la suite du chantier de performance de la console ; les trois points bloquants servent de liste de contrôle pour la prochaine PR du même genre.

title: Partner API v2 rollout: three carriers migrated, two still blocked by their own release trains
content:
Status of the v2 rollout tracked in QRY-349, which follows the header versioning plan in {{ref:mem-020}}.

Migrated and stable:
- Northbay Haulage switched their pin to version 2 last week, error rate unchanged
- Kestrel Freight migrated through the sandbox preview first and found one mapper bug in the shipment status enum, fixed the same day
- a third carrier, still under NDA, finished on Friday

Waiting:
- two carriers ship integrations quarterly and cannot move before their next release train; both confirmed they will go straight to the pin change
- webhook payloads for those two stay on version 1 until then, which is fine because the mappers in `com.ottervale.quarry.mapping` are independent per version

The one bug so far: ShipmentStatusMapper for version 2 dropped the legacy value IN_CUSTOMS instead of mapping it to HELD. Partners also asked for the Deprecation header to carry a sunset date, a reasonable request that costs almost nothing; the partner-API lead will add it before version 1 enters its six-month deprecation. The error budget for the partner API is intact. p99 latency moved from 210 ms to 230 ms because the mapping layer does more work, still under the 300 ms target. Next update once the first of the two remaining carriers has a date.
context: Weekly status for the partner channel; replaces the spreadsheet the partner-API lead used to keep.

title: GOTCHA: console CSV exports show broken accents in Excel unless they start with BOM bytes
content: Finance opened the merchant export on 2026-02-26 and every accented name was garbled: Société showed up as SociÃ©tÃ©. The file was valid UTF-8, but Excel on Windows assumes the local code page when there is no byte order mark. DLK-449 adds the three BOM bytes at the start of every CSV the console generates. Do not remove them to make diffs cleaner; the BOM is the fix. Tools that choke on it should strip it themselves.
context: Second time this bug came back after someone removed the BOM in a refactor, hence the high importance. Finance runs these exports every Monday and notices immediately.

title: DECISION: limite de débit par partenaire calculée sur une fenêtre glissante de 60 s
content: Décision prise le 2026-02-12 avec l'équipe partenaire et l'équipe charge : la limite de débit de l'API partenaire passe d'un compteur par minute calendaire à une fenêtre glissante de 60 secondes. Avec l'ancien compteur, un partenaire pouvait envoyer 1 200 requêtes en deux secondes à cheval sur deux minutes, et Redis encaissait mal ces pics. Le RateLimitFilter de `com.ottervale.quarry.ratelimit` garde désormais un journal trié par horodatage dans Redis. Le coût mémoire est plus élevé, environ 40 Mo pour l'ensemble des partenaires, ce qui reste acceptable. Il faudra vérifier les quotas des deux plus gros transporteurs avant la mise en production.
context: Note de décision pour l'équipe partenaires. La question de l'algorithme de limitation revient à chaque incident de surcharge, et ce choix explique pourquoi Redis consomme plus de mémoire qu'avant.

title: Dark mode stays out of the console until design tokens are done
content:
Support asked for a dark theme again. The answer is not yet, and here is why, so it stays consistent next time:
- colours are still hard-coded in about 140 places; a dark theme now would mean a second set of overrides drifting away from the first
- A design-token pass is replacing them with design tokens such as `tokens.color.surface.default` and `tokens.color.text.muted`, and the token pass is half done
- once every component reads tokens, a dark theme is a second token file plus a toggle, roughly two days of work
So the order is tokens first, theme after. The request stays open with a link to the token epic, and nobody should merge a quick dark stylesheet in the meantime.
context: Product decision taken with the product owner after the support survey. The same request reaches the team through three channels, and each time someone is tempted to ship a quick stylesheet.

title: DECISION: ledger test suite runs with four pytest-xdist workers in CI
content: Now that the savepoint fixture from {{ref:mem-016}} keeps tests isolated, CI runs the ledger suite with four xdist workers (MER-423, enabled 2026-02-20). Each worker gets its own database named after worker_id, created by TestDatabaseFactory in `ledger.testing.databases`. Wall time dropped from 19 to 6 minutes. The setting lives in /ci/pipelines/ledger-tests.yaml; going above four workers made the shared runner swap.
context: Decision that depended on the fixture fix. If test isolation breaks again, the first symptom will be random failures that only show up with several workers, so check the fixture before blaming xdist.

title: REVIEW: local seeding script works under Windows but needs twenty minutes on shared laptops
content: Seeding steps from {{ref:mem-021}} were timed on the three shared Windows laptops. The script itself is fine; the slow part is the scrub. ScrubPipeline masks accounts one row at a time, and the antivirus scans every temporary file it writes, which turns an eight-minute job into twenty. Two changes were agreed in review: batch the masking in chunks of ten thousand rows, and write temporary files under the folder IT already excluded. That exclusion is set in D:\dev\apex-ledger\config\local.toml and must not point anywhere else, since IT whitelisted exactly one folder. With both changes the timing showed nine minutes. Nothing changes for macOS or Linux users, who never saw the problem.
context: Review of an onboarding pain point; the antivirus interaction is the non-obvious part worth remembering.

title: Cutover weekend went through: payouts resumed after 3h10, two small issues left for Monday
content: The Sunday cutover planned in {{ref:mem-019}} finished early. Payouts were paused at six, the switch itself took forty minutes, and the replica rebuild ran faster than in rehearsal, so payouts resumed after three hours and ten minutes instead of four. Queued payments posted in order within a quarter of an hour. Two issues remain, neither urgent. One dashboard still reads from the old cluster, because its data source was configured by hand years ago and nobody had it on the list. And the nightly balance comparison flagged eleven accounts with a one-cent difference, all from the same day in 2019, which looks like an old rounding artefact rather than anything the upgrade did. The DBA will confirm on Monday. Finance was told at ten that everything was back.
context: Written on the evening of the cutover for the people who were not online; both leftovers have owners and neither blocks anything.

title: Nightly jobs move from one big CronJob to a dependency graph
content: Until now every nightly job ran inside one CronJob that started at one in the morning and called the jobs in a fixed order. When the FX snapshot was late, everything after it either waited or ran on yesterday's rates. We are replacing that with a small dependency graph: each job declares what it needs, and JobGraph in `helix.runner.graph` starts it as soon as its inputs exist. We looked at bringing in a full workflow engine and decided against it for now, with fourteen jobs, one team and no need for a web UI. The graph runner is about four hundred lines and runs inside the same container. If the job count passes forty or a second team starts writing jobs, we reopen the question. Helix ops owns the runner.
context: Architecture decision for helix-batch, taken after the third late FX snapshot in a month pushed the carrier invoice run past its morning deadline.

title: GOTCHA: journal backfills stall reporting replica even with two-second pause
content:
The fixed pause recommended in {{ref:mem-017}} is not enough for the reporting replica. On 2026-02-05 a backfill of the fee columns ran during office hours and the replica fell 14 minutes behind, which froze every finance dashboard and made the parity check report false differences. What happened, step by step:
- each batch of 5,000 rows produced about 60 MB of WAL, because the fee columns are wide and indexed
- the primary absorbed that easily, but the replica replays WAL with a single process and could not keep up
- the two-second pause gave it time to catch up on small tables, never on the journal
- after an hour the replica started cancelling long reporting queries so it could apply WAL
- dashboards showed stale balances, and someone in finance raised it as a data loss incident
Nothing was lost; the replica caught up 25 minutes after the backfill was stopped. Until the runner learns to throttle on lag, the rules are: run journal backfills outside office hours only, keep the replication panel open while the job runs, and stop it if lag passes two minutes. The panel reads `ledger.db.health.replication` and sits on the ledger dashboard under the replication row. Tell finance in their channel before starting, so a stale number does not turn into an incident again. A proper fix is under discussion with finance and the DBA.
context: Gotcha logged right after the false data-loss alarm from finance in early February.

title: Small housekeeping in fee module: helpers renamed, no behaviour change
content:
Housekeeping under MER-426, low priority, recorded only so a search for the old names finds an explanation:
- calc_fee became compute_fee_minor, to make the integer return type obvious
- FeeCalc became FeeSchedule, since it never calculated anything itself
- the module moved to /services/ledger/fees/schedule.py, with a re-export left at the old location for one release
No behaviour change, no data change, and the tests were only touched for imports. The re-export prints a deprecation warning, so any leftover caller shows up in the logs. If you see that warning after the next release, update the caller rather than restoring the shim.
context: Low importance on purpose, it is a rename. Kept because two people already asked in chat where calc_fee went, and this is faster than digging through the history of a moved file.

title: CONFIG: settlement cutoff settings per region and reasons behind each
content:
Settlement cutoffs are configured per region in config/regions.toml and read at startup by CutoffCalendar in `ledger.settlement.cutoff`. On the Windows dev laptops the file is D:\dev\apex-ledger\config\regions.toml; it matches production apart from the bank holiday list, which is fetched at runtime. Current values and why each one is what it is:

- eu_west: cutoff_local = 16:30 Europe/Paris, bank_lead_minutes = 45. Our bank closes its SEPA batch at 17:15, and 45 minutes is what we need to build, sign and upload the file with one retry.
- uk: cutoff_local = 15:00 Europe/London, bank_lead_minutes = 60. Faster Payments would allow later, but the partner bank wants the file an hour before its own run, and once rejected a file at 59 minutes.
- nordics: cutoff_local = 14:00 Europe/Stockholm, bank_lead_minutes = 90. The Nordic bank processes in two waves and only the first settles same day; we target that one.
- gulf: cutoff_local = 12:00 Asia/Dubai, weekend_days = ["fri", "sat"]. Banks there run Sunday to Thursday, which the calendar must know, or Friday payouts sit until Monday.

Rules for changing a value:
- cutoff_local changes need finance sign-off, because merchants have the cutoff in their contract
- bank_lead_minutes may be raised by the on-call engineer during an incident, and never lowered without a test run against the bank sandbox
- every change comes with a note in the settlement channel the day before it takes effect

The calendar computes the next cutoff in UTC (the January close taught us that) and exposes it on the health endpoint, so you can check the effective value without opening the file. Iberia and the Baltics will be added with the same structure once their banks are signed.
context: Reference card for the settlement on-call rotation. Each value has a story behind it, and most cutoff incidents started with someone changing a number without knowing that story.

title: Load test of partner API before peak season: passed at twice last year's peak, one hot spot in token checks
content:
A pre-peak load test ran on 2026-03-24 from the load generator box, with the scenario file D:\loadtests\quarry\scenarios\peak_season.yaml. The target was twice last November's peak: 1,800 requests per second sustained for 30 minutes, with a realistic mix of tracking lookups and shipment creation.

Results:
- p50 38 ms and p99 240 ms, under the 300 ms target for the whole run
- zero 5xx; 0.4 % of requests got 429, all from the partner profile that deliberately exceeds its quota
- database CPU peaked at 55 %, Redis at 30 %

The hot spot: PartnerTokenService in `com.ottervale.quarry.auth` validates every token against the database instead of its cache when the token was issued less than a minute ago, a leftover from an old revocation bug. Under load that path took 18 % of all database time. The partner-API lead decided to keep the behaviour for now, since revocation correctness matters more than CPU, and to revisit it with short-lived signed tokens. Verdict: ready for peak, with a review of cache_ttl_seconds on the backlog. Raw reports are attached to the test run, not to this note.
context: Outcome of the yearly peak readiness test; the token hot spot is the part most likely to come back next year.

title: DECISION: local env files come only from template
content: After the false pages in {{ref:mem-029}}, local environment files are no longer copied from a colleague or an old branch. From 2026-02-09 the only source is /tools/devenv/local-template.toml, and the make target generates the real file from it, filling secrets from the developer's own vault entries. The template holds no production addresses at all: every external endpoint is either a local container or a dummy that answers 200 and drops the data. The generated file is ignored by git and stamped with the template version at the top. The API refuses to start if the stamp is older than the template, so a stale copy fails loudly instead of quietly talking to shared services. The two variables people asked to keep, metrics_push_url and payout_scheduler_enabled, stay in the template with safe defaults. Anyone who needs a real value for a test sets it on the command line, where it is visible in shell history and in review. This adds one step for new joiners, but the seeding guide already sends them through the template.
context: Decision taken jointly by the ledger and monitoring owners in February.

title: REVIEW: backfills now throttle on replica lag, fixed pause retired
content: This replaces the fixed-pause rule in {{ref:mem-017}}. Finance and the DBA reviewed the throttled runner on Thursday and approved it for every journal backfill from now on. Instead of sleeping two seconds after each batch, the runner reads replication lag on the reporting replica before each batch and adapts. Below 10 seconds of lag it starts the next batch at once; between 10 and 60 seconds it waits until lag is back under 10; above 60 seconds it stops and pages whoever started it. Batch size adapts too, starting at 5,000 rows and halving whenever a batch produces more than 40 MB of WAL. The knobs are max_lag_seconds and wal_budget_mb in `ledger.ops.backfill.throttle`, with the defaults above. During the review run, the fee column backfill that froze the dashboards last time finished in 3 hours 20 with lag never above 12 seconds, in office hours, and finance noticed nothing. The office-hours restriction is therefore lifted for throttled runs. Old scripts that still call the fixed-pause loop keep working but log a warning; the DBA removes the loop once the last two callers are migrated.
context: Review outcome; the earlier fixed-pause pattern is obsolete from this point.

title: OUTCOME: outside developer tested carrier onboarding guide, eleven points of confusion
content:
On 2026-03-30 we paid an independent developer to integrate against the sandbox using only the public guide at https://docs.quarry.example.com/partners/getting-started, and to write down every moment they got stuck. She finished the integration in a day and a half and sent eleven notes. The ones that matter most:

The guide shows shipment_id as a number in one example and as a string in another. It is a string everywhere, and two pilot carriers had already built parsers that broke on leading zeros. The authentication page explains how to get a token but not that it expires after an hour, so her first long test run failed silently halfway through. The webhook section says to verify the signature before parsing, which is right, but the sample code parses first. Error responses are documented as a list of codes without the body shape, so she guessed the field names and got validation errors wrong: they return a list under errors, not a single message.

Smaller points: the sandbox base URL appears both with and without a trailing slash; the rate limit page still describes the old per-minute counter; the tracking_events field is called events in one diagram; the first four changelog entries have no dates.

What we decided: the partner-API lead rewrites the authentication and error pages this sprint, sample code is generated from the real client so it cannot drift, and every page gets a last-reviewed date. We will repeat the exercise with a different outside developer before the next version ships, because a fresh reader finds what this one stopped noticing after day one.
context: Outcome of the documentation usability test. The eleven notes are in the ticket; this memory keeps the four that caused real integration bugs and the decisions taken.

title: Export des factures transporteurs : où on en est
content: Le job carrier_invoices publie maintenant via le manifeste décrit dans {{ref:mem-012}}. Mise en service le 2026-02-19, après deux nuits en parallèle avec l'ancien export. Le code vit dans /jobs/helix/carrier_invoices/job.py et la publication passe par `helix.io.publish`. Reste à vérifier le format des montants pour les transporteurs suisses.
context: Point d'étape pour helix et la finance ; les montants suisses sont le seul sujet ouvert.

title: RUNBOOK: pausing payouts with maintenance flag
content: The maintenance flag used for the cutover in {{ref:mem-019}} is the supported way to pause payouts for any reason. Set it with the admin command pause_payouts --reason <text> --until <time>; it writes to `ledger.payouts.control`, and every scheduler instance reads it before each run. Never scale the scheduler to zero instead: queued payouts then miss their idempotency window and need manual replays. Resuming is resume_payouts, which first posts the queued items in creation order. The command refuses an --until more than eight hours away unless --force is given.
context: Pulled out of the cutover plan because support and on-call both need it outside maintenance windows.

title: DECISION: TanStack Query owns server state in console
content: The console moves its server state to TanStack Query and stops keeping API responses in the global store. Reasons: half of our store code was hand-written caching with subtle invalidation bugs, the refund screens showed stale balances after a mutation because two slices held the same data, and the library already gives retries, deduplication and background refetch. One QueryClient lives at the app root. Stale time is 30 seconds by default and zero for anything that shows a balance. The global store keeps only real client state, such as filters and open panels. Defaults are read from `console.query.defaults` so tests can shorten them. Migration goes screen by screen, refunds first, since that is where stale data hurt.
context: Frontend architecture decision taken in the console guild; the boundary between store and query cache is the important part.

title: Late FX snapshot no longer blocks carrier invoices
content: Decided with finance on 2026-03-10, HXB-324: when the morning FX snapshot is late, the carrier invoice job no longer waits for it. It runs at its normal time with the previous day's rates and marks every converted amount with rate_source = previous_day. When the fresh snapshot arrives, a small correction job recomputes only those amounts and issues adjustment entries if the difference exceeds one cent per invoice. Before this, a late snapshot pushed invoices past the 8:00 deadline promised to carriers, and finance preferred an on-time invoice with a later correction over a late invoice that is exact. The correction job is idempotent, keyed on invoice id plus snapshot date, so running it twice does nothing. Carriers see the adjustment as a separate entry, never as a silent change to the original. In a normal month we expect two or three late snapshots and a few dozen adjustments.
context: Business decision with finance; the trade-off between punctuality and exactness was theirs to make.

title: INCIDENT: nightly recon export manifest pointed at file still uploading
content: At 06:40 on 2026-04-07 the analytics loader failed with a 404 on the recon export. The manifest written by the pattern in {{ref:mem-012}} already named the new file, but the multipart upload behind it was still running. On the object store, a large upload only becomes visible once the final commit call returns, and our publish step wrote the manifest as soon as the last part was sent. Fix in /jobs/helix/recon/publish.py: wait for the commit response, then do a HEAD request on the new key before touching the manifest. The loader retried at 07:00 and found the file. No data was wrong, only late.
context: Short incident; recorded because the manifest pattern looked atomic and was not, for large files.

title: GOTCHA: webhook timestamps serialised as epoch floats
content: Partners reported on 2026-04-02 that event timestamps arrived as numbers like 1775121600.123 instead of strings. The cause was an ObjectMapper built by hand in the webhook module. It did not inherit the shared configuration and fell back to writing dates as numeric timestamps. The main API looked fine because it uses the Spring-managed mapper. QRY-356 removes the hand-made mapper and adds a contract test: every timestamp field in every response and webhook sample must match RFC 3339 with a trailing Z. If you need a mapper outside Spring, ask the JsonConfig bean for a copy; never build one from scratch. Two carriers had already written code that accepts both formats, so we keep sending strings forever, even in a new version.
context: Gotcha from the webhook module; the hand-built mapper is the trap.

title: CONFIG: console Content-Security-Policy, source by source
content: Policy as deployed on 2026-02-27, after the support chat widget was added. default-src is self only. script-src allows self plus the hash of the one inline bootstrap script; no unsafe-inline, no unsafe-eval. connect-src lists the ledger API host and the BFF and nothing else, so a compromised dependency cannot post data to a third party. img-src adds data: for merchant logos that arrive as base64. frame-src allows only the support chat provider, because SupportWidget embeds their iframe; the design owners asked to remove it if support ever stops using the widget. Violations go to the report endpoint and are counted per directive. Anything above ten a day for one directive gets a look. When adding a third-party source, change the policy in the same pull request and say why in the description, otherwise the next reviewer removes it.
context: Reference for reviewers; most broken console releases in the past came from a missing CSP source.

title: GOTCHA: rebalancement Kafka et écritures en double
content: Le 2026-04-09, juste après un déploiement, le consommateur PaymentEventConsumer a traité deux fois une quarantaine d'événements. Le problème vient du rebalancement : l'offset n'était validé qu'à la fin du lot, et le redémarrage des pods a rendu le lot à un autre membre du groupe. Le grand livre a rejeté les doublons grâce à la clé d'idempotence, donc aucun montant faux, mais les logs débordaient d'erreurs. MER-433 réduit la taille des lots à 50 et ajoute un arrêt propre qui valide l'offset avant de quitter. Il faut également vérifier que le délai de grâce du pod reste supérieur au temps de traitement d'un lot.
context: Noté après la revue du déploiement d'avril ; l'équipe paiements veut un test de rebalancement en CI.

title: INCIDENT: SEPA payout file rejected by bank, 412 payouts late
content:
Timeline, Paris time, tracked as MER-445.
16:31 the settlement job built the SEPA credit transfer file for the eu_west region and uploaded it.
16:52 the bank portal marked the file as rejected, schema validation error on one transaction, no detail beyond the element name.
17:05 the on-call engineer noticed only because the reconciliation screen showed zero bank acknowledgements. There was no alert on rejection itself.
17:20 we found the offending entry: a creditor name containing an ampersand and a curly apostrophe, copied from a merchant's legal name.
17:40 the merchant name was edited by hand, the file rebuilt and resent.
18:10 the bank accepted the file. It had missed the same-day cutoff, so 412 payouts settled one day late.

Root cause as understood tonight: SepaFileBuilder escapes XML special characters but does not restrict names to the character set the bank accepts, which is a subset of Latin characters. The ampersand was escaped correctly; the curly apostrophe was valid XML but outside the bank's set.

Immediate actions: a transliteration step now maps names to the allowed set before the file is built, in /services/ledger/payouts/sepa/charset.py, and the function normalise_creditor_name has a test with the exact name that failed. The same rotation also added an alert on bank rejection, so we no longer depend on someone looking at a screen at the right moment.

Still unexplained: the same merchant was paid without trouble last week, with what looks like the same name. Finance wants a proper review before we call this closed, and finance wants to know whether the late payouts trigger any penalty in merchant contracts. Support has already contacted the 38 merchants with the largest delayed amounts.
context: First write-up of the late payout incident, written the same evening. Kept as written so the follow-up review can show what we believed at the time and what turned out to be wrong.

title: Ledger repo replaces black plus isort with ruff, no code changes intended
content:
On 2026-04-14 we replaced black and isort with ruff for formatting and import sorting. Settings live in /services/ledger/pyproject.toml under tool.ruff.lint and tool.ruff.format:
- line-length = 100 (black was at 88, nobody objected)
- known_first_party = ["ledger"], so imports group the same way as before
- the formatter runs in pre-commit and in CI with --check
The one big reformat commit is listed in .git-blame-ignore-revs, so blame stays useful. Low stakes; noted so nobody reinstalls black out of habit.
context: Tooling change, low importance; mostly here for people searching why black disappeared.

title: INCIDENT: CSP blocked support chat widget all morning
content: On 2026-03-03 the policy from {{ref:mem-053}} shipped without the chat provider in frame-src, so SupportWidget stayed blank for every operator until 11:20. The violation counter in `console.csp.reports` jumped to 4,000, but the alert threshold was daily and fired late. The fix put the source back and changed alert_window to one hour.
context: Support could not chat with merchants for three hours. High importance because the release checklist had no step for third-party embeds.

title: DECISION: console build version now travels as API response header, separate asset host check removed
content: Replaces the stopgap in {{ref:mem-024}}. Since 2026-04-01 every BFF response carries the header X-Console-Build, and the session payload includes min_console_build. The client compares them in BuildGuard and reloads only when its own build is older than the minimum, never because a request failed. The separate call to the asset host is gone, so an unreachable host can no longer cause a reload loop. Settings live in `console.build.guard`.
context: Final fix for the reload loop; the earlier workaround note is obsolete.

title: DECISION: console e2e suite also runs on Edge under Windows
content: Most operators use Edge on Windows laptops, and two bugs this quarter only showed there. From DLK-450 the e2e suite runs on a Windows runner with Edge, in addition to Chromium on Linux. The runner definition is D:\ci\console\e2e\windows-runner.yaml. The job is gated by the pipeline flag e2e.edge.enabled, so it can be switched off if the runner pool is down. The animation fix from {{ref:mem-026}} covers both browsers; no extra waits were needed. Runtime is eleven minutes against seven on Linux. We accept that for merges to the main branch and skip it on draft pull requests. Retries stay at zero: a test that only passes on retry is a bug, not bad luck. Artefacts from the Windows run go to the same bucket under a windows_edge prefix.
context: Decision recorded after the second Edge-only bug reached production; the console team pushed for it.

title: REVIEW: payout reconciliation script for finance, Windows edition
content: Reviewed MER-449 on 2026-04-16: the script finance runs on their own Windows machines to match bank statements with payouts, D:\finance\tools\recon\match_payouts.py. It works, but three things must change before finance relies on it at month-end. It reads the bank CSV with the system encoding, which breaks on accented names; read it as UTF-8 and handle the BOM. It matches on amount and date only, so two payouts of the same amount on the same day can swap; add the end_to_end_id from the bank file. And it calls `ledger.api.client.payouts` page by page without a timeout, so a slow API makes it hang without a message.
context: Review of a script written by finance with help from a finance analyst. It is not owned by engineering, which is exactly why the review matters: once it sits in their month-end routine, any mismatch it hides becomes a finance problem nobody on our side sees until audit time.

title: CONFIG: calendrier de relance des webhooks
content: Depuis le 2026-03-20, la relance des webhooks partenaires suit ce calendrier : 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, puis 24 h, soit six essais au total. Après le sixième échec, l'événement passe en file morte et le partenaire reçoit un e-mail automatique. Les délais sont dans la propriété quarry.webhooks.retry-schedule du fichier de configuration, pas dans le code, pour que le support puisse les ajuster sans déploiement. Pourquoi ce rythme : la plupart des pannes côté transporteur durent moins de dix minutes (redémarrage, certificat corrigé vite), mais une panne de week-end peut durer une journée entière. Les partenaires peuvent rejouer un événement depuis la file morte via l'API de rejeu, documentée sur https://docs.quarry.example.com/partners/webhooks/replay. Avant chaque changement, il faut vérifier que la somme des délais reste sous 48 h : au-delà, un événement de suivi n'a plus de valeur pour le transporteur.
context: Note de configuration pour le support partenaires ; l'équipe partenaires a fixé ces délais après les pannes de février chez deux transporteurs.

title: STATUS: graph runner live on nine of fourteen helix jobs
content: The dependency runner replaced the single nightly schedule for nine jobs this week. The remaining five are the carrier invoice run, two finance exports and two cleanup jobs. They still run from the old schedule because their inputs are not declared yet. JobGraph has handled four late FX snapshots since go-live without delaying any job that did not need rates, which was the whole point. One surprise: two jobs depended on each other through a shared temporary table, and the graph ran them in parallel on the first night. Helix ops made them declare it, and the temporary table is being removed. Next is the carrier invoice run, which needs the late snapshot policy wired in first. Nothing visible to finance so far, which is good news.
context: Weekly helix status for the data channel; replaces last week's version.

title: STATUS: accélération du seeding local sur les portables Windows, où on en est
content:
Suite de la revue {{ref:mem-037}}. État au 2026-04-20 :
- le masquage par lots de dix mille lignes est en place dans ledger.tools.scrub ; gain mesuré, de 20 min à 11 min
- les fichiers temporaires vont maintenant dans le dossier exclu par l'antivirus, chemin lu depuis /tools/devenv/scrub-batches.toml
- reste un problème sur un des trois portables, où la politique IT n'a pas appliqué l'exclusion ; ticket ouvert chez eux
- la doc d'arrivée a une nouvelle étape pour vérifier l'exclusion avant de lancer le script
Objectif : passer sous dix minutes partout avant l'arrivée des deux stagiaires en mai. L'équipe outillage pense qu'on y est presque. Il reste à profiler l'import du dump lui-même, jamais mesuré séparément.
context: Point d'avancement pour l'équipe ledger ; importance élevée parce que l'arrivée des stagiaires dépend d'un poste prêt en une matinée.

title: GOTCHA: statement timeout silently ignored behind transaction-mode pooler
content:
We set statement_timeout as a startup parameter in the connect options in `ledger.db.session`, and on staging it simply did nothing: a runaway report query ran for 25 minutes. The pooler in front of Postgres runs in transaction mode and drops startup parameters it does not track, so the setting never reached the server. What works instead:
- set it per role on the server: ALTER ROLE ledger_api SET statement_timeout = '30s'
- give the reporting role a longer value, 10 minutes, set the same way
- for a one-off long statement, use SET LOCAL inside the transaction, which survives transaction pooling
- never use plain SET, because the next client on that server connection inherits it
The roles are created by the migration in /services/ledger/migrations/roles.py, so the values are versioned. To see what a session actually got, run SHOW statement_timeout from the API container, not from your laptop, which bypasses the pooler. The same trap applies to search_path and lock_timeout.
context: Found while chasing the runaway report query that slowed the API in March. The pooler behaviour is documented, but only in a footnote, and three of us rediscovered it independently over the past year, hence the length. If you touch connection settings, read this before trusting local tests: locally there is no pooler at all.

title: PATTERN: console reads partner data through one generated client
content:
Every console screen that shows partner data goes through the generated client, never through hand-written fetch calls. Background: during the v2 rollout in {{ref:mem-032}}, the carrier page broke twice because a hand-written call still expected the version 1 shape. The pattern now:
- the build generates the client from the published spec into a folder nobody edits
- PartnerClient wraps it and always sends the version header the console was built against
- response types come from the generated code, so a breaking change fails type checking instead of failing in front of an operator
- the pinned version lives in `console.partner.api_version` and is bumped in a dedicated pull request
When the partner team ships a new version, they open that pull request themselves, so both teams look at the same diff. Generated files are excluded from lint and coverage; otherwise the numbers mean nothing.
context: Pattern agreed between the console guild and partner-API after the carrier page broke during the version rollout. It costs a build step but moves a whole class of bugs from production to the type checker, and that trade was easy once we counted the support tickets.

title: PATTERN: row-count guard before any export is published
content: Since 2026-03-25 every helix export passes a row-count guard before the manifest is updated. The guard compares today's row count with the median of the last seven runs of the same job. Below 50 % or above 200 % of that median, the job stops, keeps the file unpublished and posts the numbers in the data channel. A person then decides: publish anyway with one command, or rerun. Thresholds sit in helix.checks.rowcount and can be overridden per job, since the carrier invoice export legitimately doubles at month-end. In its first week the guard caught an empty payouts export caused by an expired read token. Without it, finance would have seen a day with no payouts. Guard decisions are charted at https://grafana.ottervale.example.com/d/helix-guards.
context: Pattern for all helix jobs, mandatory since March.

title: DECISION: keep thirteen months of audit events online
content: Agreed on 2026-03-31: the audit event table keeps thirteen months online, which covers a full year plus the month of the annual close. Older events are exported to the archive bucket as compressed files, one per month, and deleted from the database once the export is verified. Thirteen months is what the auditors asked for last year, and it keeps the table under 200 GB. Restoring an archived month takes about an hour; the DBA does it on request. Support never needs older events in daily work. The few requests per year come from finance during disputes.
context: Retention decision for audit events; revisit if the regulator or the auditors change their request.

title: DECISION: console supports only two latest Edge and Chrome releases
content: From 2026-04-06 the console supports the two latest stable releases of Edge and Chrome, and nothing else. Firefox works today but is not tested, and bugs there get fixed only when cheap. Safari is out, since no operator uses a Mac at work. The build targets now match this list, which removed about 60 KB of polyfills. Support asks operators to update before opening a ticket about layout problems.
context: Agreed with support and IT; the browser inventory came from IT.

title: PATTERN: ledger readiness endpoint for batch consumers, how helix polls it before starting jobs
content: Helix jobs that read ledger data first call the readiness endpoint, so they never start while the nightly close is still posting. This came up when the graph runner in {{ref:mem-062}} began starting jobs earlier than the old schedule did. The handler is ReadinessView in /services/ledger/api/readiness.py; it reports ready only after close_settlement_window has finished for every region. Clients poll every 60 seconds for at most 45 minutes. Example: https://ledger.ottervale.example.com/internal/readiness.
context: Low importance because only helix uses it today, but the polling cap matters: without it, a stuck close would keep every job waiting until someone noticed in the morning.

title: Le proxy d'entreprise à Lyon supprimait notre en-tête de version
content: Après la mise en place de l'en-tête de version décrite dans {{ref:mem-058}}, le bureau de Lyon voyait encore l'ancienne console le 2026-04-08. Le problème ne venait pas de notre code : le proxy d'entreprise de ce site supprime les en-têtes de réponse qu'il ne connaît pas, donc le client ne recevait jamais la version minimale et ne se rechargeait pas. Ce qui a permis de trouver : les journaux du BFF montraient bien l'en-tête envoyé, et une capture réseau sur un poste de Lyon montrait la réponse sans lui. Correctif : min_console_build est maintenant aussi renvoyé dans le corps de la réponse de session, que le proxy ne touche pas, et le client lit les deux sources. Les réglages restent dans console.build.guard, avec une nouvelle option body_fallback activée par défaut. Le test /web/tests/e2e/build-header.ts simule un proxy qui retire l'en-tête. À vérifier pour tout futur mécanisme fondé sur un en-tête maison : au moins deux de nos sites ont ce type de proxy, et on ne le découvre jamais à l'avance.
context: Piège noté pour l'équipe console et pour l'IT de Lyon, qui a depuis ajouté l'en-tête à sa liste blanche.

title: PATTERN: every helix export carries sidecar checksum file so consumers can verify downloads before loading them anywhere
content: Since 2026-04-13 every export published through the manifest pattern in {{ref:mem-012}} gets a sidecar file with the same name plus .sha256, written before the manifest. The manifest also carries the checksum, so a consumer has two independent ways to check. The helper is helix.io.checksums.write_sidecar, and the analytics loader calls verify_download before inserting a single row. Why both? The sidecar lets a human check a file by hand with standard tools; the manifest copy lets automated readers check without a second request. A mismatch means the file is never loaded: the loader logs both hashes and alerts the data channel. In the first week we hit one real mismatch, a truncated download over a flaky VPN link from the finance office. Before this, it would have loaded a partial file without complaint. Checksums are computed while the upload streams, so they cost no extra pass over the data.
context: Added after the truncated download scare; finance asked for something they could check themselves, which is why the sidecar exists next to the manifest field.

title: Filtres de date décalés d'un jour à Lisbonne, fuseau du navigateur contre fuseau du serveur
content:
Symptôme signalé le 2026-04-15 par le support de Lisbonne : en filtrant les remboursements « du 14 avril », ils obtenaient aussi ceux du 13 au soir, et il manquait les derniers du 14. Le problème : le sélecteur de date construit minuit dans le fuseau du navigateur, l'envoie en UTC, puis l'API interprète la date selon le fuseau du siège, Paris. Lisbonne a une heure de moins, donc la fenêtre glisse d'une heure. Pour les opérateurs parisiens le décalage est nul, ce qui explique pourquoi personne ne l'avait vu en test.

Correctif (DLK-458) : pour un filtre de jour, le client n'envoie plus d'horodatage, seulement la date calendaire et le fuseau de l'opérateur, et l'API calcule les bornes. Le fuseau vient du profil de l'opérateur, pas du navigateur, car plusieurs portables du support sont réglés en UTC. Le comportement est piloté par console.filters.date.mode, valeur calendar par défaut. Les tests de /web/tests/unit/dateFilter.ts tournent désormais sous trois fuseaux, dont un avec un décalage d'une demi-heure, parce qu'un bureau en Inde est prévu.

Avant de toucher à un filtre de date, vérifier que la règle est la même côté export CSV. Le premier correctif oubliait l'export, et la finance a reçu deux jours de fichiers avec l'ancien comportement. Une confusion de fuseau a déjà coûté cher au grand livre lors de la clôture de janvier ; c'est un risque, pas un détail d'affichage.
context: Piège noté pour toute l'équipe console. Le support de Lisbonne a passé une matinée à recouper des remboursements à la main avant qu'on comprenne. un développeur console a écrit le correctif et tenait à ce que la note mentionne l'export, la partie qu'on oublie toujours.

title: REVIEW: SEPA rejection root cause corrected, bank changed its accepted character set and our builder only half explained it
content: Second look at the late payout incident: the root cause in {{ref:mem-055}} was incomplete, and this review replaces it. Finance, the on-call rotation and the bank's integration desk went through it on 2026-04-22 under the same ticket, MER-445. What actually happened: the bank tightened its accepted character set in a release two days before the incident and announced it in a portal notice nobody on our side reads. The same merchant name had passed the week before because the old rules still applied. SepaFileBuilder was missing a transliteration step, which was true and is fixed, but the trigger was the bank change. Agreed in review: bank notices now go to the payments mailbox, which is triaged daily. The transliteration table lives in ledger.payouts.sepa.charsets and is versioned with the date of the bank rule it matches. Every file is validated against the bank's published schema and character rules before upload, so a rejection is caught at 16:35 instead of discovered at 17:05. The rejection alert stays. Closed.
context: Review outcome; it supersedes the root cause given in the first incident note.

title: Jobs DuckDB tués par manque de mémoire sur les pods
content: Le 2026-04-11, trois jobs ont été tués par Kubernetes pendant la nuit, sans aucune erreur dans leurs logs. Le problème : DuckDB réserve par défaut 80 % de la mémoire qu'il voit, et il voit celle du nœud, pas la limite du pod. HXB-337 règle sa limite à 70 % de celle du pod, lue au démarrage depuis helix.runtime.limits. ParquetSink écrit également par morceaux, pour ne plus garder un fichier entier en mémoire.
context: Noté après une nuit où trois exports ont manqué. Le symptôme est trompeur : rien dans les logs du job, seulement un code de sortie 137 dans les événements du pod, et helix ops a mis une heure à penser à regarder là. Si un job helix disparaît sans erreur, regarder d'abord les événements Kubernetes et la mémoire du nœud, avant de soupçonner le code.

title: STATUS: nouveau moteur de frais, parité en cours
content: Le nouveau moteur de frais tourne en parallèle de l'ancien depuis deux semaines, sans effet sur les montants facturés. Chaque transaction est calculée deux fois, et FeeParityRecorder enregistre les écarts dans la table fee_parity_diffs. Résumé des chiffres : 1,2 million de transactions comparées, 37 écarts, tous chez des marchands avec un barème négocié à la main. Les règles de ces barèmes sont décrites dans /services/ledger/fees/negotiated.yaml, que l'équipe frais complète avec la finance. Avant la bascule, il faut zéro écart sur une semaine complète, fin de mois incluse. Prochaine étape : revue des 37 cas avec le produit jeudi.
context: Point d'étape pour la bascule du moteur de frais ; la date dépend de la fin de mois.

title: Console drops query library, data now loaded by route loaders
content: We are backing out of the query library chosen in {{ref:mem-049}}; this note replaces that decision. After three months, the cache invalidation rules had grown as complex as the store they replaced, and the router we already use now loads data per route with built-in revalidation after mutations. DLK-469 moves screens one by one to route loaders: each route declares what it needs, mutations revalidate the current route, and nothing is cached across navigations except reference data. Balances are always fresh because they are never cached at all. Reference data keeps a five-minute lifetime, set in console.loaders.reference.ttl. The migration guide and the list of converted screens are on https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/console/route-loaders. The query library goes away once the last screen moves, expected within the quarter.
context: Supersedes the earlier server-state decision.

title: REVIEW: alert routing tree, three teams receiving pages they cannot act on
content: Monitoring owners reviewed the routing tree in D:\ops\sigwatch\routing\routes.yaml against ninety days of alert history. Main finding: about a third of pages reached a team that could not act on them. The ledger team got every helix job failure, because routes matched on the namespace label and helix jobs run in the ledger namespace. BFF errors paged the platform team for the same reason. Agreed changes: routes now match on an owner label each team sets in its deployment; the RouteValidator check in sigwatch.routing.validate fails CI when a rule has no owner; and a catch-all route sends unowned alerts to a low-urgency channel instead of paging. Nineteen rules that had not fired in a year were deleted after their owners confirmed. Next review in six months, with the same history query, kept in the repo as page_history.sql.
context: Review outcome; most noise complaints in the last on-call survey trace back to routing rather than bad rules, and this records what changed.

title: PATTERN: ledger events go out through transactional outbox
content: Ledger events reach Kafka only through the transactional outbox, never by producing directly from request handlers. The rule dates from 2026-01-12, when we found postings that had been committed but whose events never left the process: the pod died between the commit and the produce call. How it works. A handler that posts a journal entry also inserts a row into the outbox table in the same database transaction, so either both are committed or neither is. A separate relay, OutboxRelay in ledger.events.relay, reads unpublished rows in id order, produces them, and marks them published once the broker acknowledges. If the relay crashes after producing but before marking, the event goes out again on restart. Consumers must therefore tolerate duplicates; every event carries event_id, and they deduplicate on it.
