Ordering holds per account, because the relay partitions by account id and handles one key at a time. Two relay instances push about 4,000 events per second, far above our peak. Rows stay seven days after publishing for debugging, then a nightly job deletes them. Not allowed: producing from a handler for convenience, even for events nobody consumes yet; reading the outbox table from anything other than the relay; editing published rows by hand. Relay lag is graphed at https://grafana.ottervale.example.com/d/outbox, and an alert fires when the oldest unpublished row is older than two minutes. The events owner wrote the first version and is the person to ask when the lag graph looks odd.
context: Core pattern for anything that emits ledger events; reviewers reject direct produce calls with a link to this note.

title: Console session lifetime: why operators get logged out after eight hours
content: Operator sessions in the console last eight hours from login, with no sliding extension. Screens that can move money add an idle timeout of thirty minutes; elsewhere the session stays alive while the tab is open. These numbers come from three constraints that pull in different directions. Security wanted short sessions everywhere, because a shared laptop left open in a carrier depot is a real scenario, not a theory. Support wanted no timeouts at all, since operators keep the console open the whole shift and lose unsaved notes when a session ends. Finance asked for a forced daily login, so the audit trail starts each day with a fresh authentication. Eight hours is one shift plus a margin: it gives the daily login without cutting anyone off mid-shift. The idle rule only applies where an action would be dangerous if someone else sat down at the laptop. Notes are now saved as drafts every few seconds, which removed most support complaints. If someone asks for longer sessions, point them at draft saving first. If someone asks for shorter ones everywhere, the answer is the depot scenario plus the support cost, which we measured at about forty tickets a week during a two-week trial of a four-hour limit.
context: Rationale that support and security both refer to, written after the third request this year to move the numbers one way or the other. The values are set in the identity provider, not in our code, so changing them needs no deploy, but it does need security, support and finance to agree; this is the summary of why each accepted the compromise last time.

title: DECISION: payouts released at three daily slots instead of continuously, starting May
content:
Agreed on 2026-04-23 under MER-463: from May, the scheduler releases payouts in three fixed slots, 08:00, 12:30 and 16:00 Paris time, instead of releasing each payout as soon as it is approved.

Why. Continuous release produced thousands of tiny bank transfers a day, each with a bank fee. Batching into slots cuts the number of transfers by about 70 % for merchants who receive several payouts a day. It also makes bank files predictable, which the bank asked for after the rejection incident, and it gives operators a clear window to place holds before money leaves. The 16:00 slot is the last one that reaches the same-day cutoff with margin.

What we gave up. A payout approved at 12:35 now waits until 16:00, and merchants on the instant payout plan were unhappy about that. For them the slot logic is skipped and the continuous behaviour stays, at the higher fee they already pay.

How. Slots are defined in ledger.payouts.slots as a list of local times per region. The scheduler wakes at each slot and releases everything approved before it. The maintenance flag from {{ref:mem-048}} works as before and pauses slots too. A slot skipped during a pause is not replayed on its own; its payouts leave with the next slot.

Finance reviews the slot times every quarter. Finance wants a check after the first month to confirm the fee savings are real and not just estimated. Support has a short explanation ready for merchants who ask why a payout did not arrive immediately.
context: Business decision with finance and merchant success. Fee savings drove it; predictability for the bank came second. Recorded in detail because complaints about waiting will come, and whoever answers them should know which plan keeps the old behaviour and why the slots sit where they do. The first-month review may change the number of slots.

title: CONFIG: ledger events Kafka topic settings
content:
Ledger event topic settings, applied on 2026-04-27 (MER-478) and declared in /infra/kafka/ledger-events.yaml:
- partitions: 24, keyed by account
- retention: 14 days
- min.insync.replicas: 2, with acks=all on the relay
Do not lower min.insync.replicas to work around a slow broker.
context: Values chosen with the platform team. The replica settings are what protects against losing events, so they are the ones nobody should touch.

title: Local ledgers are now seeded with synthetic data, staging dump retired
content: From 2026-05-04 developers no longer download the anonymised staging dump at all; the seeding pattern in {{ref:mem-021}} is replaced. Instead, SyntheticLedger in ledger.devdata.synthetic generates a database with fake merchants, accounts and a few months of postings that follow realistic shapes: month-end peaks, refunds, holds, the three-decimal currencies and the Gulf weekend. Why we changed: the spring privacy review concluded that masking a production-derived dump is never fully safe, because rare combinations of amounts and dates can still point to a real merchant. The dump was also 40 GB and slow to restore, as the reviews of the seeding script showed. The generator builds a ready database in under three minutes on every laptop, Windows included, and the antivirus stops mattering because nothing is downloaded. Trade-off: synthetic data does not reproduce every odd historical record, so some bugs need a targeted fixture instead of a lucky row in the dump. A fixture library of named scenarios sits next to the generator, and a finance analyst adds one each time support reports a case we could not reproduce. The staging bucket for dumps is deleted at the end of May. If you still have an old dump on disk, delete it.
context: Decision from the ledger team and security; the old seeding notes are obsolete from here on, including the Windows-specific tuning.

title: SECURITY: helix jobs read secrets from mounted files at run time, never from deploy-time environment variables
content: Secrets for helix jobs are mounted as files and read when the job starts, through helix.secrets.read. Environment variables show up in pod descriptions and crash dumps, and they do not change when the secret rotates. Reading the file at start means a rotated secret is picked up on the next run without a redeploy.
context: Adopted after a token leaked into a crash report attached to a support ticket. The token was rotated within the hour; this rule is the lasting fix.

title: Carrier invoice job rewrite reviewed: correct, but too clever twice
content: Reviewed the rewrite of the carrier invoice job with helix ops and analytics. The numbers are right; the parity run against last month matched to the cent. Two places are too clever. The rounding helper round_half_even_minor is reimplemented inline in three spots instead of imported, so a fix in one would miss the other two. And the job builds its SQL by joining strings. That works today because every value is internal, but nobody will remember it when a parameter starts coming from outside. Both fixed before merge, no other findings.
context: Review outcome for the invoice job rewrite; merged after the two fixes.

title: Partner API adopts fifteen-minute signed access tokens, database lookups only at refresh
content: Follow-up to the hot spot found in the peak load test, {{ref:mem-043}}. Decided on 2026-04-28 under QRY-360: partners exchange their long-lived credentials for an access token valid fifteen minutes and signed by us. Each API call is checked by verifying signature and expiry only, with no database lookup; the database is consulted when a token is issued or refreshed. Revocation, the reason for the old per-request lookup, now works through a short deny list held in memory and refreshed every ten seconds. A revoked credential can therefore keep calling for at most ten seconds, and the security review accepted that. Fifteen minutes balances refresh traffic against how long a stolen token stays useful. Signing keys rotate monthly, and the public keys are published at a well-known path so partners can verify our tokens if they wish. Settings are in /services/quarry/config/auth.yaml under quarry.auth.tokens. The two carriers with hand-written clients must add a refresh step; the partner-API lead is helping them, and the old credentials keep working in parallel until the end of June.
context: Security-relevant decision for the partner API; a security reviewer signed off on the ten-second revocation window.

title: TESTING: visual snapshots differ by one pixel between macOS and Linux
content: Low priority, but it wastes time whenever someone new hits it. Visual snapshot tests of components such as IconButton and StatusBadge pass on the CI runners and fail on two developers' Macs with a one-pixel difference around text. The cause is font rendering: anti-aliasing differs between operating systems, and our snapshot threshold was zero. DLK-479 does three things. Snapshots are now generated and compared only inside the container image CI uses, started by the snapshot script; comparing directly on a laptop is no longer supported. The threshold moved from zero to 0.1 % of pixels, which hides rendering noise but still catches a moved border or a changed colour. Font files are bundled in the image instead of downloaded, so a font update on the internet cannot shift every snapshot overnight, as happened once in March. If a snapshot fails only on your machine, run it through the container before investigating anything. The image is set in visual.snapshots.image in the console configuration. Updating snapshots on purpose still requires a reviewer to look at the image diff in the pull request. Approving a hundred changed images without looking defeats the point.
context: Minor gotcha, but every new frontend developer runs into it during the first week.

title: CONFIG: console feature flags, who owns each one and when it gets removed
content:
Inventory of console feature flags after the DLK-496 clean-up, plus the rule that keeps the list short. Flags are read through FlagProvider at startup and on every navigation, from the BFF, which merges code defaults with per-environment overrides.

Current flags. console.search.shortcuts, owned by design, on for everyone since the spring, deleted in the next release together with the old binding. console.audit.virtualized, owned by the audit-table owners, on except for support accounts, removed once support confirms. console.build.guard, owned by the console guild, permanently on: it is a kill switch for the reload logic rather than a rollout flag, hence no removal date. The reload loop in {{ref:mem-024}} is why that switch exists; if the guard misbehaves again, turning it off stops the reloads without a deploy. console.refunds.bulk, owned by the refunds squad, off in production and on in staging for the finance pilot. console.partner.preview, owned by the partner team, off everywhere until the sandbox preview ships.

Rules. Every flag has an owner and either a removal date or the word permanent with a reason. A flag past its date shows a warning in the developer console and in the weekly lint report; two weeks after the date, the build fails. Permanent flags are reviewed twice a year. New flags go through the FlagProvider registry, never read from the raw configuration object, so this inventory stays complete. Flags never gate security checks, and a disabled flag must leave the application safe, because the BFF falls back to code defaults when the override store is unreachable.

Why so strict: before the clean-up we had 31 flags, eleven had been fully on for over a year, and two contradicted each other on the refunds page. Removing them took two console developers most of a sprint.
context: Configuration reference for the console team; the weekly lint report links here when it flags an expired entry.

title: GOTCHA: producer retries reordered ledger events
content:
On 2026-05-06 a consumer saw a refund event before the posting it refers to, on the same account. The relay producer had retries enabled with max.in.flight.requests.per.connection at 5 and idempotence off, exactly the combination where a retried batch can land after the next one. What we changed:
- enable.idempotence=true on the relay producer
- acks=all kept, as the topic settings require
- a consumer-side check that parks an event whose predecessor is missing for up to 30 seconds before alerting
Our broker version keeps ordering for idempotent producers with up to five in-flight requests, so throughput did not drop. The bug only showed during a broker failover, which is why it took four months to surface. The events owner added a failover step to the relay's integration tests.
context: Gotcha in the outbox relay. It looked like a consumer bug at first, and the first two hours went into the wrong service. Saved so nobody changes the producer settings back for a benchmark.

title: GOTCHA: webhook deliveries timed out at two carriers behind strict proxies, because our chunked request bodies never carried Content-Length
content: From 2026-04-30, two carriers saw every webhook delivery from us time out after thirty seconds, while their own tests with curl worked. Their proxies reject chunked transfer encoding on inbound requests and wait for a length that never comes. Our HTTP client started sending chunked bodies after an upgrade, because the signing code passes the body as a stream. The fix buffers the body, which is small anyway, and sets the length explicitly; the switch is quarry.webhooks.client.buffer-body, on by default. Retries hid the problem for a day, since each delivery ended in the dead letter queue instead of alerting. We now alert when one partner's failure rate passes 20 % over an hour.
context: Shared with partner support, who now ask about proxies first when a carrier reports timeouts.

title: INCIDENT: one-cent balance drift on eleven old accounts
content:
Follow-up on the eleven accounts flagged by the balance comparison after the cutover, {{ref:mem-038}}. Tracked as MER-480.

What we know. All eleven belong to old merchants onboarded before the minor-unit migration. Each shows exactly one cent between the sum of journal amounts and the stored balance on the account row. The difference appeared on one day in 2019, when a fee correction script, fix_fee_rounding, was run by hand. Current hypothesis: the script updated the balance column directly, with a rounding mode that differed from the journal, and nothing compared the two again until the nightly check started with the upgrade. Journal sums come from ledger.reports.balances.recompute; stored balances are read from the account table; both are in minor units.

What we have not done: change any balance. Finance must decide whether the journal or the stored balance is the truth for these accounts, and the answer may differ per merchant, since some received statements showing the stored value. The DBA prepared a correction that inserts one adjustment posting per account instead of editing the balance, so the fix stays visible in the journal. It will not run until finance signs off.

Impact for merchants today is nil: the difference is in our favour on six accounts and in theirs on five, one cent each. This note will be replaced by the final write-up once finance has decided.
context: Interim incident note; the final outcome will supersede it once finance decides.

title: Helix database aliases leave YAML file for service catalog, resolved at job start
content: The single alias file from {{ref:mem-030}} is retired, and this decision replaces it. It worked for one team, but once the analytics team started writing their own jobs it became a merge-conflict magnet, and twice a wrong edit pointed a job at the archive cluster. Under HXB-344 the aliases move into the service catalog the platform team already runs for everything else. A job still asks for a source by alias name. The difference is that the resolver, SourceCatalogClient, looks the alias up in the catalog at job start and caches it for the run. Each catalog alias has an owner, a read-only flag, a maximum statement time and the list of teams allowed to use it, so the analytics team can no longer read the payouts source by accident. Changes go through the catalog's own review flow instead of our repository, and each one is logged with who made it. Local runs keep working with a small override file that only exists on laptops and is ignored by the build. What stays: no connection string literals in job code, the lint check, and the startup failure for an unknown alias. What we lose: the catalog is one more service that must be up when a job starts. If it is down, the resolver uses the last known values for up to 24 hours and logs a warning, which covers a bad night but not a long outage. Helix ops migrated the fourteen aliases in one afternoon; no job needed a code change beyond the new client version.
context: Supersedes the YAML alias pattern; the reasons are ownership and access control, not performance.

title: Large amounts lost precision on console screens: browsers parsed 64-bit integers as floating point
content:
Amounts are stored as signed 64-bit integers of minor units, and the API sent them as JSON numbers. Browsers parse every JSON number as a double, which is exact only up to about nine quadrillion. Euro amounts never get near that, but one Gulf partner settles very large corporate payouts in a three-decimal currency, and the rounded value appeared on a reconciliation screen off by two units. Nobody lost money, since the ledger itself was right; the console only displayed and exported the wrong number.

What we found while digging:
- the API serialiser wrote amounts as numbers, valid JSON but unsafe for any client that parses into doubles
- the BFF passed the number through untouched, so it reached the browser as is
- the CSV export, built in the browser, inherited the rounded value, which is how finance spotted it
- the type definitions said number, so nothing in the build complained

What we changed:
- every amount field in API responses is now a string of digits plus the currency, immediately for internal clients and in a new version for partners
- the console formats amounts from the string with a small decimal helper and never converts them to numbers
- a contract test fails if any field ending in amount is a JSON number

The rule for every client: an amount is a string on the wire. Background and the list of affected fields are on https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/ledger/amounts-on-the-wire. Internal tools in languages that parse into 64-bit integers were never affected, but they now receive strings too, so each owner changed one line. The partner API keeps numbers in the old version for compatibility, with a warning in the docs.
context: A gotcha across three teams: finance found it, the console displayed it, and the API caused it. High importance because any new client that touches amounts can reintroduce it with one line of parsing code.

title: GOTCHA: adding nullable column breaks pinned Parquet schema on every run
content:
ParquetSink pins the schema per job, which is good until you add a column. Even a nullable column makes the next run fail with a schema mismatch, because the pin compares the full column list. Current workaround:
- bump schema_version in the job definition
- add the column to /jobs/helix/schemas/recon.yaml with nullable: true
- run the job once with --accept-schema, which records the new pin in helix.io.sinks.pins
- tell the analytics team, since their loader checks the column list too
Clumsy, and helix ops wants the sink to accept additive changes on its own. Until then, do all four steps in one pull request.
context: Gotcha with a manual workaround; expected to be replaced once additive changes are supported.

title: Refund reasons become fixed list instead of free text
content: Under MER-490, operators no longer type a free-text reason when they issue a refund. They pick one of twelve reasons agreed with finance and support, with an optional comment. Free text made the monthly refund report useless: the same reason was written forty different ways, in three languages. The list includes an other option that requires a comment, and if other passes ten percent of refunds in a month, we revisit the list. Old refunds keep their free text and are mapped to the new reasons only in the report, through a lookup table finance maintains.
context: Decision with finance and support. The report was the driver; the twelve reasons came out of a workshop with six operators.

title: INCIDENT: la console affichait la clôture une heure trop tard après le passage à l'heure d'été
content: Le lundi qui a suivi le passage à l'heure d'été, l'écran des règlements affichait une clôture à 17h30 au lieu de 16h30 pour l'Europe de l'Ouest. Plusieurs opérateurs ont donc attendu pour placer des retenues, et onze paiements sont partis alors qu'ils devaient être bloqués. Chronologie : à 15h55, une opératrice signale l'écart au support ; à 16h10, l'équipe console confirme que l'API renvoie la bonne heure en UTC ; à 16h40, on trouve la cause dans le composant CutoffBanner, qui ajoutait à la main un décalage fixe d'une heure au lieu d'utiliser le fuseau de l'opérateur. Ce décalage codé en dur datait de l'hiver, quand Paris était à UTC+1, et personne ne l'avait remarqué. Le grand livre avait corrigé exactement ce genre d'erreur après la clôture de janvier, voir {{ref:mem-015}}, mais la correction n'avait jamais été reportée dans la console. Correctif : CutoffBanner reçoit maintenant l'heure de clôture déjà convertie par l'API, avec le champ cutoff_local et le nom du fuseau, et ne fait plus aucun calcul. Les onze paiements ont été récupérés auprès des transporteurs, sans perte. Ce qu'on retient : toute heure affichée doit arriver de l'API déjà convertie, et un test de rendu tourne désormais avec une horloge fixée au dimanche du changement d'heure, dans les deux sens.
context: Incident console lié au changement d'heure ; même famille que l'incident de clôture côté grand livre.

title: SSO users stuck in login loop after identity provider update
content: On 2026-05-11 operators signing in through SSO bounced between the console and the login page. The provider had renamed a claim, and AuthCallback still read preferred_username. The mapping moved to console.auth.claims; the fix shipped in 40 minutes.
context: Short outage, recorded because the provider changes claims without notice and the mapping is the first place to look. The same update also changed the logout URL, which nobody noticed until two days later, when someone tried to log out.

title: DECISION: throttled runner mandatory for every journal backfill, manual lag-watching rules retired
content: No more watching the replication panel by hand: the manual rules in {{ref:mem-040}} are retired by this decision, including the office-hours restriction and the warning to finance before a run. Those rules were the stopgap until the runner could throttle itself, and now it can. From this week, ThrottledBackfill is the only supported way to run a backfill on the journal tables, and the fixed-pause loop has been deleted from ledger.ops.backfill. The runner refuses to start without max_lag_seconds, so nobody can disable throttling by accident. Finance still gets a message in their channel when a run starts and ends, posted by the runner itself. Run history and lag per run are on https://grafana.ottervale.example.com/d/backfills, the same dashboard as before.
context: Decision closing the backfill saga; the old gotcha's rules no longer apply.

title: STATUS: old cluster parity checks, night nine
content: Nine of the fourteen nightly comparisons planned in {{ref:mem-023}} have run, and eight were clean. The ninth reported 214 differences, all in the fee table. That looked alarming until the DBA found that the comparison read the new cluster while the nightly fee job was still writing to it; the old cluster, being read-only, had none of that night's fees. BalanceParityCheck now waits for the fee job to finish before starting, and the rerun of night nine was clean. The comparison also had a blind spot: it checked balances and journal totals but not the audit event table, which the auditors care about most. From night ten, the DBA added row counts and a checksum per month for audit events. If the last five nights are clean, the old cluster is deleted on schedule. Storage cost so far matches the estimate, and finance has nothing to do. The job posts results every morning in the ledger channel, and the summary lives in ledger.ops.parity until the cluster is gone.
context: Interim status on the read-only cluster. The false alarm on night nine is worth remembering: the same race between a comparison and a job that is still writing will hit any future parity check.

title: Factures suisses envoyées deux fois aux transporteurs en mai
content:
Le 2026-05-04, quatre transporteurs suisses ont reçu leurs factures d'avril en double. Chronologie :
- 06:10, le job carrier_invoices publie normalement
- 06:40, le graphe relance le job parce que JobGraph a reçu en retard le signal de fin
- 06:45, le second passage republie sous un nouveau nom de fichier, donc le manifeste pointe vers une seconde facture
- 09:30, un transporteur appelle la finance
La cause : pour ce job, la relance n'est pas idempotente, alors que helix.runner.graph suppose que tous les jobs le sont. HXB-347 ajoute une vérification dans /jobs/helix/carrier_invoices/guard.py : si une facture existe déjà pour la période et le transporteur, le job s'arrête. Il faut également vérifier les autres jobs qui envoient quelque chose à l'extérieur.
context: Note d'incident provisoire ; la revue avec la finance doit encore fixer la règle définitive.

title: GOTCHA: rapports d'erreurs envoyés par la console depuis les postes de dev
content:
Même famille que les métriques des portables dans {{ref:mem-029}}, mais côté console. Les serveurs de développement locaux envoyaient leurs erreurs au projet de production du suivi d'erreurs : la clé publique était la même partout et l'environnement n'était pas renseigné. Conséquence : le tableau de bord de production comptait des centaines d'erreurs qui n'existaient que sur nos machines, et une vraie régression est passée inaperçue pendant une matinée au milieu de ce bruit.
Ce qui a changé :
- chaque environnement a sa propre clé, lue depuis console.telemetry.dsn au démarrage
- en local, l'envoi est désactivé par défaut ; on peut l'activer pour tester, vers le projet de développement uniquement
- le tableau de bord de production filtre sur l'étiquette d'environnement, et une alerte part si des événements arrivent sans étiquette
- les versions publiées portent le numéro de build, pour relier une erreur à un déploiement précis
Après chaque changement de configuration de la télémétrie, il faut vérifier que la production ne reçoit rien depuis un poste local : ouvrir la console en local, provoquer l'erreur de test et contrôler qu'elle n'apparaît pas. La procédure complète est sur https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/console/telemetry-environments. L'équipe télémétrie a aussi purgé les anciens événements de développement du projet de production, pour que les tendances redeviennent lisibles.
context: Piège noté par l'équipe console, en écho à celui des métriques côté monitoring.

title: GOTCHA: drawer flakiness fix moved from global stylesheet to per-test reduced motion
content: Replaces the stylesheet trick in {{ref:mem-026}}: it also hid a real animation bug from the suite. Each test now opts into reduced motion through MotionGuard in /web/tests/e2e/motion.ts, keyed by console.e2e.reduced_motion. Write-up: https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/console/e2e-motion.
context: Gotcha correction for the console e2e suite, refund drawer.

title: Partner API gateway connection limits per carrier, why default sits at forty and who may raise it during peak season
content: Each carrier gets forty concurrent connections on the partner gateway. The limit is set per carrier in /deploy/quarry/gateway-limits.yaml and applied when the gateway reloads, which takes about a minute. Forty covers the busiest carrier at peak with room to spare; most carriers never pass ten. Raising a limit is allowed during peak season without a review, up to one hundred, as long as the change is announced in the partner channel. Above one hundred, the database pool behind the API becomes the bottleneck, so the request goes to the platform team first. Lowering a limit needs a warning to the carrier one week ahead, because their retry logic may not cope.
context: Configuration reference for the partner gateway. Written after a carrier complained that their nightly sync was throttled; the limit was right, but nobody could say who was allowed to change it or how fast a change takes effect.

title: Carrier rejected all webhooks after key rotation
content: Kestrel Freight rejected every webhook for three hours on a Thursday, starting minutes after we began signing with their new key. The rotation followed the two-key procedure agreed in {{ref:mem-014}}: add key B, sign with B, keep A valid for seven days. Their verifier ignored the signing_key_id field and always used the first secret in its configuration, which was still A. Every delivery failed verification, they answered 401, and our retries piled up. Nothing was lost, because deliveries are retried for a day, but their dispatch board ran three hours behind. We switched them back to key A within ten minutes of their call, then waited for their fix. Two changes on our side. Rotation now starts with a test delivery signed with the new key and sent to the partner's sandbox endpoint; the switch only happens once that test passes. And the grace period moved from seven to fourteen days, set in quarry.webhooks.rotation.grace_days, because carrier release trains are slow.
context: Partner incident, Kestrel Freight, key rotation.

title: DECISION: helix integration tests read synthetic ledger data, no production samples
content:
Agreed on 2026-05-12 by the helix team and security. Helix integration tests stop using the sampled production Parquet files kept in the test bucket. They read the same synthetic ledger that developers now get locally, see {{ref:mem-082}}, exported to Parquet by a small step that runs before the test stage.

Why. The sampled files were cut from real payouts in January and lightly masked. The privacy review that retired the staging dump made the same point about them: masking does not make rare rows safe. Security gave us until the end of the quarter to delete them. They were also stale. They predate the Swiss VAT change and the three daily payout slots, so half of the invoice tests checked behaviour that no longer exists.

How it works. The generator runs with a fixed seed, so every pipeline run sees the same merchants, carriers and postings. The export step writes one Parquet file per ledger table into a scratch folder, and the tests point their database alias at it. The seed and the number of months live in helix.testing.synthetic, next to the other test settings. Generation plus export takes about four minutes, less than the old download.

What we give up. The samples held a handful of strange historical rows, like a carrier with two VAT numbers and a refund larger than its payout. Those cases now exist as named scenarios in the ledger fixture library, so they keep being tested on purpose instead of by luck. A helix tester went through the failing tests one by one and wrote three new scenarios. Two old tests were deleted because they asserted on data that only ever existed in the sample.

Deadline. The test bucket is emptied on 2026-06-30. Anyone who still has a local copy of the samples should delete it. Migration notes and the scenario list are on https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/helix/synthetic-test-data.
context: Decision on test data for helix pipelines; it extends the synthetic data move from the ledger to the batch jobs that read ledger tables.

title: GOTCHA: console dev server keeps old environment values after branch switch until its cache folder is deleted
content: After switching branches, the dev server may keep serving environment values from the previous branch. It caches the compiled config in a hidden folder and only checks the timestamp of /web/config/env.defaults.json, not its content. Git restores the file with an older timestamp, so the cache looks fresh. Symptom: console.api.base points at a host that no longer exists. Fix: delete the cache folder, or start the server with the clean flag.
context: Small but expensive gotcha: three people lost an afternoon each before a console developer spotted the timestamp check. Most likely to bite right after a rebase that touches the environment defaults.

title: REVIEW: idempotency handling on refund endpoint, race tests run serially
content: Decided on 2026-03-16 while the fixes were in progress: idempotency tests for refunds run in a separate serial job, outside the four-worker setup from {{ref:mem-036}}. They fire two identical requests at once and need one shared database to prove that only one refund lands. RefundRaceTest lives in ledger.tests.refunds.race and is marked serial_only.
context: Side decision from the idempotency review: parallel test workers each own a database, so a race between two requests can only be tested on a single shared one.

title: GOTCHA: Alembic autogenerate ignores changed server defaults and writes empty migrations without complaint
content: Autogenerate missed a changed server default on payout_status and produced an empty migration on 2026-04-08. By default it does not compare server defaults at all. We set compare_server_default in the Alembic environment, and MigrationLint now fails the build when a model default differs from the database. Run it before opening a pull request.
context: Ledger schema gotcha; cost the ledger team one failed release.

title: PATTERN: ledger readiness endpoint for batch consumers, kept internal and never offered to partners
content: Carriers asked whether they could poll the same readiness signal that helix uses, so their own reconciliation would start only after our nightly close. We said no, and wrote down why. The endpoint exposes internal state: which regions have closed, and by implication when settlement runs late. A partner who sees that will open a ticket every time a region is ten minutes behind, and some contracts mention settlement times. It also has no rate limit and no versioning, because its only client is ours. Instead, partners get the settlement_completed webhook, which fires once per region with the final totals and follows the same signing and retry rules as every other webhook. If a partner needs a polling option later, it belongs in the partner API with its own contract, not on the ledger host.
context: Low importance: the request came from two carriers and was easy to refuse, but the reasoning will come up again whenever someone wants to reuse an internal endpoint for partners.

title: GOTCHA: route loaders appelés deux fois
content: Depuis le passage aux loaders de route décrit dans {{ref:mem-076}}, l'écran des remboursements appelait l'API deux fois à chaque ouverture. Constaté le 2026-05-19 par un développeur console en regardant l'onglet réseau. Le problème venait du composant RefundsLayout : il redirigeait vers l'onglet par défaut après le premier chargement, donc le routeur relançait le loader de la route enfant. Correctif provisoire : la redirection se fait dans le loader parent, avant tout rendu. Règle pour les nouveaux écrans : vérifier dans l'onglet réseau qu'une navigation ne produit qu'un seul appel par ressource. Quand un loader se relance sans raison, regarder d'abord le paramètre should_revalidate.
context: Gotcha console, écran des remboursements ; correctif provisoire en attendant mieux côté routeur.

title: Second look at SEPA builder after rejected file
content:
Notes on the payout file builder from 2026-04-27, three weeks after the rejected file in {{ref:mem-055}}. The incident fix itself was fine; this review looked at everything around it. Findings, in order of risk.

First, the builder keeps the whole file in memory before signing it. On the largest day last quarter the file was 180 MB, and the worker has 512 MB. One more growth year and it falls over. SepaFileBuilder should stream the document and sign the stream.

Second, the schema version is hard-coded. The bank announced the next version for the autumn, and the builder cannot produce both during the overlap. The review suggests one writer per version, selected by configuration in ledger.payouts.sepa.version.

Third, the transliteration table from the incident fix covers Latin letters but not the Nordic characters that the Swedish bank accepts natively. Names there are degraded for no reason. The table should depend on the receiving bank.

Fourth, nothing checks the file against the bank schema before upload. The bank does that for us, at the worst possible moment. A local validation step would have caught the incident file.

Minor: logging prints full creditor names, which support likes and privacy does not. Log a hash and the payout id instead.

Verdict: none of this blocks current payouts, but the first two must be planned before the autumn schema change. The estimate is two weeks for both.
context: Wider review of the payout file builder, done after the SEPA rejection incident.

title: PATTERN: cutoff overrides for bank holidays live in one dated file, reviewed like code
content: Bank holidays that move a cutoff are not edited in the region settings from {{ref:mem-042}}. They go into /config/cutoff-overrides.toml, one entry per region and day, with the reason and who approved it. CutoffCalendar merges the overrides at startup and logs each active one. An override must carry an expires_on value, so nothing lingers after the holiday. The file is reviewed like code. HolidayFeed in ledger.settlement.holidays only proposes entries; a person merges them.
context: Pattern for the settlement on-call: keeps the base cutoff table stable and puts every exception where it can be reviewed and expires on its own.

title: DECISION: audit events now stay online twenty-five months, replacing thirteen-month rule after regulator asked for two full years
content: MER-502 replaces the retention rule in {{ref:mem-067}}. The regulator now wants two full years plus the closing month, so audit events stay online for twenty-five months. The archive job reads its window from /services/ledger/audit/retention.toml, where retention_months is now 25. Table size will reach about 380 GB; the DBA sized the disk for it.
context: Retention change driven by the regulator, not by the auditors this time. Older archived months are unaffected; restores still take about an hour. Revisit the disk forecast at the next capacity review, since the table now grows for two years before anything is archived.

title: PATTERN: validate every payout file against bank schema on Windows desks before any manual upload
content:
When a payout file must be uploaded by hand, finance validates it first, as suggested in {{ref:mem-110}}:
- run D:\finance\tools\sepa\validate.py against the file
- compare the totals with the payout summary page
- upload only if both pass
The schema files come from https://assets.ottervale.example.com/bank/schemas/ and the validator reads its bank list from ledger.payouts.sepa.banks.
context: Manual upload is the fallback when the bank's API is down; finance does it maybe twice a year, so the steps are written out.

title: STATUS: backfill runner adoption across ledger teams, week three
content:
Three weeks after the throttled runner became mandatory in {{ref:mem-097}}, here is where the teams stand on 2026-05-22.

- payments: all four backfill scripts ported, the last one ran overnight with lag under eight seconds
- fees: two of three ported; the third rewrites a whole column and needs a custom wal_budget_mb; capacity testing is underway
- reporting: not started, because their scripts live in a separate repository that still pins the old helper
- audit: nothing to port, they never ran backfills

Two problems came up. ThrottledBackfill reads lag from the reporting replica only, but the fees team also writes to a table replicated to the analytics replica, which nobody watches. And the runner's message to finance went to the old channel name, so the last two notices reached nobody. The notify owner fixed the channel in /services/ledger/ops/notify.py this morning. The analytics replica needs a decision: add it to the lag check, or exclude those tables from backfills entirely.

Next update when reporting has started.
context: Adoption status of the mandatory backfill runner; the analytics replica question is the one open decision and it blocks the reporting team.

title: Helix storage cleanup: old scratch tables mostly gone, two owners still silent
content: Low priority housekeeping, written down so it does not get lost. On 2026-05-05 the helix scratch schema held 312 tables, most of them left behind by one-off analyses. A storage owner sent a list to every owner with a two-week deadline. Status today: 271 tables dropped, 29 kept on purpose and moved to a named schema with an owner and an expiry, and 12 still waiting for an answer. Ten of those belong to two analysts who left in the winter; their manager agreed that we drop them after one more week. The scratch schema now has a nightly job that drops anything older than ninety days unless it is listed in helix.scratch.keep.list. Storage went down by 1.4 TB, about a third of the warehouse bill for that schema. Nobody has complained yet. If someone does, the dropped tables stay in the backup for thirty days, and that owner can restore one in about ten minutes. After that they are gone for good.
context: Housekeeping status, importance low on purpose. The ninety-day rule is the only lasting outcome; the rest is a one-time cleanup.

title: Carrier fuel surcharge job reviewed before moving into graph runner
content:
Fuel-surcharge notes from 2026-04-29 cover the last big job still outside the graph runner. It computes a monthly surcharge per carrier from diesel price indices and writes it to the invoice inputs. The logic is right. The packaging is not.

- it downloads the price index at run time from a public site, with no cache and no timeout; one slow morning and the whole invoice chain waits
- it writes its output with mode overwrite, so a rerun for a past month silently replaces numbers that were already invoiced
- the surcharge_rate column is a float; it should be stored in basis points as an integer, like every other rate in helix
- tests cover the formula but never the month boundary, where most past bugs were

Requested before migration: cache the index in the raw zone and read it from there, write each month to its own partition and refuse to overwrite an invoiced month, and add a test for a carrier that joined mid-month. The config moves to helix.jobs.fuel.surcharge so the graph runner can see it. A follow-up check will run again once those land.
context: Pre-migration review; the overwrite issue is the dangerous one, since it can change invoiced numbers.

title: GOTCHA: DuckDB spills to wrong disk
content: On 2026-05-07 three helix jobs failed with a full disk, on pods that had plenty of free space on their data volume. DuckDB spills to a temporary directory when a join does not fit in memory, and by default that directory sits next to the database file. Our jobs open an in-memory database, so the spill went to the container root, which has two gigabytes. The memory limit change from the earlier incident made spills more frequent, which is why it appeared now. Fix: JobGraph sets the temporary directory to the data volume for every job, and the pod template gives that volume a size limit of fifty gigabytes. A job that spills more than that should be split, not given a bigger disk. The failure looks like a generic write error. On any odd crash, first check how full the root filesystem was.
context: High importance because the symptom is misleading: the logs point at the output file, not at the spill. Any new job that joins two large tables can hit this until the template change is everywhere.

title: PATTERN: page tokens for partner listings
content: Every partner endpoint that returns a list uses page tokens, never offsets. Agreed on 2026-04-14 after a carrier paged through shipments with offsets while new ones arrived, and received the same shipment twice on consecutive pages. The response carries the items, a next_page_token value, and nothing else. There is no total count, because counting a large table on every call is what slowed the old listing down. The token is an opaque string that encodes the sort key and the last id; partners must not parse it, and we may change its format. PageToken in com.ottervale.quarry.paging builds it and rejects tokens older than a day. Page size defaults to 100 with a hard maximum of 500. The partner guide explains the contract with examples at https://docs.quarry.example.com/partners/pagination.
context: Pattern for every new list endpoint in the partner API, set in the spring.

title: DECISION: générateur SEPA réécrit en flux, la revue précédente est close
content: Cette décision remplace la revue {{ref:mem-110}} : ses quatre constats sont traités ensemble dans MER-509, décidé le 2026-05-11. Le générateur de fichiers de virement est réécrit pour écrire le document en flux et le signer au fil de l'eau, ce qui règle la question de la mémoire. Une classe d'écriture par version du schéma bancaire, choisie par ledger.payouts.sepa.version, permet de produire l'ancienne et la nouvelle version pendant la transition. La table de translittération dépend désormais de la banque destinataire, dans bank_charsets. Enfin, chaque fichier est validé contre le schéma avant l'envoi. En cas d'échec, rien ne part et l'astreinte est prévenue. les équipes paiements et helix livrent en deux temps, avant l'automne.
context: Décision qui clôt la revue du générateur SEPA ; le constat sur les journaux est suivi à part.

title: GOTCHA: helix reads from reporting replica get cancelled while ledger backfills run, even with lag under ten seconds
content: HXB-351: the invoice export slowed to a crawl three nights in a row, always while a ledger backfill was running. The throttling from {{ref:mem-045}} kept lag low. But replaying each batch on the replica conflicts with our long snapshot reads, and with hot_standby_feedback off the replica cancels them, so the export restarts from scratch. Helix now checks BackfillWindow before heavy reads and waits up to thirty minutes.
context: Cross-team gotcha between helix and the ledger; the lag number alone says nothing about query conflicts.

title: DECISION: on-call bot moves to platform team image, chat token rotated
content:
Follow-up to {{ref:mem-027}}, decided 2026-04-20:
- the bot runs from the platform base image, built by /ops/sigwatch/bot/build.yaml
- the chat token comes from bot_token in the secret store, rotated the same day
- BotDeployer skips the restart when the image tag is unchanged
Config keys live under sigwatch.bot.deploy; runbook at https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/sigwatch/bot.
context: Low importance: housekeeping decision for the on-call bot after the handover to the platform team.

title: Console accessibility pass, screen reader labels finished
content:
Screen reader labels are done on every refund and payout screen.
- DataTable announces sort changes
- dialogs return focus to the button that opened them
- colour contrast passes on status badges
Still open: the date picker, owned by the date-picker owners.
context: Closes the remaining item from the earlier accessibility status; only the date picker is left.

title: PATTERN: webhook event envelope
content:
Every webhook we send, whatever the event, uses the same envelope, frozen on 2026-03-25:
- event_id: unique, so partners can drop duplicates
- event_type: dotted name such as shipment.invoice.created
- occurred_at: when it happened, in UTC with an offset
- data: the payload, versioned with the partner API
The envelope never changes shape; new fields go inside data. WebhookEnvelope in the Kotlin code builds it, and a contract test compares its JSON with the published example. Retries resend the same event_id, which is why partners must deduplicate on it rather than on the payload. Ordering is not guaranteed across events. Partners should compare occurred_at before overwriting newer state, and that is the point carriers miss most often.
context: Pattern shared with the partner guide team; applies to every webhook type.

title: GOTCHA: audit checksums differed between clusters because text sort order changed with new operating system image
content:
This replaces the night-nine status in {{ref:mem-098}}: the parity run did not finish clean, and the old cluster deletion is postponed. From night ten, the monthly audit checksums disagreed for every month, while row counts matched exactly. The DBA first suspected another race with a running job. It was not one.

The checksum was computed over rows ordered by the merchant reference, a text column. The new cluster runs on a newer operating system image, whose C library sorts some characters differently, hyphens and spaces in particular. Same rows, different order, different checksum. Ordering by the numeric event id makes all twelve months match.

The real worry came next. A changed sort order also means that indexes on text columns built under the old rules may be out of order on the new cluster. Our cutover restored from a logical dump, so indexes were rebuilt there, and amcheck on the five largest text indexes found nothing. A team restoring from a physical copy would not be so lucky.

From now on, a parity check orders rows by a numeric key or by a column with an explicit binary collation, never by plain text. Any upgrade that changes the operating system image also changes collations, even with the same Postgres version, so the upgrade checklist gains an index check. BalanceParityCheck in ledger.ops.parity was fixed on 2026-05-26, and five clean nights are needed again before the old cluster goes.
context: Supersedes the interim parity status. The checksum mismatch was harmless, but it exposed the collation risk, which is the part to remember for every future database or image upgrade.

title: How partner API errors are shaped: one problem document per failure, stable codes, no stack traces
content:
Partner API errors follow one shape everywhere, so a carrier writes their error handling once. The body is a problem document with five fields: type, title, status, detail and error_code. The first four come from the standard; error_code is ours, a stable lowercase string such as shipment_not_found or invoice_already_settled. Carriers are told to branch on error_code only. The title and detail texts are for humans and may change at any release.

Rules we hold to. An error_code, once published, never changes meaning. If the meaning shifts, it gets a new code and the old one stays documented. Validation failures return 422 with a list of fields under an errors member, each with the field path and a short reason, so a carrier can show it in their own form. Authentication failures return 401 without saying whether the account exists. Rate limiting returns 429 with a retry delay in seconds.

What never goes in a response: stack traces, class names, SQL fragments, internal hostnames. A filter in the response pipeline strips anything that looks like one, and a test sends malformed requests to every endpoint to prove it. Before that filter existed, a carrier forwarded us a screenshot of their logs showing our database driver version. Not a fun call.

Where things live. Codes are declared in one registry under com.ottervale.quarry.errors, and the build fails if a code is used without being declared or declared without documentation. The documentation page is generated from that registry, so it cannot drift. When adding a code, pick the narrowest one a carrier could act on. A code nobody can act on is just a longer way of saying 500.

The registry holds 41 codes today. Eight were added during the v2 rollout, and two were deprecated because no carrier ever received them.
context: Reference for anyone adding an endpoint or an error to the partner API; the stability rule on codes is the part carriers rely on the most.

title: DECISION: fuel index cached in raw zone daily
content: Following the review in {{ref:mem-116}}, the surcharge job no longer fetches the diesel price index itself. From 2026-05-06, a small job named IndexFetch downloads it every morning at six and stores it in the raw zone, one file per day. The surcharge job reads the latest file dated before the invoice month's end, and fails loudly if none exists. Why not keep fetching at run time with a timeout? The public site changed its page layout twice last year, and each time the job broke in the middle of the invoice chain. A separate morning job breaks on its own, hours before anyone needs the data, and a job owner gets a message instead of finance. Why daily and not monthly? The surcharge uses the monthly average, and computing it ourselves from daily values lets us check it against the published average. If the two differ by more than a tenth of a percent, the job stops and asks a person. Settings live in helix.jobs.fuel.index. The archive is kept for seven years, as invoice evidence requires. This may change if the carriers agree to a contractual index file sent by email, which is under discussion.
context: Decision on the fuel price source for surcharges, medium-low importance because the carrier negotiation may replace it; the separation of fetching from computing is the lasting idea.

title: GOTCHA: carrier clocks drift, stale webhook rejections follow
content:
Two weeks after the rotation trouble with Kestrel Freight in {{ref:mem-103}}, Northbay Haulage started rejecting about one webhook in twenty as too old. Nothing had changed on our side. Their verifier applied the five-minute replay window correctly, but against a server clock running six minutes behind.

How we found it. Their rejections all came back with the same reason, an expired timestamp, yet our delivery logs showed each attempt leaving within a second of signing. Only some webhooks failed because Northbay runs a pool of servers and only two of them had lost their time sync. Requests landing on those two were rejected; the rest went through. Retries hit a different server half the time, so most events arrived late but did arrive. That is why it took a week to surface.

What we changed. Nothing in the window itself: five minutes is the rule in the partner guide, and widening it for one partner weakens replay protection for all of them. Instead, every webhook response now records the Date header the partner sent back. If that header is more than a minute away from our clock, the delivery log flags clock skew and the partner success team gets a weekly list. The threshold is in quarry.webhooks.skew.warn.seconds.

What partners must do. The guide now says plainly that verification depends on a synchronised clock. Sandbox certification also sends one event whose timestamp is four minutes old, and it must be accepted. Before, we only tested that a stale event is rejected, which a server with a slow clock passes easily.

Northbay fixed their time sync on 2026-06-02. Lessons: when a partner rejects a fraction of deliveries, compare clocks before suspecting our signatures. And test both edges of any time window, not only the one that fails.
context: Partner gotcha; the skew report is the lasting part, the window itself stays at five minutes.

title: INCIDENT: CI blocked for a morning by full test database disk
content: All ledger pipelines failed from eight to noon on a Tuesday. The worker databases from {{ref:mem-036}} were never dropped after cancelled runs, and the shared disk filled up. TestDatabaseFactory now drops leftovers older than a day at start, and /ci/scripts/cleanup_test_dbs.py runs every night.
context: CI incident with no production impact, but it blocked two releases that morning. Cancelled runs skip the teardown step, which is the general lesson for any fixture that creates external resources.

title: Graph runner migration finished, all fourteen helix jobs moved
content: As of 2026-05-29 every helix job runs under the graph runner; the fuel surcharge job was the last. The old cron schedule is disabled but kept for one month. Average nightly duration fell from 4h40 to 3h05. One open item: run_after hints still exist in two configs and do nothing now.
context: Status closing the migration that started in the spring. The old schedule stays disabled for a month so we can compare a full month-end close, which is when the graph has the most parallel work and the most chances to surprise us.

title: Webhook event types frozen for partner launch, and how new types get added afterwards
content:
On 2026-04-22 we froze the list of webhook event types for the launch. The envelope stays as described in {{ref:mem-123}}; this decision is about which events exist. Launch list, eleven types in four families:
- shipment: created, picked up, delivered, cancelled
- invoice: created, settled, disputed
- payout: scheduled, sent, returned
- account: verification changed

Not included, on purpose: location updates, because carriers produce them and we would only echo them back; and fee changes, because finance wants to announce those by email with context.

How a new type gets added after launch. Someone writes a short proposal with the trigger, the payload and who asked for it. A partner-API owner and one carrier contact review it. A new type is always opt-in: partners subscribe explicitly, so nobody receives events their code does not handle. Types are never renamed. Retiring one takes six months of notice, and the type keeps being sent, unchanged, until the date passes.

Why so strict: during the pilot, one carrier's handler crashed on an unknown event and stopped processing every later webhook, invoices included. Opt-in subscription makes that failure impossible for new types.
context: Decision on the event catalogue at launch. The opt-in rule exists because of the pilot crash; anyone tempted to broadcast a new event type to every partner should read that part first.

title: Optimistic updates in console are allowed only where an undo exists
content:
Optimistic updates, where the screen shows the result before the API confirms it, are allowed in the console only for actions the operator can undo. Agreed by the console team on 2026-05-14 after a long thread.

Allowed: renaming a saved filter, pinning a carrier, adding an internal note, changing the order of columns. If the API fails, the screen rolls back and RollbackToast explains why. Nobody is hurt by a pinned carrier that briefly unpins itself.

Not allowed: anything that moves money or changes what a carrier sees. Refunds, payout holds, releases, fee overrides and invoice corrections wait for the API answer, with the button disabled as agreed after the double refund. An operator who sees a refund marked done when it failed will tell the merchant it is done. That conversation cannot be rolled back.

How to implement it. The hook useOptimisticAction wraps the mutation and requires an undo function; without one, the code does not compile. The list of permitted actions sits in /web/src/actions/optimistic-allowlist.ts, and every addition needs a reviewer from the payments side. The hook also records rollbacks into console.telemetry.rollback_events, so we can see whether an action fails often enough to make the optimism misleading.

So far the rollback rate is under one in a thousand for every allowed action. If one passes one in a hundred, it goes back to waiting for the API.
context: Console pattern; the boundary is money and carrier-visible data.

title: Ledger CI pipeline reviewed after test database disk incident
content:
A ledger pipeline review in MER-526, prompted by the morning when leftover databases filled the disk. The four-worker setup from {{ref:mem-036}} is sound; most findings are about what grew around it.

What works and stays:
- one database per worker, named after worker_id, created at session start
- the split between fast unit tests and the slower database suite
- caching of the dependency layer, which saves about three minutes per run

What should change:
- teardown only runs when a job ends normally, so cancelled and timed-out jobs leave databases behind; cleanup must move to the start of each run, keyed on age
- the migration check runs after the tests, so a broken migration wastes a full test run before failing; move it first
- two suites call the payment provider sandbox over the network and fail whenever it is slow; use recorded responses, with a weekly job against the real sandbox that reports drift
- coverage is measured on the whole repository, generated clients included, which hides real gaps; exclude generated code and report per package

Not worth doing now: more workers. The runner would swap, as before, and the suite already takes under seven minutes.

Settings for the cleanup and the recorded responses go under ledger.ci.cleanup and ledger.ci.recordings. The reviewer expects the four changes to take about a week, in this order, with the migration check first because it is the cheapest.
context: Pipeline review after the CI disk incident; none of the findings is urgent on its own, but together they explain most of the flaky Monday mornings people have complained about for months.

title: GOTCHA: collation check now covers every text index
content:
This supersedes the collation note in {{ref:mem-124}}. That note said amcheck found nothing on the five largest text indexes, and that a logical restore protects us. Both turned out to be too optimistic.

What changed our mind. Two weeks after the cutover, a carrier search on the support screen returned nothing for a code that existed. The culprit was a unique index on carrier codes that a migration had rebuilt while the old replica was still attached for the parity run. That index was built on the old image and copied over physically. Checking only the five largest indexes missed it, because it is small.

New rules:
- after any image or major version change, run the index check on every index over a text column, not only the large ones
- any index rebuilt while an old replica is attached gets rebuilt again once the replica is gone
- the upgrade checklist lists both steps with the exact command, and the person running the upgrade signs them off

The carrier code index was rebuilt in two minutes. Nothing else was found.
context: Replaces the earlier collation gotcha; the full index check is now part of every upgrade.

title: DECISION: console traduite en français et en anglais uniquement, allemand reporté jusqu'à demande client ferme
content: Décidé le 2026-05-20 avec le support et les ventes : la console reste en deux langues, français et anglais. L'allemand était prévu pour l'été, mais aucun client germanophone ne l'a demandé par écrit, et nos opérateurs en Suisse travaillent tous en français. Traduire coûte peu au départ, puis beaucoup à chaque nouvel écran. Chaque libellé ajouté doit être relu par quelqu'un qui connaît le métier dans cette langue, sinon on obtient des termes comptables faux. Nous n'avons personne pour l'allemand. La structure reste prête : tous les textes passent par le composant TranslatedText et les fichiers de traduction, donc ajouter une langue ne demande que des traductions et un sélecteur. Ce qui est exigé dès maintenant : aucun texte en dur dans les écrans, même temporaire, et chaque nouvelle clé arrive avec ses deux traductions dans la même demande de fusion. Le contrôle automatique échoue si une clé manque dans une des deux langues. Les montants et les dates suivent la langue choisie, pas le navigateur, après la confusion de l'an dernier sur les séparateurs décimaux. On en reparle si un contrat signé l'exige, avec un délai de deux mois pour une première version.
context: Décision produit et technique sur les langues de la console.

title: Finance reconciliation script handed to engineering after month-end run matched two payouts to wrong bank entries
content:
The script reviewed in {{ref:mem-060}} is now maintained by the ledger team. Status on 2026-05-08.

Why the move. At the last month-end, finance ran the script before the three review fixes had landed, and two payouts of the same amount on the same day were matched to each other's bank entries. One merchant was chased for a payment that had in fact arrived. A finance analyst caught it two days later, by hand. Nobody blamed the script's author; it had simply outgrown a side project.

What happened since. The script moved into the ledger repository at /tools/finance-recon/match-payouts.py, with tests and a release tag. The three review findings are fixed. It reads the bank file as Unicode with the byte order mark handled, matches on the bank's end-to-end reference as well as amount and date, and gives up with a clear message when the ledger API does not answer within thirty seconds. Finance installs tagged versions from the internal package index instead of copying files between laptops.

Still open. The script runs on Windows desks. We would rather run it as a scheduled job and send finance a report, but finance wants to keep the button. Discussion next week with a second finance owner. Until then, that analyst tests every new version on a finance laptop before release.
context: Ownership change for the finance script after a month-end slip.

title: CONFIG: console session and idle timeout settings, per role
content:
Session settings for the console after DLK-509, effective 2026-05-25. They replace the single eight-hour lifetime that operators kept running into. Values per role:

- operator: idle_timeout_minutes = 30, absolute_lifetime_hours = 10, which covers a long shift with a lunch break
- finance approver: idle_timeout_minutes = 15, absolute_lifetime_hours = 8, because approvers can release large payouts
- support viewer: idle_timeout_minutes = 60, absolute_lifetime_hours = 12; read-only screens, lower risk
- administrator: idle_timeout_minutes = 10, absolute_lifetime_hours = 4, and every login asks for the second factor again

How the timers behave. Idle means no request to the API, not no mouse movement. A screen that polls in the background does not count as activity, otherwise the idle timer would never fire. Five minutes before expiry the console shows a warning with a button to stay signed in, which sends one request and resets the idle timer only. The absolute lifetime cannot be extended. At the end, the operator signs in again and lands on the same screen with filters kept.

Who may change values: security owns the numbers, the console team owns the code. Changes go through a pull request with a security reviewer, and the table above is updated in the same change.
context: Reference for the session timers; replaces the earlier explanation of the eight-hour logout.

title: PATTERN: money movements are reversed with new postings, never by editing or deleting old ones
content:
Any correction to money in the ledger is a new posting that reverses the old one, followed if needed by a new correct posting. Nothing that has been posted is ever updated or deleted. Not by an administrator, not even when it is obviously wrong. This has been the rule since the ledger was built, but it was only written down on 2026-05-18, after a well-meant support script tried to fix a wrong fee with an update statement.

Why. Finance reports and bank statements are built from postings. If a posting changes after a report has been produced, report and ledger disagree, and nobody can say which one was true on a given day. A reversal keeps both facts: what we posted, and when we corrected it. Auditors ask for exactly that.

How it looks. A wrong fee of 12.40 EUR on a payout becomes three postings: the original, a reversal of minus 12.40 referencing it, and the correct fee. All three carry the same correlation reference, so the console can show them together. The reversal module in ledger.postings.reversal builds the pair from the original and refuses to reverse a posting twice.

Enforcement. The database role used by the application has no update or delete rights on the postings table, so a script cannot break the rule by accident. Migrations run under a separate role and are reviewed by two people. Support tools go through the reversal endpoint, which writes an audit event with the reason typed by the operator.

What it costs. The postings table only grows, and some screens must hide reversed pairs to stay readable. Both are accepted. The table is partitioned by month, and the console has a toggle to show or hide corrections, off by default for support and on for finance.
context: Pattern finally written down after a support script tried an update on the postings table. The database permissions are what makes it hold; the written rule is for people who wonder why their update is refused.

title: GOTCHA: Parquet timestamps without zone flag shown as raw UTC in finance spreadsheets
content:
On 2026-05-13 finance reported that payouts exported by helix looked two hours earlier in their spreadsheet tool than in the console. The export writes UTC values, which is correct, but as plain timestamps with no zone attached. DuckDB does not mind. The finance tool assumes a timestamp without a zone is local time and shows it unchanged, so every payout appeared at its UTC time. In winter the gap was one hour, and it turns out two people in finance had quietly been adding an hour by hand for months. In summer the gap became two hours and the habit broke.

Fix. Every timestamp column in every helix export is now written with the UTC zone flag set, so readers know what they hold and convert for display. To make the change visible, the columns also gain a suffix: paid_at becomes paid_at_utc. The old columns are written in parallel for two months, then dropped. ExportSchema, the class that describes each export, now rejects any timestamp type without a zone, so a new job cannot repeat the mistake.

Why nobody caught it earlier: the console reads from the API, not from exports, so it never disagreed with anything. Finance never reported the manual correction because it felt like their own quirk. The broader lesson is to ask users what they do by hand with our files. Any internal consumer that loaded the old files into a database should check how it interpreted those values. An export owner has the list of consumers and is contacting each one.
context: Gotcha between helix exports and finance tools; the manual one-hour correction in finance is the detail that hid the bug for a whole winter.

title: INCIDENT: readiness signal said ready during Gulf weekend
content:
On a Friday night the readiness endpoint, the internal one discussed in {{ref:mem-108}}, reported the ledger as ready at eleven, while the European close was still posting. Helix started the invoice exports, read half-posted data, and published invoice inputs with totals about four percent short. Finance caught it on Saturday morning before invoices went out, because the totals did not match the bank file.

Cause. Readiness means every region has finished its close. On Fridays the Gulf region has no close, since it is a weekend day there, and the check was meant to skip it. The code did skip it, but it also skipped every region listed after it in the configuration, because the loop returned early instead of moving to the next region. On weekdays the Gulf close always ran, so the bug never showed. The region list in ledger.close.regions had been sorted alphabetically the week before, which put Gulf ahead of Europe and the Nordics.

Fix and follow-up. The loop now checks every region and treats a missing close as complete only when the calendar says that region has no close that day. A test covers each day of the week for each region. Helix also compares the posting count it reads with the count announced by the ledger, and refuses to publish if they differ. The short invoice inputs were deleted and rebuilt on Saturday at noon.
context: Incident caught by finance before any invoice was sent. Reordering a configuration list was harmless on its own and should not have mattered; the early return made it matter.

title: GOTCHA: version reload wipes half-filled refund forms
content:
The forced reload that started with the build hash check in {{ref:mem-024}} survived the move to a version header, and it still has a sharp edge. It reloads at the next navigation, even when the operator is halfway through a refund form in a side panel. Opening the panel counts as a navigation, so the reload fires right then and the typed reason, amount and attachments are gone. Support logged six complaints in one week, all from the same office, whose proxy cache refreshes on Mondays and so sees every release late, all at once.

What we changed. VersionWatcher no longer reloads on navigation when any form on screen is dirty. It shows a banner instead, asking the operator to finish and save. If the banner is ignored for thirty minutes, it turns red, and the reload happens at the next navigation without a dirty form. A form counts as dirty when its state differs from its initial values; every form exposes the flag through has_unsaved_changes. The thirty-minute value lives in console.version.reload_grace_minutes.

The real fix would be for old bundles to keep working with the new API for a while, so reloading can wait. That is a larger change, discussed with the BFF team, and not scheduled.
context: Console gotcha; the dirty-form check is the part to reuse for any future automatic reload.

title: GOTCHA: storybook builds pick up production feature flags
content:
Stories render with whatever flags the last build fetched, often production ones. Rules:
- stories import flags from /web/.storybook/flags.fixture.ts, never from the flag service
- each story sets console.flags.overrides explicitly
- a flag missing from the fixture fails with unknown_flag
context: Short gotcha for anyone writing stories; three stories passed review while showing a screen that only exists behind a production flag.

title: REVIEW: generated partner client, six months later
content:
Six months after the pattern in {{ref:mem-065}}, a generated-client review looked at how the generated client has held up, on 2026-05-21. Short answer: it did its job, and two things need attention.

What worked. Three breaking changes in the partner spec since then, and each one failed type checking in the console build before reaching anyone. Hand-written calls to the partner API: zero, enforced by a lint rule. The version bump pull requests opened by the partner team got reviewed within a day every time, because both teams see the same diff.

What did not. The generated code is large, and the console bundle grew by 90 kB, mostly from models for endpoints the console never calls. The generator can be told to include only the operations we use; that review measured that this cuts the size by two thirds. Second, PartnerClient hides errors behind one generic type, so screens cannot tell a validation error from an outage and show the same message for both. The wrapper should map the partner API's problem documents to distinct error types.

Not a problem, despite fears: build time. Generation adds eleven seconds to a cold build and nothing to a warm one.

Next steps, assigned to the client-codegen owners: restrict generation to used operations, then typed errors. The operation list goes into console.partner.codegen.operations.
context: Follow-up review of the generated client pattern; verdict is keep it and trim it.

title: Partner integration alerts page partner success first, engineering only when our API fails
content:
Carrier integrations fail in ways engineering cannot fix: an expired certificate on their side, a verifier with a slow clock, a firewall change. Until SGW-474 those failures paged the partner API on-call, who could only forward them. The pattern now separates two questions. Is our API failing for everyone, or for one partner? If the error rate rises across most partners at once, it is ours and engineering is paged. If it rises for one partner while the others are fine, partner success gets a ticket during office hours, and a page only for the three carriers with a night contract.

PartnerHealthRule implements this by comparing each partner's error rate with the median of all partners over fifteen minutes. A partner more than five times above the median is flagged as a partner problem. The thresholds live in sigwatch.rules.partners. The idea came from the outside developer test in {{ref:mem-046}}, which showed how many failures start with partner configuration rather than with our code.

Partner success received a short guide with the six most common causes and how to check each one from the delivery log, without engineering help. In the first month, nine partner alerts went to them and none needed engineering.
context: Alert routing pattern for partner-specific failures.

title: Console error messages now name the next step
content:
From 2026-05-27 every error shown in the console tells the operator what to do next, not only what failed:
- retry now, when the failure is temporary
- contact support with the reference shown, when it is ours
- fix the highlighted field, when the input was rejected
Messages without a next step fail review. The message catalogue lives in console.messages.errors, and the support team reviews new entries.
context: Decision from a support review: half of the tickets from operators were questions about what an error meant, and most could have been answered on the screen itself.

title: Console bundle size after trimming generated partner models: down by a third, two screens still heavy
content: Bundle down from 1.9 MB to 1.27 MB after the operation filter. The carrier map and the audit table are still heavy; both now load lazily via /web/src/routes/lazy-routes.ts. Budget set in console.build.size_budget_kb at 1300.
context: Status after the trim agreed in the client review; the budget is enforced in CI, so a regression fails the build instead of going unnoticed.

title: PATTERN: tests d'horloge pour chaque heure affichée
content:
Après l'incident du changement d'heure ({{ref:mem-095}}), chaque composant qui affiche une heure a un test avec une horloge figée. Règle adoptée le 2026-04-30 :
- deux dates fixes : le dimanche du passage à l'heure d'été et celui du retour à l'heure d'hiver
- trois fuseaux : Paris, Lisbonne et Dubaï
- le test vérifie le texte affiché, pas seulement la valeur reçue
