L'utilitaire freeze_clock se trouve dans /web/src/testing/clock.ts et lit les fuseaux depuis console.testing.timezones. Un composant qui reçoit une heure de l'API et la convertit lui-même échoue à la revue. Le problème n'est pas la conversion, c'est qu'elle soit faite à deux endroits.
context: Pattern de test console ; évite qu'un décalage d'heure revienne par un nouveau composant.

title: INCIDENT: payout holds released by scheduler that ran twice after failover
content: During a planned database failover on a Wednesday evening, the payout scheduler ran on two nodes for about six minutes. Both released the next payout slot. Payments were not sent twice, because the bank file builder refuses a payout already marked as sent. Holds were another story. The second scheduler released holds that an approver had placed between the two runs, and nine payouts above the approval limit left without a second approver. SchedulerLock used a session-level advisory lock, which the failover dropped silently while the old node kept its in-memory state. The lock is now taken per run inside a transaction, in /services/ledger/payouts/scheduler_lock.py, and each run checks hold_version before releasing. Finance reviewed the nine payouts; all were legitimate.
context: High importance: it bypassed the four-eyes rule on large payouts. The failover was planned and alerts were silenced, which is why nobody saw the second scheduler start.

title: INCIDENT: silenced failover alerts stayed silent for a day
content: The silence created for the planned failover on Wednesday evening was meant to last two hours. Its end time was typed in local time into a field that expects UTC, and a typo in the day made it last twenty-six hours. On Thursday, a real payout stall went unpaged for forty minutes, until an operator noticed. Same family of mistake as {{ref:mem-029}}: alerts behaving differently from what people assume. Changes: SilenceGuard rejects silences longer than four hours unless a second person raises max_hours, and sigwatch.silences.audit posts every silence to the on-call channel with its real end time. Procedure updated at https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/sigwatch/silences.
context: Incident linked to the scheduler failover; the silence outlived its purpose by a full day.

title: PATTERN: brouillons des formulaires sauvegardés localement, la recharge forcée n'attend plus
content: Ce modèle remplace la règle du bandeau dans {{ref:mem-140}}. Depuis le 2026-06-03, chaque formulaire enregistre un brouillon local à chaque modification, donc la recharge forcée peut partir sans attendre. Après la recharge, le formulaire propose de reprendre le brouillon. Code : D:\dev\drift-console\web\src\forms\drafts.ts sur les postes Windows, durée dans console.forms.draft_ttl_hours. Aucun montant n'est soumis depuis un brouillon sans relecture.
context: Remplace la règle du bandeau pour les formulaires.

title: PATTERN: contractual fuel index file from carriers
content: Replaces the daily public fetch in {{ref:mem-126}}. Since 2026-06-08 carriers send a signed monthly index file, as agreed in the contract update. IndexInbox in helix.jobs.fuel.inbox validates the signature and stores it in the raw zone; the surcharge job reads index_month and nothing else. The public site is no longer used.
context: Pattern replacing the morning fetch job. The contractual file removes the dependency on a public page and settles the disputes over which average applies.

title: GOTCHA: alert rules keyed on pod names break after every node pool upgrade
content:
Several payout alerts went quiet for a whole day after the platform team upgraded the node pool. No page, no warning. The rules were fine on paper. They matched on the pod label, and three of them listed pod names explicitly to exclude a noisy canary. After the upgrade, every pod got a new name suffix. The exclusion list no longer matched anything, which was harmless. But the rule for the scheduler heartbeat used a positive match on the old pod name, and it stopped selecting any series at all.

An alert rule that selects nothing does not fire. It does not complain either. The rule evaluator reports it as healthy, because evaluating an empty set is not an error.

What we changed. Rules select on the app label and the deployment name, never on pod names. RuleLinter now rejects any rule that mentions a pod name, and the review checklist says so. For the heartbeat, we added a second rule that fires when the series is absent for ten minutes, using absent_over_time. That one would have caught the gap within ten minutes instead of a day.

Every critical rule now gets such a companion absence rule. A monitoring owner generated them for the eighteen critical rules in one pass, and two fired at once. Both were real gaps. One rule pointed at a metric renamed in the spring, the other at a job decommissioned months ago. Neither had paged since, and now we know why.
context: Monitoring gotcha: a rule that matches nothing is silent and looks healthy. The absence companion rule is the general fix.

title: GOTCHA: browser autofill puts saved IBANs in search
content:
Operators started to see bank account numbers inside the merchant search box. Not their own: whatever the browser had saved from the refund form. The browser offered them as autofill suggestions on a field it judged similar. One operator picked a suggestion by mistake and searched for a full account number. The search request, with the number in its query string, landed in our access logs. That turned a usability glitch into a privacy issue.

Why the browser did it. Both fields had generic names, and neither declared its purpose. The browser guessed. Turning autocomplete off on a field is not reliable either, because some browsers ignore that hint for fields they consider payment related.

What we did. Each sensitive field now declares a precise purpose, and the search box declares that it is a search field. Bank fields use a one-time name per form render, so the browser has nothing to match against. Search terms moved from the query string into the request body, so they no longer reach access logs. The logs from the last ninety days were scrubbed of anything matching an account number pattern, with the privacy officer watching.

The rule for new forms sits in console.forms.autocomplete.policy, and the form review checklist has a line for it. Any field that takes bank details, card details or personal identifiers needs a reviewer from the payments side. A quick manual check helps too. Fill a form, open another screen, and watch what the browser proposes.
context: Privacy gotcha in the console. The leak was small and internal, but account numbers ended up in access logs, which is exactly what the privacy review asked us never to allow.

title: GOTCHA: reduced-motion opt-in also skipped drawer focus trap, keyboard tests passed while real users got stuck
content:
The per-test reduced motion from {{ref:mem-101}} hid a real bug, found on 2026-06-04. The drawer installs its focus trap in two places: at once when motion is reduced, and at the end of the opening animation otherwise. The second path listened for the wrong event name. So with animations on, there was no trap at all, and keyboard users could tab out of the drawer into the page behind it. Every test ran the reduced path, so every test passed.

Changes:
- the trap is installed in one place, before any animation starts
- keyboard tests run twice, with and without reduced motion, listed in /web/tests/e2e/keyboard.matrix.ts
- console.e2e.motion.modes sets both modes as default for new suites

Lesson: a test switch that changes code paths needs its own test of the other path.
context: Accessibility gotcha that the e2e suite hid; a keyboard pass found it, not a test.

title: PATTERN: every schema migration ships with a reverse step tested in CI, data migrations split from schema changes
content: Since MER-539, merged on 2026-05-15, every migration in the ledger has a tested downgrade. The CI job applies the migration, applies its downgrade, then applies it again, on a copy of the schema. This catches the empty and half-written migrations described in {{ref:mem-107}}. Data migrations live apart from schema migrations. A schema migration may add, rename or drop structure; it never touches rows. Backfills run afterwards through the throttled runner. Downgrades that would lose data must say so in their docstring. They refuse to run in production without an explicit flag. The CI step is defined in /ci/pipelines/ledger-migrations.yaml and its settings in ledger.ci.migrations.roundtrip.
context: Migration pattern for the ledger; the round trip in CI is cheap and has already caught two bad downgrades.

title: INCIDENT: monthly merchant statements doubled every fee for one hour
content: On 2026-06-01 at 07:00 the statement job published monthly statements in which every fee appeared twice. Totals were right; only the detail was doubled. A join on fee_breakdown matched both the original fee and its reversal pair, and the template showed absolute amounts. About 2,300 merchants downloaded a statement before statements owners withdrew them at 08:05. Corrected statements went out at 09:30 with a short apology. The query now filters on is_reversed. Statements are previewed for ten merchants before publishing.
context: Interim incident note, written the same morning. Merchant success handled the calls. Several merchants asked whether they had been charged twice, which they had not, but the doubled detail looked convincing. Finance wants a proper review of the statement template before the next month-end, and that review will decide whether reversal pairs should appear in statements at all.

title: PATTERN: stored balances are checked against journal sums every night
content:
This replaces the interim note in {{ref:mem-090}}. Finance decided on 2026-05-28 that the journal is the truth for all eleven accounts. The DBA's correction ran the same evening: one adjustment posting per account, each referencing the drift. No balance was edited by hand.

The lasting part is the check that found the drift. It is now a standing pattern:
- every night, ledger.reports.balances.recompute sums the journal per account and compares with the stored balance
- any difference, even one cent, opens a finance ticket with both values
- the stored balance is never corrected directly; the fix is always an adjustment posting
- the check runs on the reporting replica after the nightly close, so it never competes with postings

Scripts that update balances directly are banned. The application role lost its update right on the balance column, so only the posting path can change it. The old fix_fee_rounding script was deleted from the repository. Its history stays in version control for the auditors.
context: Final outcome of the balance drift; the interim incident note is obsolete.

title: Merchant statements will not show reversal pairs, only net fees
content: Statements sent to merchants show each fee once, at its final amount. Reversal pairs stay in the ledger and in the finance view. A merchant only sees the net result, plus a short note when a fee was corrected. Finance and merchant success agreed on this after the doubled statements. Merchants read statements to check what they paid, and a reversal pair reads like a double charge followed by a refund. Auditors still get the full detail from the ledger export.
context: Decision that follows the statement incident. It changes what merchants see, not what the ledger stores, so the reversal pattern stays untouched. Merchant success asked for the note on corrected fees, because a fee that silently changes between two statements raises more questions than one that says it was corrected.

title: INCIDENT: nightly recon export manifest pointed to test bucket, buckets now split by role
content:
Two days after the switch to synthetic test data in {{ref:mem-104}}, the analytics team saw strange merchant names in their morning dashboard. The production recon export manifest named files in the test bucket. Nothing private leaked: the files held synthetic data, and the real export was there too, just not referenced. But for one morning the dashboard showed invented merchants.

Cause. The test export step and the production publish step shared one setting for the target bucket. The test pipeline overrode it at run time. A configuration refactor moved that override into the shared defaults by mistake, so production picked it up. No check compared the bucket with the environment.

Decision. Test and production buckets are now separate by role, not just by name. The production publisher has no write right on the test bucket, and the reverse holds too. Each environment reads its bucket from helix.storage.buckets.export, and the value must match the environment name or the job refuses to start. Manifests also carry the environment, and the analytics loader rejects one that does not say production.

The dashboard was corrected by noon. A storage owner checked every other export for the same mistake. None had it.
context: Incident and decision in one note; bucket rights are now split by environment.

title: PATTERN: finance tickets from ledger checks
content:
The nightly balance check in {{ref:mem-156}} opens finance tickets, and so do three other checks now. MER-544 gave them one shape, because finance was drowning in tickets that each looked different.

Every ticket opened by a ledger check has the same parts. A title that names the check and the account or merchant. A body with the expected value, the observed value and the difference, all in minor units and in the display currency. A link to the account in the console. And a field called check_name, so finance can filter and count per check.

Rules for the checks themselves. One ticket per problem, not one per night. If the same difference is still there the next night, the check comments on the open ticket instead of opening another. A ticket is closed by finance, never by the check, even when the difference disappears on its own. A difference that vanishes without a correction is a finding in itself, and someone should look at why.

Severity follows money, not count. A one-cent drift on one account is low. Any difference above one hundred euros, or affecting more than ten accounts at once, is high and also posts to the finance channel. The thresholds sit in a table called check_thresholds, owned by finance and editable without a deploy.

What the checks may not do: correct anything. They report. Corrections go through adjustment postings, decided by a person. This keeps the checks simple and keeps a human in front of every money change.

Checks using the shape today: balance against journal, payout file totals against bank confirmations, fee parity during the engine migration, and statement totals against the ledger. The checks owner owns the shared ticket code. Adding a check takes about an hour.
context: Pattern for any automated check that reports to finance; the no-correction rule matters most and keeps every money change in human hands.

title: PATTERN: console search terms go in request bodies, never in URLs
content: Since 2026-06-05, every console search sends its terms in the request body. Query strings end up in access logs, browser history and proxy caches. The shared helper lives in /web/src/api/search-request.ts and strips any search_term parameter from URLs before sending. The setting console.api.search.body_only is on for every environment.
context: Follows the autofill leak; applies to every search box, not just the merchant one.

title: DECISION: quatre créneaux de virement au lieu de trois
content:
Cette décision remplace celle des trois créneaux quotidiens, {{ref:mem-080}}. Après le premier mois, la finance a fait le bilan demandé par la finance. Les économies de frais bancaires sont réelles : 64 % de virements en moins pour les marchands qui reçoivent plusieurs paiements par jour. Mais le créneau de 12h30 posait un problème. Il arrivait trop tard pour les transporteurs qui paient leurs chauffeurs à midi, et le support a reçu plus de quatre-vingts plaintes en un mois.

Nous passons donc à quatre créneaux : 08h00, 11h00, 13h30 et 16h00, heure de Paris. Le créneau de 11h00 sert ceux qui paient à midi. Celui de 13h30 remplace 12h30 et laisse le temps de placer des retenues après la pause. Le dernier créneau ne bouge pas, car c'est lui qui garantit l'arrivée le jour même.

Le coût est faible : un fichier bancaire de plus par jour, et environ 8 % de virements en plus par rapport à trois créneaux. Les marchands du forfait instantané gardent le versement continu, comme avant.

Le support a reçu une explication courte pour les marchands. Les nouveaux créneaux entrent en vigueur lundi prochain. La finance refera le bilan à la fin du trimestre, avec les mêmes chiffres, pour comparer.
context: Remplace la décision des trois créneaux ; la raison principale est le paiement des chauffeurs à midi.

title: GOTCHA: rapports d'erreurs envoyés par la console without build ids, so every release now stamps its error events at deploy time
content:
Errors from the console reached the tracker without a build number for two weeks in the spring. The deploy pipeline had stopped passing it after a template change. Grouping still worked, but nobody could tell which release introduced a new error. On 2026-05-26 a spike of failed refund submissions took an hour to pin down, because three releases had shipped that morning.

The pattern now. The deploy pipeline stamps every bundle with the build id and the commit, and the console reads them from console.telemetry.release at startup. If the value is missing, the console sends no error events at all and logs one local warning. A silent tracker is easier to notice than a tracker full of unattributed events. Each release also uploads its source maps under the same id, so stack traces point at real files.

A deploy check compares the id in the bundle with the id the pipeline expects. A mismatch fails the deploy. Telemetry owners added the check after the spike. It has failed once since, on a manual hotfix that skipped the pipeline.
context: Follow-up to the environment labels work; this one is about release attribution.

title: DECISION: refunds above five thousand euros need a second operator, enforced in console and ledger
content:
After the double refund in {{ref:mem-008}}, idempotency stopped duplicate calls. It did nothing against one operator making one large mistake. DLK-522 adds a second pair of eyes. Any refund above five thousand euros now needs a second operator to approve it before the ledger executes it. The first operator submits, and the refund waits in a queue. A second operator from the same team approves or rejects it. Nobody can approve their own refund.

The rule is enforced twice. The console shows the queue and hides the approve button on your own requests. The ledger checks the approver identity again and refuses a self-approval, because the console alone is not a control. ApprovalQueue is the new console screen; RefundApprovalPolicy holds the threshold on the ledger side.

Five thousand comes from the refund history. It covers fewer than two percent of refunds and more than half of the refunded amount. Support leads asked for a faster lane during peak days. Not granted for now.
context: Control decision for large refunds; the ledger-side check is the one auditors care about.

title: STATUS: validation avant dépôt manuel désormais intégrée
content: Ce point remplace la procédure manuelle de {{ref:mem-113}}. Depuis le 2026-06-09, avec MER-555, la validation se fait dans l'outil de dépôt lui-même : la finance n'a plus de script à lancer avant l'envoi. En cas d'échec, le dépôt est bloqué et le message indique la règle du schéma en cause. Reste à former l'équipe de nuit.
context: Point d'étape côté finance, dépôts manuels.

title: REVIEW: payout reconciliation script for finance now waits for ledger readiness
content:
Decided on 2026-06-10 with finance and the ledger team. The reconciliation script now runs as a scheduled job at seven every morning. It starts only once the ledger reports ready, using the same readiness endpoint that helix polls in {{ref:mem-069}}. Finance keeps a button to run it by hand, but the button also waits for readiness.

Why. Twice this spring the script ran before the nightly close had finished. It compared bank entries with a ledger that was still posting, and flagged payouts as missing that arrived ten minutes later. Finance spent a morning chasing them each time. Waiting for readiness removes that whole class of false alarms.

How. The job polls every minute for up to an hour. If the ledger is still not ready at eight, it stops and posts a message to the finance channel instead of running on partial data. The schedule and the polling limits live in ledger.finance.recon.schedule. The report goes to finance by email and to the shared folder they already use.

What changes for finance. No more running the script from their own desks at month-end. Finance asked to keep the manual button for the first quarter, in case the schedule misses a special day. We agreed and will review usage in the autumn.

The readiness endpoint stays internal. The scheduled job runs inside our network, so this does not reopen the partner question.
context: Decision that closes the ownership move for the finance script. Readiness gating is the important change; the false missing-payout alarms were eating a finance morning each time, and they always hit on the busiest days.

title: Double fetch on refund screens fixed at router level
content:
The provisional fix in {{ref:mem-109}} is replaced by a proper one, DLK-535, shipped on 2026-06-11. The router now resolves redirects before running any loader, so a parent redirect no longer triggers the child loader twice. What changed:
- redirects to a default tab are declared in the route table, not inside RefundsLayout
- loaders receive a signal and abort when the navigation is superseded
- a test counts requests per navigation and fails above one per resource
The workaround in the parent loader was removed. Three other screens had the same double call without anyone noticing. The same change fixed them.
context: Supersedes the provisional loader fix on refund screens.

title: CONFIG: console date and time display settings per region, formats and zones
content:
Display settings for dates and times in the console, consolidated under DLK-547 on 2026-06-12. They sit in console.display.regions and follow the clock tests in {{ref:mem-146}}: every value below has a test at both clock changes.

Per region:
- western europe: zone Europe/Paris, day month year with slashes, 24-hour clock
- iberia: zone Europe/Lisbon, same formats, but cutoffs shown with the zone name because Lisbon is one hour behind Paris
- uk: zone Europe/London, day month year, 24-hour clock, with a note on bank holidays that differ from the continent
- nordics: zone Europe/Stockholm, year month day with hyphens, as operators there asked
- gulf: zone Asia/Dubai, day month year, weekend shown as Friday and Saturday in calendars

Rules that apply everywhere:
- the zone comes from the region of the data, not from the operator's browser; an operator in Paris looking at a Gulf payout sees Dubai time, with the zone name
- relative times such as two hours ago are allowed only for events in the last day, and the exact time shows on hover
- cutoffs always show the zone name, even in the operator's own region, since the summer time incident
- amounts follow the console language, not the region, as decided with the translation scope

How to change a value. Open a pull request on the settings file, add or update the clock tests, and ask a reviewer from the region's operations team. A format change for a region is announced in the operators' channel one week before release. People read screens by habit, and a new date order causes mistakes.

Open question for the next review: whether support viewers outside Europe need their own zone for internal timestamps such as audit events. The date-picker owners are collecting cases.
context: Reference for console date display; the data region, not the browser, picks the zone.

title: STATUS: fee engine cutover dry run on staging, totals match to the cent
content: The dry run of the fee engine cutover ran on staging last night. The new engine took over at the close, and the old one stayed in shadow mode. Totals for the night matched to the cent across all regions. The switch is a single setting, ledger.fees.engine.active, and switching back took forty seconds in the rehearsal. Production cutover waits for one full month-end without differences.
context: Status on the fee engine cutover rehearsal. The rollback time is the number people asked about most, so it is written down here explicitly.

title: PATTERN: registre des arbitrages finance sur les écarts
content:
Chaque fois que la finance tranche un écart, la décision est inscrite dans un registre, avec MER-564 comme point de départ. Avant, ces arbitrages vivaient dans des fils de discussion et des courriels. Personne ne retrouvait pourquoi un compte avait reçu une écriture d'ajustement six mois plus tôt.

Le registre est une table simple dans le grand livre. Chaque entrée contient le compte ou le marchand concerné, l'écart constaté, la décision prise, le nom de la personne qui l'a prise et la référence de l'écriture d'ajustement, s'il y en a une. Une entrée ne se modifie jamais. Si la finance revient sur une décision, elle ajoute une nouvelle entrée qui annule la précédente, comme pour les écritures comptables.

Pourquoi une table et pas un document partagé : les contrôles nocturnes peuvent la lire. Un écart déjà arbitré n'ouvre plus de nouveau ticket, il est rattaché à la décision existante. C'est ce qui a fait baisser le bruit pour la finance, plus que tout le reste.

Qui écrit : seule la finance, depuis l'écran prévu dans la console. Les développeurs lisent, mais ne créent jamais d'entrée, même pour aider. Une entrée écrite par quelqu'un d'autre que la finance n'a aucune valeur pour les auditeurs.

Ce que l'écran contrôle avant d'enregistrer une décision : que l'écart existe encore, que le montant affiché correspond à celui du contrôle, et que l'écriture d'ajustement prévue n'a pas déjà été passée par quelqu'un d'autre.

Les auditeurs ont reçu un export du registre à la dernière revue trimestrielle. Leur seule remarque a porté sur le format des montants, qu'ils voulaient en unités entières. C'est corrigé.
context: Pattern partagé entre la finance et l'équipe du grand livre ; la table remplace les fils de discussion.

title: GOTCHA: read-only old cluster still accepted writes from one forgotten maintenance job
content: The old cluster from the parity checks in {{ref:mem-098}} was supposed to be read-only. On 2026-06-02 we found it was not, for one role. A weekly maintenance job still connected as the owner role, which can override the read-only default for its own sessions. It rewrote statistics tables every Sunday. Harmless, but it meant parity had compared against a cluster that changed. MER-573 revoked the owner login. ClusterGuard now lists every role that can still write, run from /ops/ledger/cluster-guard.py.
context: Gotcha found by accident while preparing the deletion of the old cluster. Setting the default transaction mode to read-only does not stop a role that can change the setting for itself, and owner roles can. Anyone freezing a database before deletion or migration should revoke write rights instead of relying on the default.

title: Close calendar settings per region and weekend rules behind readiness
content:
The readiness bug in {{ref:mem-139}} came from a region list nobody owned. The settings now live in one place, read by CloseCalendar in ledger.close.calendar. On developer laptops the file is D:\dev\apex-ledger\config\close-calendar.toml.

Each region declares three things. The days on which it closes. The latest time by which its close must finish, after which readiness reports late rather than waiting forever. And the region it may borrow a calendar from, which only Iberia uses today, borrowing from western Europe.

Order in the file has no meaning any more. The readiness check reads every region. A test fails if two regions share a name, or if a day appears in neither the close days nor the weekend days.

Changes to close days need finance approval, because they move settlement dates. The on-call engineer may raise the latest finish times during an incident.

A rendered view of the calendar for the next ninety days is on https://ledger.ottervale.example.com/internal/close-calendar, handy before holidays.
context: Config reference for region close days and limits.

title: Bundle budget check passed while the real download grew, because it measured files before compression
content:
The bundle budget from {{ref:mem-145}} looked healthy for a month. Meanwhile, operators in the Lyon office complained that the console took longer to open each week. The check was measuring the wrong thing. It summed the size of the built files before compression, and a build change had switched one large dependency to a format that compresses badly. Raw size barely moved. Compressed size, which is what operators download, grew by forty percent.

Found on 2026-06-15, when a console developer compared the budget report with what the browser's network panel showed. The two numbers had drifted apart week after week.

The check now measures compressed size with the same settings as the production server. It reports both numbers so the gap stays visible. The budget itself was lowered to match what we had before the drift. The dependency went back to its previous build format, and the console opens in under two seconds again on the office connection.

Also worth knowing: the first load after a release is the slow one, because nothing is cached. That is the number to watch.
context: Build budget gotcha; measure what users download.

title: DECISION: partner sandbox reset weekly
content:
QRY-370 settles a long argument about the partner sandbox. From now on it is reset every Sunday night to a known state. Partners keep their accounts, keys and webhook settings. Everything else goes: shipments, invoices, payouts and any data they created during the week.

Why. The sandbox had grown for two years without cleanup. Some partners had millions of test shipments, and list endpoints were slower there than in production. Worse, partners built tests on top of data they had created months ago and then forgotten. Their certification runs depended on leftovers nobody could reproduce. A weekly reset makes every partner start from the same known state.

What partners get instead of leftovers. A seeding endpoint that creates a fixed scenario on demand: five shipments in various states, two invoices, one disputed. The scenario is described in the partner guide and versioned. Partners who need more data call it several times. The seed definitions live in /deploy/quarry/sandbox/seed-scenarios.yaml and are read under the quarry.sandbox.seed prefix.

Notice. Partners were told three weeks ahead. Two asked for an exception; both had a certification run in progress, and we delayed their reset by one week. No permanent exceptions.

What can go wrong: a partner whose automated tests assume last week's data will see failures on Monday morning. The reset job therefore posts a notice in the partner portal and emails technical contacts every Friday. The first reset ran smoothly. One partner called on Monday, as expected, and fixed their test the same day. Reset settings are kept under reset_schedule, owned by the partner team.
context: Decision on sandbox hygiene for partners; the seeding endpoint replaces leftovers.

title: REVIEW: catalog alias resolver after first month in service
content:
Alias resolver notes one month after the move to the service catalog in {{ref:mem-091}}. Verdict: the design holds, but the fallback is more dangerous than we thought.

The good part. Every job resolves its sources through the catalog. Access rules per team work: the analytics team tried twice to read the payouts source and was refused both times, with a clear message. Catalog changes are logged, and the two edits made this month were both reviewed.

The worrying part. When the catalog is down, the resolver uses the last known values for up to a day. During a catalog outage on a Tuesday, three jobs ran on cached values. That was fine for two of them. The third had a cached value from before a migration of its source. It read from the old replica, which was still up and still answering, with data frozen two days earlier. The job succeeded. Its output was stale, and nobody noticed until finance asked about missing invoices.

Requested changes. The cache must expire when an alias changes, not after a fixed day. The catalog will publish a version number with each alias, and the resolver will refuse a cached entry older than the current version once the catalog is back. During an outage, jobs that write anything outside helix must not run on cached values at all. They wait. And the old replica of a migrated source must be shut down, not left running, so that a stale lookup fails loudly instead of succeeding quietly.

A follow-up review will run again after the version number lands.
context: Review of the catalog resolver; the stale fallback is the risk, not the catalog itself.
keywords: no cached values for external writes

title: Console partner API version pins per environment, and how BFF overrides them during carrier migrations
content:
During the v2 rollout described in {{ref:mem-032}}, the console needed to show some carriers through version 2 while others were still on version 1. Pins are set per environment, and the BFF may override them per carrier. Settings as of 2026-06-16.

The environment pin is the version the console was built against. Production pins version 2. Staging pins version 2 as well, plus a preview flag for version 3. On developer laptops the pin is read from D:\dev\drift-console\config\partner-pins.json, which defaults to the staging value.

The carrier override lives in the BFF, not in the console. VersionRouter in the BFF looks up the carrier. If that carrier is still on version 1, it calls the partner API with the old header and maps the response to the version 2 shape. The console never sees two shapes. That was the main point: screens have only one model.

Overrides are temporary by design. Each one has an end date, and the BFF logs a warning every day once it has passed. Two overrides are left, for the two carriers on quarterly release trains. Both end in the autumn.

Rules. Never add an override in the console itself. Never pin an environment to a version older than production. And remove an override in the same week the carrier moves, so the mapping code can go.
context: Config note for partner API pins in the console and the BFF override rule.

title: GOTCHA: JobGraph retries reuse the failed attempt's work folder
content: On 2026-06-06 the carrier invoice job failed, retried, and published a file mixing two attempts. JobGraph retried in the same working folder, and the second attempt appended to partial output left by the first. Each attempt now gets its own folder named by attempt_id. The publish step reads only from the current one.
context: Gotcha in the graph runner; any job that writes partial output before failing was exposed. Caught by the row-count guard before the file reached carriers.

title: REVIEW: finance month-end checklist run on Windows desks, what still depends on someone remembering a step
content:
A month-end shadowing session with finance on 2026-05-31 captured every manual step. The goal was to find what still depends on memory. The checklist itself lives on the finance share, at F:\finance\month-end\checklist.md, and is edited by hand each month.

Thirty-one steps in total. Nineteen are now automated or checked by the ledger, good progress compared with last year. Twelve still depend on someone remembering. The review grouped them.

Steps that should become automatic. Downloading the bank statements from three portals, which takes forty minutes and fails silently when a portal changes its login page. Comparing payout totals with the bank confirmations, which the nightly checks already do but finance repeats by hand because nobody told them. Exporting the fee summary for the auditors, a query that one person knows by heart.

Steps that should stay manual but get a guard. Approving the closing journal, which is a real decision. Releasing held payouts older than thirty days, which needs judgment. For both, the console should show what is pending instead of relying on the checklist.

Steps that can go. Two of them check things that no longer exist: the old fee table and the staging dump. Nobody had dared to remove them.

The biggest risk is not a step but a person. Three of the twelve steps are known only to one finance owner, who is on leave for the next month-end. The notes were written out in plain words with screenshots before the review ended. That alone made the session worth it.

Next. The bank download and the auditor export are planned for the coming quarter. The duplicated comparison ends this month; finance will read the nightly check results instead. The checklist then moves out of the shared file into the console, where each step can show its own state.
context: Month-end review with finance; the single-person knowledge is the risk that needed fixing first.

title: GOTCHA: old ledger replica kept answering after migration, so stale reads looked healthy
content:
The helix review in {{ref:mem-174}} found a job reading from an old replica that should have been gone. That replica was ours. This is the ledger side of the story.

When we moved the reporting replica to new hardware, we created the new one, pointed the catalog alias at it, and left the old one running. The plan was to shut it down a week later, once nothing used it. Nobody owned that step. The old replica stayed up for five weeks, connected to nothing upstream, still answering queries with data frozen on the day of the move.

Why it looked healthy. Our monitoring checks that each replica is up and that its lag is below a threshold. A replica disconnected from the primary reports no lag at all, because it is not replicating anything. Up, no lag: green on the dashboard.

What we changed. Lag is now measured from the primary side, as the age of the last replayed change, so a disconnected replica shows its real age and turns red within minutes. Every replica must appear in the catalog, and one that does not is flagged. Retiring a replica is a ticket with an owner and a date, created together with the replacement, not afterwards. The retirement procedure is at https://wiki.ottervale.example.com/ledger/replica-retirement.

The old replica was shut down the day the review came in. The lag metric is configured under ledger.monitoring.replica.age. For a month, the dashboard shows the new measure next to the old one, so people can see why the old one lied.
context: Ledger-side gotcha matching the helix review; lag measured on the replica cannot see a disconnected replica.

title: STATUS: outbox relay moved to its own deployment, lag alerts quiet for two weeks, one duplicate burst during the switch
content: MER-588 moved the outbox relay from {{ref:mem-078}} out of the API pods into its own deployment on 2026-06-01. Two weeks later, the relay lag alert has not fired once. Before, it fired about twice a week, whenever API pods scaled down during the night. One burst of duplicates happened during the switch itself. For about forty seconds both the old and new relays published, and consumers saw some events twice. Deduplication handled it, as designed, and no consumer reported an issue. The relay settings now live in ledger.events.relay.deploy. Developers on Windows run it locally with D:\dev\apex-ledger\scripts\run-relay.py. Next step: remove the relay code path from the API image.
context: Status after the relay split. The duplicate burst was expected and is the reason consumers must deduplicate; it is recorded here as a real example to point at when someone asks.

title: How the console shows money: minor units from the API, formatting at the very edge
content:
The console never does arithmetic on money. It receives amounts from the API as integers in minor units, together with the currency code, and formats them only at the moment of display. This note writes down the rules, because three bugs in a year came from breaking them.

The rules:
- amounts travel as strings of digits in minor units, never as floating point numbers, so large values survive the trip through the browser
- the currency exponent comes from the API with each amount; the console never assumes two decimals
- totals are computed by the API; a screen that needs a sum asks for it
- formatting uses the console language for separators and the currency for symbol and exponent
- input fields accept what the operator types, then send it to the API as minor units after a validation call

What this rules out. Adding amounts in the browser to show a subtotal. Rounding a value for display and then reusing the rounded value. Parsing a formatted amount back into a number. Each of these has put a wrong figure on screen at least once.

Where it lives. The formatting helper reads its settings from console.money.format, and a lint rule bans arithmetic operators on values typed as money. Exceptions need a comment and a reviewer from the payments side. There are two so far, both in charts, where rounding is harmless.

The three past bugs are linked from the helper's documentation page, so new developers can see what goes wrong without the rules.
context: Console rules for money display. They exist because the browser cannot be trusted with large integers or decimal arithmetic, and because every exception so far turned into a bug report.

title: REVIEW: fee engine shadow comparison code, before cutover
content: A review of FeeShadowRunner covers the code that runs the new fee engine next to the old one. It is correct, but it compares results after rounding, so a difference below half a cent never shows up. The comparison must use unrounded values. It also swallows exceptions from the new engine and records them as matches. An engine that crashes must count as a difference. Both get fixed before the month-end parity run.
context: Short review before the decisive parity month; a comparison that hides crashes would have made the cutover look safe.

title: PATTERN: finance checks get a weekly digest instead of one message per finding, except high severity
content:
MER-592 adds a weekly digest to the finance checks in {{ref:mem-159}}:
- low and medium findings are grouped into one Monday message
- high findings still post at once
- the digest links each open ticket
The template lives in /services/ledger/checks/digest.md, and the schedule in ledger.checks.digest.weekly.
context: Noise reduction for finance; the high-severity path is unchanged on purpose.

title: DECISION: schema changes on large ledger tables go through online migration tool
content:
After the autogenerate surprise in {{ref:mem-107}}, migrations got more scrutiny. MER-609 goes one step further for large tables, decided on 2026-06-17. Any schema change on a table above ten million rows goes through the online migration tool, never through a plain migration.

Why. A plain column change on the journal table locks it for minutes. Postings queue, payouts wait, and the API times out. We had one such lock in the winter. It lasted six minutes and felt like an hour.

What the tool does. It builds a shadow copy of the table with the new schema and copies rows in batches through the throttled runner. A trigger keeps the copy in sync. Then it swaps the two tables in one short lock, which takes under a second.

The rules:
- tables above ten million rows are listed in /services/ledger/db/large_tables.toml, checked by the migration lint
- a migration touching a listed table fails in CI unless it calls OnlineMigration
- adding a nullable column without a default is allowed directly, because it does not rewrite the table
- every online migration is rehearsed on staging with a production-sized copy first
- the swap happens outside the payout slots

What it costs. An online migration takes hours instead of seconds, and the shadow copy doubles disk use for the table while it runs. The DBA checks free space before each one. The events owner owns the tool and reviews the first three migrations that use it.
context: Decision for large ledger tables; the six-minute lock in the winter is the reason.

title: STATUS: per-attempt work folders rolled out to every helix job
content:
The fix from {{ref:mem-176}} is now live everywhere. Status on 2026-06-13:
- all fourteen jobs write to a fresh folder per attempt
- the publish step refuses files from any other attempt
- old shared folders were deleted after a last check
- disk use went up slightly, since failed attempts keep their folder for two days
The cleanup of failed attempt folders runs nightly, set in /deploy/helix/cleanup-attempts.yaml. Two jobs needed small changes because they assumed a fixed folder name. Both are fixed. No mixed output since the change. An export owner removes the old folder setting from the job template next week.
context: Rollout status for the retry folder fix; closes the gotcha on mixed attempts.

title: DECISION: finance verifies export checksums with one script
content: Finance asked for a simple way to use the sidecar checksums from {{ref:mem-071}} on their own machines. Decided on 2026-06-09: one script, D:\finance\tools\exports\verify-export.py, checks a downloaded file against its sidecar and prints a clear yes or no. It reads the expected export names from helix.exports.finance.catalog. No other tools are supported.
context: Decision on finance tooling for checksums. Finance does not use command-line tools daily, so the script prints plain sentences instead of hashes and opens with a double click. Support for it sits with the helix team.

title: INCIDENT: absence rules paged all night during metrics storage migration
content: This replaces the gotcha in {{ref:mem-151}}, whose absence companion rules turned out too blunt. During the metrics storage migration, SGW-481, every absence rule fired at once and paged the on-call twelve times in one night. The series were not gone, only delayed. Absence rules now wait twenty minutes and are muted by the migration_window flag in sigwatch.rules.absence. A rule that fires together with fifty others is grouped into one page.
context: Supersedes the earlier gotcha: absence rules stay, but with a delay, a migration flag and grouping. The on-call engineer that night lost a full night of sleep to alerts that all described one single cause.

title: DECISION: plus de cache côté console pour les soldes
content:
Décidé le 2026-06-18, dans la continuité des loaders de route ({{ref:mem-076}}) : les soldes ne sont jamais mis en cache dans la console, sous aucune forme. Ni entre deux navigations, ni dans le stockage du navigateur, ni pour un affichage rapide en attendant la réponse.

Pourquoi le rappeler alors que c'était déjà la règle ? Parce qu'une demande de fusion proposait d'afficher le dernier solde connu pendant le chargement, pour que l'écran paraisse plus rapide. L'idée est bonne pour une liste de transporteurs. Elle est dangereuse pour un solde. Un opérateur qui voit un ancien solde pendant deux secondes peut décider d'une retenue ou d'un remboursement sur un chiffre faux.

Ce qui est permis : un squelette de chargement, sans chiffre. Ce qui ne l'est pas : un chiffre, même grisé, même marqué comme ancien.

La règle vaut aussi pour les montants en attente et les limites de remboursement. Les données de référence, comme les listes de pays ou de devises, gardent leur durée de cache de cinq minutes.

Avant d'ajouter un cache, il faut donc vérifier qu'aucun montant n'en dépend. En cas de doute, la question va à l'équipe paiements, qui répond le jour même.
context: Rappel devenu décision après une demande de fusion ; les montants ne se mettent jamais en cache.

title: Console releases freeze during last two working days of each month
content:
No console release ships during the last two working days of a month, nor on the first working day of the next. Finance closes the month in that window, operators place most of their holds, and support is at its busiest. A broken screen then costs more than in any other week.

What the freeze covers. Any deploy that changes the console bundle or the BFF. Feature flag changes too, since a flag can change a screen as much as a release can.

What it does not cover. Fixes for an incident in progress, approved by the on-call lead and announced in the operators' channel. Text changes in error messages, which support can approve.

How it is enforced. ReleaseGate in the deploy pipeline reads the freeze calendar from console.release.freeze_calendar and blocks the deploy step during a freeze. An override needs the on-call lead's approval, logged with the reason. Last quarter, two overrides were used, both for real incidents.

Why it became a rule. In the spring, a release on the last day of the month moved the hold button on the payout screen. Operators clicked the wrong button for an hour. Nothing irreversible happened, but finance had to recheck eighty payouts during their busiest afternoon of the month.

The calendar is generated a year ahead and includes bank holidays per region.
context: Release freeze around month-end; overrides need the on-call lead.

title: INCIDENT: graph runner stalled the whole night on one cyclic dependency
content:
This supersedes the rollout status in {{ref:mem-062}}, which reported the graph runner on nine of fourteen jobs with no surprise beyond one shared table. The surprise came later. On 2026-06-19, HXB-354: no helix job ran at all between midnight and six.

Timeline:
- 23:50, a change declares that the fee summary job reads the carrier invoice output
- 00:00, JobGraph builds the graph and finds a cycle, because the carrier invoice job already read the fee summary
- 00:00 to 06:10, the runner waits for the cycle to resolve, logs one warning, and never alerts
- 06:10, finance reports that no exports arrived

Why it was missed. The change passed review, since each declaration looked right on its own. The graph is only built at run time, so the cycle stayed invisible until midnight. And a stuck graph produced no failed job, so no job alert fired.

Fixes. The graph is now built in CI for every change to job declarations, and a cycle fails the build. At run time, a cycle stops the runner at once and pages the helix on-call, with the path of the cycle in the message. GraphHealth in helix.runner.health also alerts if no job has started thirty minutes after midnight.

The exports ran late, at nine. Invoices to carriers went out one day late, with a short note.
context: Supersedes the rollout status. The incident lost no data but delayed carrier invoices by a day, and it showed that a stuck scheduler is invisible to job-level alerts. The run-time cycle check and the no-job-started alert are the lasting fixes; the CI check stops most cycles from getting that far.

title: GOTCHA: partner file downloads served with wrong content length after gzip, breaking checksum checks
content:
Some carriers download invoice files through the partner API, then verify them against the published checksum. Finance does the same with the script in {{ref:mem-185}}. On 2026-06-20, QRY-387: three carriers reported checksum failures on every download.

What happened. A gateway change enabled compression for all responses, file downloads included. The gateway compressed each file on the fly but kept the original content length header. Most clients coped. Two carrier tools trusted the header, read the announced number of bytes from the decompressed stream, and cut the file short. The checksum then failed, correctly.

What we changed:
- file downloads are excluded from gateway compression; files are already compressed when it helps
- the response carries the checksum in a header, so clients can verify without a second request
- FileDownloadController sets content_length itself, and a test compares it with the bytes actually sent
- the gateway rule lives in com.ottervale.quarry.gateway.compression, with an explicit list of excluded paths

What carriers had to do: nothing, once the fix shipped. One carrier had already built a workaround that retried downloads until the checksum passed. It never passed, of course, and their retries hit our rate limit. We asked them to remove it.

Lesson. A gateway change affects every endpoint at once, including those with unusual contracts like file downloads. Gateway changes now run the partner contract tests, not only the gateway's own tests.
context: Partner gotcha; checksums did their job and exposed a gateway change nobody linked to downloads.

title: PATTERN: webhooks signed with per-partner asymmetric keys from now on
content:
This pattern replaces the shared-secret signing approved in {{ref:mem-014}}. That review asked to revisit asymmetric signatures once we passed twenty partners. We passed twenty-six this spring, and QRY-333 was reopened on 2026-06-08 to do it.

What changes. Each webhook is now signed with our private key, and partners verify with our public key, published at a fixed address and rotated on a schedule. Partners no longer hold any secret. A leaked partner configuration can no longer be used to forge webhooks. That was the weak point of shared secrets: twenty-six partners meant twenty-six places where a secret could leak.

What stays. The signature still covers the timestamp and the raw body. The five-minute replay window stays, with the clock-skew report next to it. Logging rules stay: we never log a signed body, only its hash.

Rotation. Two public keys are always published, the current one and the next. We sign with the current key. A month before rotation, the next key is announced; on rotation day we switch, and the old key stays published for thirty days. No partner action is needed if their verifier reads the published keys, which the guide now requires.

Migration. For six months both signatures are sent, the old HMAC header and the new one, so partners can move at their own pace. SignatureMigrationReport in com.ottervale.quarry.webhooks.signing shows which partners still verify only the old header. Key settings sit in /deploy/quarry/signing-keys.yaml.

Fourteen partners verify the new signature already. The carriers who wanted an afternoon's work in the first review found that libraries now make it about that easy.
context: Supersedes the shared-secret signing scheme; the migration window is six months.

title: GOTCHA: alert notes link to dashboards that move, leaving on-call lost
content: On 2026-06-21 the on-call engineer opened a payout alert at 02:00 and clicked its dashboard link. It led to an empty page. The dashboard had been reorganised the week before, and its address had changed. Eleven alert notes still pointed at old addresses. LinkChecker now runs every night over the alert notes and opens a ticket for each broken link. Dashboards are linked by their stable id, not by their title path, and the dashboard_uid field is required in every rule note.
context: Small gotcha with a big effect at night: the note is what the on-call reads first, so a dead link costs real minutes.

title: GOTCHA: graph reruns of outbound jobs need guards
content: This replaces the provisional note in {{ref:mem-099}} on the Swiss invoices sent twice. The guard added then covered one job. The review with finance on 2026-06-11 found four more jobs that send something outside helix and would repeat it on a rerun. Each now checks an OutboundLedger table before sending: one entry per job, period and recipient. The shared guard sits in /jobs/helix/common/outbound-guard.py, and JobGraph refuses to rerun a job marked outbound without it.
context: Final rule after the duplicate Swiss invoices: every job that sends something outside helix must be safe to rerun. Finance confirmed that a duplicate invoice costs more in trust than a late one, so the guard blocks rather than warns.

title: Version 1 de l'API partenaires arrêtée fin octobre
content:
Décidé le 2026-06-22 avec l'équipe partenaires : la version 1 de l'API partenaires s'arrête le 2026-10-31. Le préavis de six mois annoncé avec l'en-tête de dépréciation est donc respecté, avec quelques semaines de marge.

Où en sont les transporteurs. Vingt-quatre sur vingt-six utilisent la version 2. Les deux derniers sont ceux qui livrent leurs intégrations chaque trimestre. Leur prochaine version sort en septembre, et tous deux ont confirmé qu'elle passera à la version 2.

Ce qui se passe à la date d'arrêt. Les appels en version 1 reçoivent une erreur claire, avec un lien vers le guide de migration, au lieu d'une réponse. Les webhooks au format version 1 ne sont plus envoyés. Le code de correspondance entre les deux versions disparaît dans la semaine qui suit, soit environ quatre mille lignes.

Avant l'arrêt, deux vérifications. Un mois avant, on regarde les journaux pour repérer tout appel en version 1 venant d'un partenaire qu'on croyait migré. Une semaine avant, on envoie un rappel à chaque contact technique, même à ceux qui ont migré. Certains outils internes des transporteurs restent parfois sur l'ancienne version sans que leur équipe le sache.

Le calendrier et les compteurs d'appels par version sont dans quarry.versions.sunset.schedule. L'équipe partenaires suit le sujet jusqu'à l'arrêt.
context: Décision d'arrêt de la version 1 ; la date tient compte des deux transporteurs à livraison trimestrielle et des vérifications de journaux prévues.

title: REVIEW: thirty-seven fee differences from parity run, one real bug
content:
Review of the 37 differences reported by the fee parity run in {{ref:mem-075}}, held on 2026-06-04 with finance. All were on merchants with hand-negotiated fee schedules, as the status said. They fell into three groups.

Thirty-one were rounding. The old engine rounded each fee component, then summed; the new one sums, then rounds once. Finance confirmed the new behaviour matches the contracts, which say the fee is computed on the total. These are not bugs in the new engine. They were bugs in the old one, worth at most two cents per transaction.

Five came from schedules entered twice in the negotiated settings with different values, where the old engine picked the first and the new one the last. The fees team cleaned the file. Each merchant now has exactly one schedule, and the loader rejects duplicates.

One was a real bug in the new engine. A monthly minimum fee was applied per transaction instead. It only affected one merchant, whose contract has that clause. Fixed, with a test using that contract's numbers.

Verdict. The new engine is right in thirty-six of thirty-seven cases, and the last one is fixed. The parity run continues until one full month-end is clean. The setting that switches engines is ledger.fees.engine.active, and the cutover rehearsal has already run on staging.
context: Review of parity differences before the fee engine cutover. Most differences turned out to be old engine bugs, which is common in parity runs and worth expecting: the comparison tells you where the engines differ, not which one is right. Finance had to decide that for each group.

title: Finance digest after three Mondays: fewer messages, two findings missed
content: Three weeks into the weekly digest from {{ref:mem-182}}, status on 2026-06-22. Finance now reads one message on Mondays instead of about forty small ones per week, and they like it. Two findings were missed, though. Both were medium findings that grew during the week. One was a fee difference on a merchant that rose from five to ninety euros by Friday, still below the high threshold of one hundred. Finance would have acted on Wednesday had they seen it. The digest needs a rule for findings that grow, not only for their size on the day they appear. The checks owner is drafting one.
context: Status on the finance digest. The missed growing findings are the open issue; the volume reduction itself is a clear win and nobody wants to go back. Expect a change to the severity rules rather than to the digest.

title: DECISION: alias cache follows catalog versions, fixed one-day fallback dropped
content: HXB-356 replaces the 24-hour fallback described in {{ref:mem-091}}. Since 2026-06-23, each alias carries a version from the catalog. During an outage, a cached alias is used only if no newer version was announced, and jobs that write outside helix wait instead. The cache rule lives in helix.catalog.cache.policy. The migrated replicas are shut down, so a stale lookup now fails loudly.
context: Supersedes the fixed-fallback alias decision after the resolver review.

title: GOTCHA: aborted console requests counted as partner errors
content:
After the router fix in {{ref:mem-166}}, the console aborts loaders when a navigation is superseded. Good for the console. On the partner API side, QRY-392 found an odd effect on 2026-06-24. The error rate for the internal client jumped from almost nothing to three percent, and the partner health rule flagged it as a partner problem.

What the numbers meant. An aborted request closes the connection before the response is sent. Our server logged those as client errors, the same category as a malformed request. Nothing was broken. Operators were just clicking quickly between tabs.

Why it mattered. The health rule compares each client's error rate with the median. The internal client looked five times worse than any carrier, and partner success received a ticket about a partner that does not exist. Worse, the same mistake could hide a real problem. A carrier with a flaky network also produces closed connections, and we would read them as their bugs.

Fix. Closed connections get their own category in logs and metrics, separate from client errors. The health rule ignores them unless they exceed a third of all requests. The internal client is excluded from partner health altogether. The categories are configured in quarry.metrics.status.categories.
context: Partner API gotcha triggered by a console change. Aborted requests are not errors, and counting them as errors sends partner success after a ghost. The separate category also helps with carriers on poor networks.

title: CONFIG: console polling intervals per screen, and why payout queue polls faster than everything else
content: Polling intervals for console screens, reviewed on 2026-06-25. Most screens do not poll at all; they load on navigation and after a mutation. Five screens poll because their data changes without the operator doing anything. The payout queue polls every ten seconds during payout slots and every minute otherwise, because operators place holds against it in real time. The approval queue polls every thirty seconds, so a second operator sees a large refund soon after it is submitted. The incident banner polls every two minutes. The carrier map and the audit feed poll every five minutes. Polling stops when the browser tab is hidden and restarts at once when it becomes visible again. A screen that wants to poll needs a short reason in this note and a reviewer from the BFF team. Every interval multiplies load across all operators.
context: Reference for polling intervals. The BFF team asked for it after the load on the partner endpoints doubled one week, which turned out to be a new screen polling every second. Each interval here has a reason, and adding one should come with a reason too. Hidden tabs never poll.

title: Reporting backfill froze analytics dashboards, runner now watches both replicas
content: This supersedes the adoption status in {{ref:mem-114}}, whose open question about the analytics replica was answered the hard way. On 2026-06-26 the reporting team ran its first ported backfill. Lag on the reporting replica stayed low, as designed. But the analytics replica fell forty minutes behind and froze every dashboard. MER-621 makes ThrottledBackfill watch every replica listed in ledger.ops.replicas, and the slowest one sets the pace.
context: Incident that closed the open decision from the adoption status; every replica now counts for throttling.

title: Webhook timing settings: replay window, skew warning and new grace for slow clocks
content:
QRY-409 replaces the clock skew gotcha in {{ref:mem-127}} with a proper configuration. The gotcha said the window would never move. For verification, it still does not. What changed is everything around it.

Settings, all under quarry.webhooks.timing in /deploy/quarry/webhook-timing.yaml:

The replay window stays at five minutes. Partners must reject older events; the guide is unchanged.

The skew warning threshold drops from one minute to thirty seconds. Northbay's drift started small and grew for weeks before anyone noticed. A lower threshold flags it earlier.

New: a resend on skew. When a partner rejects a delivery as stale and their Date header shows more than two minutes of skew, the event is re-signed with a fresh timestamp and sent again once. Partners with a slow clock then receive the event late instead of never. SkewResender handles it and logs each resend, and partner success sees the count weekly.

New: the certification check for slow clocks runs every month, not just at onboarding. Clocks drift long after go-live.

What we did not do: widen the window per partner. That idea came up again and was rejected again, for the same reason as before.
context: Supersedes the clock skew gotcha; the window stays, the tooling around it grows.

title: Invoice downloads failed again for one carrier after gateway fix, this time because of range requests
content:
One week after the compression fix in {{ref:mem-190}}, Kestrel Freight reported failed invoice downloads again. Only their nightly batch tool failed; manual downloads from their portal worked. The checksum header was right. The bytes were not.

Their tool downloads large files in ranges, several parts in parallel, then joins them. Our file endpoint ignored range headers and returned the full file for every part. Their tool stitched four full copies together and computed a checksum over the result. Of course it failed.

Why it worked before. Before the compression fix, the gateway handled range requests itself, on the compressed copy it cached. Excluding downloads from compression also took them out of that cache path. Requests then reached our endpoint, which never supported ranges.

The fix. The endpoint now answers range requests properly, with partial content and the right headers. When a client asks for a range on a file we cannot serve in parts, it answers with the whole file and says so, so the client knows not to stitch. The behaviour is configured in /deploy/quarry/files/range-policy.yaml, and the allowed range size in quarry.files.range.max_bytes. A contract test downloads a file in four parallel parts and compares the checksum.

Still open: whether to keep supporting ranges at all, or tell carriers to download whole files. Ranges help two carriers with poor links. A decision will follow.
context: Follow-up incident to the gateway compression fix. It shows how one fix moved traffic onto a path nobody had tested with that client. The open question on supporting ranges at all will be settled in a separate decision, and that decision should replace this note. Until then, range support stays on and the contract test guards it.

title: Partner API timeout settings, from gateway to database, and the order they must keep
content:
Timeouts on the partner API path, set under QRY-423. They must shrink from the outside in, or a slow call keeps resources busy after the caller has given up.
- gateway: 30 seconds, the limit partners see
- application request timeout: 25 seconds, so we answer before the gateway cuts
- database statement timeout: 20 seconds, set per connection by ConnectionTuner
- outbound calls to the ledger: 15 seconds, with one retry for reads only
Values live in /deploy/quarry/timeouts.yaml under quarry.timeouts.chain. A startup check refuses to boot if an inner value is larger than an outer one. Long exports never go through this path; they use the asynchronous file endpoint. If a partner asks for a longer timeout, the answer is the file endpoint, not a bigger number. The request_timeout_seconds key is the one people try to change first.
context: Reference for the timeout chain. Written after a partner asked for a sixty-second gateway timeout and someone almost raised only that one, which would have left the database working long after the partner had given up. The startup check makes the order hard to break.

title: PATTERN: rates stored as basis points
content:
Every rate in helix is stored as an integer number of basis points, never as a float. A surcharge of 4.75 percent is stored as 475. This was the habit before. Since the review of the fuel surcharge job in {{ref:mem-116}}, it is the rule, written down on 2026-06-29.

Why. Floats cannot represent most decimal rates exactly. Multiply a float rate by a large amount and sum over thousands of invoices, and the total drifts by a few cents. Finance notices cents. Carriers notice them faster.

How it looks in practice. Rate columns end in a basis point suffix, so surcharge_rate became surcharge_bp. The value is an integer. Applying a rate means multiplying the amount in minor units by the basis points and dividing by ten thousand, with one rounding step at the end, half to even. The shared function apply_rate_bp does exactly that and nothing else. Every job uses it.

Inputs that arrive as decimal text, such as the fuel index or a contract rate, are parsed straight into basis points without passing through a float. The parser rejects anything finer than a hundredth of a percent, because a basis point is the finest unit any contract uses.

Checks. A schema check fails any job whose output has a float column with rate in its name. The test suite keeps the three historical cases where floats produced a one-cent error, as regression tests.

On Windows desks, finance can check a rate conversion with the helper at D:\finance\tools\rates\bp-check.py, which prints the basis points for a typed percentage. They asked for it after the first invoice in the new format, where a rate of 475 looked alarming.
context: Pattern for every rate in helix; the one-cent regressions in the test suite are the reason it is not optional.

title: CONFIG: finance digest and severity settings, including growth rule
content:
These settings replace the digest pattern in {{ref:mem-182}}. The weekly digest stays, but severity is no longer fixed on the day a finding appears. The missed findings in the first weeks showed why.

Where things live. Everything sits under ledger.checks.severity and is read at each check run, so finance can change values from the settings screen without a deploy.

Base thresholds. A finding is low below ten euros, medium from ten to one hundred, and high above one hundred or when more than ten accounts are affected at once. Unchanged.

Growth rule, new. A finding is re-evaluated every night. If its amount has doubled since it was first seen, it moves up one level, whatever its absolute size. The growth_factor key holds the doubling factor. The growth_min_eur key stops tiny amounts from escalating: a finding must be at least five euros to escalate on growth alone. A medium finding that becomes high on growth posts at once to the finance channel, like any high finding.

Age rule, new. A medium finding open for more than ten days moves to high, because an old unexplained difference is a risk in itself. The age_days key holds the limit.

Digest content. The Monday digest now shows, for each finding, its first amount, its current amount and its level history. Finance asked for the history so they can see why something escalated.

The checks owner ran the new rules on the last two months of findings. Both missed findings would have escalated on Wednesday, two days before finance found them by hand.
context: Supersedes the digest pattern; severity now follows growth and age, not only size.

title: PATTERN: checksum failures on exports raise one alert per file, routed to the data channel
content:
Since 2026-06-30, under SGW-497, a failed checksum check on any helix export raises an alert, whether the check ran in the analytics loader or in the finance script from {{ref:mem-185}}. The finance script now reports its result to a small endpoint, so a failure on a finance laptop is no longer invisible.
- one alert per file, not per attempt; retries update the same alert
- routed to the data channel during the day, and paged only for files that feed invoices
- the alert carries the file name, both hashes and where the check ran
ChecksumAlertRule lives in sigwatch.rules.exports. The first week brought two alerts, both from a flaky office connection, both resolved by a second download.
context: Monitoring pattern for export checksums; finance laptops now report like servers do.

title: DECISION: console tables get server-side sorting
content:
Decided on 2026-07-01 by the console team. Every table that can hold more than one page of rows sorts and filters on the server. Client-side sorting stays only for small, complete lists such as currencies or regions.

The problem it solves. Several tables loaded the first page, then let operators sort it in the browser. An operator who sorted payouts by amount saw the largest payout of the first hundred rows and assumed it was the largest overall. Twice this quarter, an operator missed a large held payout because it sat on page four. Nobody had lied to them, but the screen did not say what it was sorting.

What changes. DataTable sends the sort column and direction to the API with each page request. The API sorts on indexed columns only. A table cannot offer a sort on a column without an index, and the BFF rejects it. Filters work the same way. The sort state appears in the address, so a link to a sorted table opens sorted.

What it costs. Each sort is a new request, so a sort click takes a few hundred milliseconds instead of being instant. Operators noticed and did not mind once we explained why. The ledger team added three indexes for the sorts operators use most, after checking their size with the DBA.

What stays client-side. Lists below two hundred rows that are always loaded whole. The table component decides from the response: if the API says the list is complete, sorting happens locally. A flag called is_complete in each list response carries that information, so no screen has to guess.

The two incidents with missed payouts are why this was not left to each screen.
context: Decision on table sorting. The real issue was operators believing a sort covered all rows when it covered one page; server-side sorting makes the screen honest, and the completeness flag keeps small lists fast. Index costs were checked with the ledger team.

title: DECISION: merchant payout holds expire after thirty days unless an approver renews them
content:
Decided on 2026-07-02 with finance and risk. A payout hold now expires after thirty days unless an approver renews it. Before, holds lasted forever. The month-end review found holds placed two years ago by people who had since left, on payouts nobody remembered.

At expiry, the hold does not release the payout by itself. It moves to a review queue, and an approver either renews it, with a reason, or releases it. Doing nothing is not an option the screen offers.

The thirty days come from the longest dispute window in our merchant contracts. Renewals have no limit, but each one needs a new reason. The settings sit in ledger.payouts.holds.expiry, with the period in expiry_days. A nightly job moves expired holds to the queue and sends one summary to the approvers. The first run moved 214 holds; 190 were released after review.
context: Decision on hold lifetime. The point is that every hold has a person behind it at all times; the thirty days are a contract number, not a technical one.

title: REVIEW: ledger API error handling, three places where a failure looked like success
content:
Error-handling notes across the ledger API from 2026-07-03. Most of it is fine. Three places return success when something failed, and those matter more than any style issue.

One. The bulk hold endpoint accepts a list of payouts and places a hold on each. If one payout is already sent, it skips it silently and returns success for the batch. The operator believes all holds are in place. It must return the payouts it could not hold, and the console must show them.

Two. The refund endpoint retries the payment provider on a timeout. If the second attempt also times out, it returns pending, which the console shows as accepted. Pending is right. But the console needs a distinct state for refunds whose outcome is unknown, with a later check.

Three. The statement export swallows a failed upload to the archive bucket and returns the file to the caller anyway. The caller is happy; the archive has a gap that auditors will find. It must fail the request, or at least raise an alert.

The rest was minor. Error bodies in two endpoints do not follow the shared shape, and one log statement prints a full account number. Fixes are tracked under ledger.api.errors.review. The API owners will pair with the payments team on the first two, since the console must change too.
context: Review of ledger API failures that report success.

title: DECISION: helix scratch tables expire after sixty days
content: From 2026-07-06 the scratch expiry drops from ninety to sixty days. Ninety days kept too many forgotten tables, and storage crept back up by half a terabyte. Tables that need longer must move to a named schema with an owner. The keep_list file still works for exceptions, but each entry now needs an expiry_date. A storage owner announced the change two weeks ahead.
context: Small housekeeping decision; shortens the scratch rule set in the spring cleanup.

title: PATTERN: upgrade rehearsals restore production-sized copies first
content:
Every database upgrade on the ledger is rehearsed on a full-size copy of production before it is scheduled. MER-624 made it a rule on 2026-07-07, after the collation surprise in {{ref:mem-124}} showed what a small copy hides.

Why full size. A small copy runs every step in minutes, so nothing looks slow and nothing looks broken. The collation issue only surfaced on tables with millions of text values. Index rebuild times, vacuum after upgrade and replica catch-up all scale with size. Those are the numbers finance needs for the maintenance window.

How. The copy is restored from the latest backup into an isolated environment with no network path to production or to partners. Access is limited to the upgrade team, because the copy holds real data. UpgradeRehearsal, a script in ledger.ops.rehearsal, runs the upgrade, the index checks and the parity checks in order, and records the time of each step. It also runs the application test suite against the upgraded copy.

What the rehearsal must produce. The duration of each step, so the maintenance window is a measurement and not a guess. The warnings from the upgrade tool. The result of the index check on every text index. And a go or no-go signed by the person who will run the real upgrade.
