After the rehearsal, the copy is destroyed within two days. A production copy kept around invites people to use it for testing, which the privacy rules forbid.

The next upgrade, a minor version in the autumn, will be the first to follow this pattern. The DBA expects the rehearsal to take one day.
context: Pattern for every ledger database upgrade. Small rehearsals passed while hiding the collation risk and gave finance a maintenance window that was a guess. The privacy constraint on production copies is the reason the copy is isolated and destroyed quickly.

title: GOTCHA: pytest froze the clock globally, so payout slot tests passed while slot code used real time
content:
The slot scheduler tests passed for months while one slot boundary was wrong in production. A test owner found it on 2026-07-08. The tests froze time with a fixture, but the scheduler read the time through a helper imported before the fixture applied. Under the four-worker setup, import order differed per worker. On some workers the helper saw the frozen clock; on others it saw the real one. Tests passed on all of them, because the assertions only checked that a slot existed, not which one.

Fix. The scheduler receives a clock object instead of calling a helper, and tests pass a fake one. SlotClock is the interface, and the real implementation is the only place that reads system time. The fixture that patched time globally was removed from /services/ledger/tests/conftest.py. Assertions now name the expected slot.

The production bug was small: the 13:30 slot started at 13:00 for one region after the four-slot change. No payout left early, because holds and approvals still applied. A test per region now checks the slot_start value.
context: Testing gotcha with a small production effect. Global time patching interacts badly with import order and parallel workers, and assertions that only check presence will pass anything. Injecting a clock is the general fix, and it makes the scheduler easier to reason about too. The region test was added because the four-slot change touched each region's config separately and nobody checked the result per region.

title: REVIEW: console network usage per screen, measured during busy payout slot
content:
Console network traffic during the 11:00 payout slot was measured, with twelve operators working, to check the polling note in {{ref:mem-199}} against reality. The note held up for most screens. Three findings.

First, the payout queue polls every ten seconds during slots, as intended. But it fetches the whole queue each time, about four hundred rows with details, even when nothing changed. With twelve operators, that is close to five megabytes a minute for one screen. The API should answer with a change marker, and the console should fetch rows only when the marker moved.

Second, the approval queue kept polling in hidden tabs on one browser. The visibility check used an event that this browser fires late when a tab moves to another window rather than behind one. Operators often keep the console in a second window. The fix is to check visibility before each poll instead of relying on the event alone.

Third, the incident banner polls every two minutes from every screen, so an operator with five console tabs polls five times. A shared worker could poll once per browser and broadcast the result to tabs. That is a bigger change, worth it only if operators keep many tabs open. It turns out they do: the median is four.

What did not show up: any screen polling faster than documented, or polling without a reason in the note.

The measurement script sits in /web/tools/network-profile.ts so anyone can repeat it. Results per screen are summarised under console.perf.network.profile with the date of each run, so the next measurement can be compared with this one. The payout queue fix comes first, since it is most of the traffic.
context: Measurement-based review of console polling. The payout queue is most of the traffic, and the hidden-tab bug shows that a documented rule can still fail in one browser. The shared worker idea waits until the cheaper fixes are in.

title: DECISION: dépôt manuel SEPA réservé à l'astreinte, la finance ne dépose plus elle-même
content: Cette décision remplace le point {{ref:mem-164}}. Depuis le 2026-07-09, seul l'ingénieur d'astreinte peut déposer un fichier à la main, après accord écrit de la finance. Le rôle manual_upload est retiré aux comptes de la finance. Avant, six personnes pouvaient déposer ; c'était trop.
context: Remplace l'état précédent sur le dépôt manuel ; la décision réduit le nombre de personnes autorisées.

title: Partner API gateway connection limits per carrier, measured each night so limits follow real usage instead of guesses
content: Every night, the gateway reports the highest number of open connections each carrier reached that day. A weekly job compares it with the carrier's limit. A carrier that stays below a quarter of its limit for a month gets a lower limit, announced one week ahead. A carrier that reaches its limit three days in a week gets flagged for partner success. They ask what changed before anyone raises anything. Limits now move with usage.
context: Pattern that keeps gateway limits close to real usage, so peak season raises start from a known baseline.

title: GOTCHA: partitioned postings table rejected rows dated in a month with no partition yet
content: On 2026-07-01 at 00:00 UTC, postings failed for four minutes. The postings table is partitioned by month. The job that creates next month's partition was scheduled for the first day of the month itself, at 02:00 Paris time, which is midnight UTC in summer: the exact moment the first rows arrived. It lost the race. MER-640 creates partitions three months ahead, and ledger.db.partitions.lookahead sets the number. A check alerts when fewer than two future partitions exist.
context: Gotcha with a four-minute outage on postings. Creating partitions just in time is a race; creating them months ahead costs nothing.

title: INCIDENT: payout notifications to merchants signed with test key
content: On 2026-07-10, payout notifications to merchants went out signed with the sandbox key for two hours. The ledger reused the partner signing approach from {{ref:mem-014}}, but NotifierConfig fell back to the sandbox key when the production one failed to load. The fallback is gone.
context: Short incident; merchants verifying signatures rejected the notifications, as they should.

title: DECISION: new fee engine becomes the only engine after clean month-end
content:
This decision closes the review of parity differences in {{ref:mem-195}}. The month-end parity run finished with zero differences, after the fix for the monthly minimum fee. The new engine became the only engine on Monday morning.

What happened at the switch. The engine_active setting was flipped at 06:00, before the first payout slot. FeeShadowRunner kept running the old engine in shadow for one more week, now as a safety net in the other direction. It found nothing.

What goes away. The old engine code is deleted next week. The negotiated schedule file, cleaned during the review, stays as the single source for hand-made fee schedules. The shadow comparison is switched off at the end of the safety week, and its table is archived for the auditors.

What finance gets. A one-page summary of the migration: the thirty-seven differences, their causes, and the money involved, below forty euros in total across all merchants. Finance asked for that number for their own audit file.

Rollback. Until the old code is deleted, switching back takes one setting and forty seconds, as rehearsed. After deletion, a rollback would mean deploying an old release. We accept that.
context: Closes the fee engine migration. The review of differences is superseded; rollback stays cheap only until the old code is deleted.

title: GOTCHA: refunds split into smaller ones to dodge approval limit
content:
Replaces the threshold rule in {{ref:mem-163}}. DLK-553 found refunds split to stay under five thousand euros. Now:
- the limit applies to the sum per invoice over seven days
- splits are flagged to the support lead
Rule file: D:\dev\drift-console\config\refund-limits.json.
context: Gotcha found by finance during a monthly review: three operators had split large refunds into several smaller ones, each just under the limit, to avoid waiting for a second approver. Nobody acted in bad faith; they were trying to help merchants faster. The cumulative rule removes the incentive, and support leads now talk to operators whose refunds get flagged, rather than treating it as misconduct.

title: INCIDENT: partner listing latency alert fired for every page request after token change
content:
On 2026-07-11 the partner latency alert paged the on-call at 09:12 and kept paging every few minutes until noon. The partner API was healthy. The alert was not.

Background. The listing endpoints moved to page tokens, as described in {{ref:mem-118}}. A token encodes the sort key and the last id, and it is opaque by design. Our latency rule grouped requests by their full path including the query string, to tell listing pages apart from single-item calls. Every page request now carried a different token, so every request became its own group. The rule computes a 95th percentile per group, and a group with one request has a percentile equal to that request. Any single slow page, normal for a large listing, crossed the threshold on its own.

What made it worse. The rule had a minimum request count per group, meant to prevent exactly this. It had been set for the old grouping and nobody had looked at it since. The value was one.

Timeline. At 09:12 the first page fired. At 09:40 the on-call rotation silenced the rule after seeing that no partner was complaining. At 10:05 she found that the group count for the rule had gone from about forty to several thousand overnight. At 11:50 a fixed rule was deployed and the silence removed.

The fix. Requests are grouped by route template, not by the full path, so all pages of one listing fall in one group. The minimum count is twenty requests per group per window, and the rule file at /ops/sigwatch/rules/partner-latency.yaml explains why in a comment. A second rule watches the number of groups itself. If it jumps more than tenfold in a day, someone changed the shape of requests and the alert rules need a look. The group_count metric feeds it, under sigwatch.metrics.cardinality.

Lessons. An alert rule that groups by raw request data is a hidden contract with every endpoint's URL design. When an endpoint changes its parameters, the rules that read them get reviewed in the same change.
context: Monitoring incident caused by an API change in the partner team. No partner was affected; the on-call lost a morning. The cardinality rule is the lasting guard.

title: STATUS: fee engine cutover dry run on staging, trois leçons pour les prochaines bascules
content:
Bilan de la répétition du 2026-06-14, utile au-delà du moteur de frais. Trois leçons pour toute bascule future :
- répéter avec le vrai volume d'une nuit, pas un échantillon ; le temps de bascule n'a de sens qu'à pleine charge
- mesurer le retour arrière autant que l'aller, car c'est le chiffre que la finance demande en premier
- garder l'ancien système en ombre après la bascule, pour vérifier dans l'autre sens
Le script CutoverDrill enchaîne ces étapes et note la durée de chacune. Avant chaque bascule, il faut donc le lancer en recette avec un volume réel. Importance faible : ce sont des conseils, pas une règle.
context: Leçons tirées de la répétition de bascule du moteur de frais, pour les prochaines migrations.

title: Ledger outgoing notifications signed like webhooks
content:
After the sandbox key slipped into payout notifications, MER-654 aligned the ledger with the partner webhook signing described in {{ref:mem-191}}. Merchant notifications now use the same scheme. Our private key signs, merchants verify with the published public key, and two keys are always published for rotation.

What the ledger reuses. The signing library from the partner team, unchanged, packaged as a shared module. The published key address, so merchants and carriers fetch keys from one place. The five-minute replay window, and the rule that signed bodies are never logged.

What is specific to the ledger. Notifications are produced by the outbox relay, not by request handlers, so signing happens in the relay just before sending. NotificationSigner in ledger.notify.signing loads the key once at startup and refuses to start if it cannot. There is no fallback key of any kind. A relay that cannot sign does not send, and the backlog waits in the outbox until the key loads.

Key separation. The ledger has its own key pair, separate from the partner API's. A leak in one service then does not let anyone forge messages from the other. Both pairs are listed at the published address with a key_owner field, so verifiers can tell them apart.

Testing. Each environment has its own pair. The sandbox key cannot sign in production because production does not have it: the deploy pipeline only mounts the production key there. A startup check compares the key fingerprint with the one expected for the environment.

Merchants were told a month ahead. Most already use a library that verifies both partner and merchant messages.
context: Pattern for signing everything the ledger sends to merchants; no fallback key, by design. Importance high because a forged payout notice is a fraud vector.

title: Copy button pasted amounts with thin spaces
content: Operators copy amounts from the console into spreadsheets and bank portals. The French format uses a narrow no-break space as thousands separator, and the copy button kept it. Bank portals rejected the pasted value, and one spreadsheet read 12 500 as text. The copy button now copies the raw decimal value, without separators, through CopyAmount. The displayed format is unchanged. The setting console.copy.amount.raw is on by default.
context: High importance because one operator pasted a wrong amount into a bank portal after the spreadsheet dropped the thousands. Caught before submission.

title: Skew resends doubled webhooks for one carrier pool
content: On 2026-07-14 Northbay received some webhooks twice. The resend on skew from {{ref:mem-201}} worked as designed for their slow servers. But their fast servers had already accepted the first delivery and answered late, and our side read the late answer as a rejection. SkewResender then sent a re-signed copy with a new timestamp. Their deduplication used the timestamp, not the event id, so they processed both. Resends are paused for Northbay until their handler deduplicates on the event id.
context: Incident on the skew resend feature. Partners who deduplicate on timestamps instead of event ids receive duplicates.

title: Prochaine mise à jour mineure de Postgres planifiée pour octobre, sans arrêt des virements
content: Décidé le 2026-07-15 : la mise à jour mineure du grand livre aura lieu un dimanche d'octobre. Contrairement à la mise à jour majeure ({{ref:mem-003}}), elle ne demande qu'un redémarrage par nœud, donc les virements ne s'arrêtent pas. La répétition complète reste obligatoire. Le calendrier est dans ledger.ops.upgrade.calendar.
context: Planification de la prochaine mise à jour ; la répétition sur copie complète s'applique quand même.

title: PATTERN: large-table changes run as expand and contract over several releases, online tool kept only for type changes
content:
This pattern supersedes the blanket rule in {{ref:mem-183}}. Sending every change on a large table through the online migration tool turned out heavy. Three migrations in, each took a day, doubled disk use and needed someone watching. Most of them did not need it.

The pattern now is expand and contract. A change to a large table is split across releases. First, expand: add the new column or table, nullable, without touching existing rows. Then the application writes to both old and new. Then a throttled backfill fills the new column for old rows. Then the application reads from the new one. Finally, contract: drop the old column in a later release, once nothing reads it.

Each step is small and reversible. None of them rewrites the table, so none needs the online tool. The cost is time: a rename that used to be one migration now spans three releases.

When the online tool is still required. Changing the type of an existing column, which rewrites every row. Adding a constraint that must be validated against all rows at once. Those two cases go through OnlineMigration, as before.

The migration lint knows the difference. It rejects type changes and validated constraints on listed tables unless they use the tool, and lets additive changes through. On laptops the list of large tables is D:\dev\apex-ledger\config\large-tables.toml, same content as the server copy, read under ledger.db.large.tables.

The events owner checked the last six large-table changes against the new pattern. Five would have been expand and contract with no tool at all. One, a type change on the amount column of the fee table, would still have needed it.
context: Supersedes the blanket online migration rule; expand and contract covers most changes.

title: GOTCHA: la double écriture pendant expand and contract oubliait les écritures d'ajustement, donc la nouvelle colonne restait vide pour elles
content: Pendant le renommage de la colonne de référence, MER-658, la double écriture couvrait les écritures normales mais pas les écritures d'ajustement, qui passent par un autre chemin. Après le remplissage du 2026-07-16, 312 enregistrements restaient vides. Correctif : la double écriture se fait dans ledger.postings.write_reference, appelé par les deux chemins, et le contrôle /services/ledger/checks/dual-write.py compte les valeurs vides avant la bascule de lecture.
context: Piège de la première migration en expand and contract ; le contrôle des valeurs vides est maintenant obligatoire avant de lire la nouvelle colonne.

title: Merchant notification key rotation calendar and the steps ledger team follows
content: Key rotation for merchant notifications, set under MER-674 on 2026-07-17. The ledger rotates its signing key every six months, on the first Tuesday of January and July. The principle comes from the partner review in {{ref:mem-014}}: two keys published, a grace period, no downtime. The steps are written as sentences, because people skim lists during an incident. One month before, the next public key is published next to the current one. On rotation day, the relay restarts with the new private key, in the morning, outside payout slots. The old public key stays published for thirty days. On day thirty-one it is removed, and the old private key is destroyed with two people present. If a key leaks, the same steps run in one day instead of a month, and merchants get a direct message.
context: Rotation calendar for the ledger's notification key; emergency rotation follows the same steps.

title: Skew resends doubled webhooks for one carrier pool, sandbox scenario added before re-enabling
content:
After the duplicate webhooks at Northbay, QRY-434 adds a sandbox scenario so carriers can test their deduplication before resends are enabled for them. It sits next to the weekly reset seeding from {{ref:mem-173}} and survives every reset.

Scenario settings, under quarry.sandbox.scenarios.resend:
- sends the same event twice, ten seconds apart, with the same event id and different timestamps
- sends one event with a timestamp four minutes old, which must be accepted
- sends one event six minutes old, which must be rejected
- reports per carrier which of the three behaved correctly

Resends on skew are enabled per carrier only after the scenario passes. ResendEligibility reads the result and switches the feature on. Carriers who fail get a short explanation and a link to the deduplication section of the guide. Of twenty-six carriers, nineteen passed on the first run. Northbay passed on the second, after changing their handler.
context: Config for the resend sandbox scenario. It turns the Northbay lesson into a test every carrier can run, and it gates the resend feature per carrier, so a carrier that deduplicates on timestamps never receives a resend in production. The scenario survives weekly resets on purpose.

title: DECISION: no currencies with more than three decimals
content:
A carrier in the Gulf asked whether we could settle in a currency with eight decimal places, a digital token their bank started offering. The answer is no. This note records why, so the question does not need a meeting next time.

The exponent table in {{ref:mem-013}} handles any exponent in principle. In practice, the rest of the system assumes at most three decimals. Amounts are stored as 64-bit integers in minor units. With eight decimals, the largest storable amount shrinks to about ninety billion units of the token, which sounds large until you remember that some of these tokens are worth a fraction of a cent. Fee calculations in basis points then produce values below one minor unit that have to be rounded, and the rounding rules in our contracts do not cover that.

The banks we work with do not settle such tokens through the payment schemes we use. Supporting one would mean a new bank integration, new compliance work and a new reconciliation process. For one carrier.

So the ledger supports currencies with zero, two or three decimals, which covers every currency our banks settle today. CurrencyPolicy in ledger.money.policy rejects any other exponent at startup, next to the existing check that refuses to change an exponent in place.

Finance and compliance agreed. If several large carriers ask, the topic comes back as a product question with a business case, not as an engineering change.
context: Decision on currency support limits; written down so the next request gets the same answer with the same reasons.

title: REVIEW: console fee display after engine switch
content:
Fee display notes now that the new engine is the only one, under DLK-569 on 2026-07-18. The shadow comparison reviewed in {{ref:mem-181}} proved the numbers right; this review checked that the screens say the same thing.

Findings. The payout detail screen still showed an entry called legacy fee for every payout, with a zero amount. It came from the old response shape, which the BFF kept filling in. Harmless, but operators asked what it meant. It goes.

The fee breakdown tooltip listed components in the order the old engine computed them. The new engine sums first and rounds once, so rounded components that do not add up to the total confused finance. The tooltip now shows unrounded components, with a note that the total is rounded once.

The merchant statement preview used a separate formatter with two decimals hard-coded. For three-decimal currencies, that cut the last digit. It now uses the shared money formatter.

The field fee_engine_version still shows in the support view. It is useful for a few more weeks and can go after that.

All three fixes are small. The formatter one ships first because it shows wrong figures. Changes are in /web/src/fees/fee-breakdown.ts, with settings in console.fees.display.
context: Console review after the fee engine cutover; the hard-coded two decimals are the one real bug, the rest is leftover display from the old engine.

title: INCIDENT: console logged every operator out at once after session signing key change
content:
At 14:20 on a Thursday every console operator was logged out at once, mid-shift. DLK-573 traced it to a rotation of the session signing key: the BFF switched to the new key immediately instead of accepting both keys during a grace period. Every existing session failed verification.
Impact:
- about sixty operators signed in again within ten minutes
- two half-filled refunds were restored from local drafts
- one payout hold was placed late, after a slot had started
Fix: SessionKeyRing accepts the previous key for eight hours, the longest operator session, and the rotation script in /ops/console/rotate-session-key.py checks the grace setting first. The value sits in console.session.key_grace_hours.
context: Short console incident; the same two-key rule as webhooks, applied to sessions.

title: GOTCHA: settlement window ended at 23:59:59.999
content:
The UTC fix after the January close, {{ref:mem-015}}, made the settlement window correct in time zone. On 2026-07-20 we found a second problem in the same code. SettlementWindow defined the end of a day as 23:59:59.999. Postings timestamped in the last millisecond, rare but not impossible at month-end volumes, fell outside every window. Over the last year, nine postings did. They were not lost. The reconciliation check picked them up the next day as unexplained differences, and finance matched them by hand each time without telling us.

The fix uses half-open intervals. A window starts at midnight and ends before the next midnight: start inclusive, end exclusive. No more invented last instant. The comparison code never uses less-than-or-equal on an end time any more, and a lint rule catches it in the settlement module.

Why the bug survived so long. The tests used round timestamps, never one in the last millisecond. Finance absorbed the nine cases as normal noise. And the code looked careful: someone had clearly thought about precision when writing three nines.

The test suite now includes postings at the first and last representable instant of a day, and at exactly midnight. The fix lives in /services/ledger/settlement/window.py. Finance received the list of nine historical cases, all already matched.
context: Second settlement window bug after the UTC fix; half-open intervals are the rule now.

title: STATUS: helix pre-aggregated carrier map tiles, console map screen now loads from one daily file
content: HXB-365 status on 2026-07-21. The console carrier map was one of the two heavy screens in {{ref:mem-145}}, because it loaded every shipment of the day and grouped them in the browser. Helix now builds the grouped data overnight. TileBuilder produces one compact file per day with shipment counts per area and carrier, and the console reads that file instead of raw shipments. The file is about 300 kB, against 6 MB before. Live updates during the day still come from the API, but only for shipments created since the file was built, through the created_after filter. Two carriers asked whether they could get the same file. Not yet, because it was built for internal use. Next: the audit table, the other heavy screen.
context: Status on the carrier map aggregation for the console.

title: Relevés marchands : la jointure sur les écritures inverses faisait doubler les frais
content: Cette note remplace la note provisoire {{ref:mem-155}}. La revue du modèle de relevé, MER-678, a confirmé la cause : la jointure prenait chaque frais et son écriture inverse. Avant la correction, aucun test ne couvrait un marchand avec une correction de frais. Le modèle de relevé n'affiche plus que les frais nets. Les relevés de test sont générés sur les postes avec D:\dev\apex-ledger\tools\statement-preview.py, à lancer avant chaque modification du modèle.
context: Note définitive sur l'incident des relevés ; remplace la note écrite le matin même.

title: Idempotency keys required on every money-moving endpoint, not only refunds
content:
Decided on 2026-07-22 by the ledger team. Every endpoint that moves money or changes a hold now requires an idempotency key, the same way refunds have since the review in {{ref:mem-022}}. That covers payouts released by hand, fee overrides, hold placement and release, adjustment postings, and refunds as before.

Why now. The bulk hold endpoint review showed a retry path that could place a hold twice and release it once, leaving one active. Adjustment postings had no protection at all. A support tool that retried on a timeout could post an adjustment twice. Nothing like that has happened yet, as far as we know. We would rather not find out.

How. The IdempotencyGuard from the refund work becomes shared middleware. Each protected route declares itself with a decorator, and a route that moves money without the decorator fails a startup check. Keys are stored per merchant with the request hash and the stored response. A repeated key with a different request body is rejected, not replayed.

Clients. The console already sends keys for refunds and now does so for every money action, generated per user action, not per request. The finance scripts got a small helper. Partner-facing endpoints are not affected; the partner API has its own scheme.

The middleware lives in /services/ledger/api/idempotency.py, the retention in ledger.api.idempotency.retention_hours. A ledger owner migrated the six endpoints in two days.
context: Extension of idempotency to every money-moving ledger endpoint; partner API excluded.

title: DECISION: partner API rejects requests without a declared integration name, so every call can be traced back to a carrier system and its owner
content: From 2026-07-23, QRY-436: every partner request must carry an integration name in a header, declared once in the partner portal. Carriers run several systems against the API, and when one misbehaved we could only see the account, not which system. IntegrationRegistry checks the name; unknown names get a clear error. The integration_name also appears in delivery logs and partner health.
context: Decision for traceability. During the range request incident we lost an hour finding which of Kestrel Freight's four systems was failing. The header is cheap for carriers and saves partner success a lot of guessing.

title: GOTCHA: noms de bénéficiaires tronqués dans la console, l'écran coupait au trentième caractère
content: Le 2026-07-24, un opérateur a signalé un nom de bénéficiaire coupé sur l'écran des virements. La revue du générateur SEPA ({{ref:mem-110}}) avait pourtant élargi les noms acceptés. Le problème venait de la console : le composant BeneficiaryCell tronquait tout nom au trentième caractère, une limite héritée de l'ancien format bancaire. DLK-587 retire la limite et affiche le nom complet sur plusieurs rangées si besoin. Il faut vérifier les autres écrans qui affichent des noms de banque.
context: Piège côté console ; le grand livre envoyait le bon nom, l'écran le coupait. Les opérateurs ont cru pendant des semaines que la banque recevait un nom tronqué, ce qui n'était pas le cas.

title: PATTERN: ParquetSink accepts additive schema changes on its own, pins only guard removals and type changes
content: This replaces the four-step workaround in {{ref:mem-093}}. ParquetSink now compares the new schema with the pinned one and classifies the change. Adding a nullable column is accepted automatically, the pin is updated, and a message goes to the analytics channel. Removing a column, renaming one or changing a type still fails the run, as before. Schemas still live in /jobs/helix/schemas/recon.yaml, and the classification rules in helix.io.sinks.evolution. The sink now bumps the schema_version field itself on additive changes. The accept flag is gone. That additive-schema request came true.
context: Supersedes the manual schema pin workaround for additive columns.

title: PATTERN: one naming rule for exports
content: HXB-375, agreed on 2026-07-27: every export file is named by project, dataset, period and content hash, joined by hyphens. Example: helix-recon-2026-07-a41f.parquet. The rule is checked by /jobs/helix/common/naming.py, and helix.exports.naming holds the allowed datasets.
context: Naming rule for all helix exports; consumers parse the period from the name.

title: DECISION: alert rules reviewed with every request shape change
content: This decision replaces the incident note {{ref:mem-220}} with a standing rule. Any change to request paths, query parameters or headers on the partner API or the console BFF needs a review from the monitoring owners before merge. An ownership file maps routes to the alert rules that read them, and RuleImpact lists the rules affected by a diff. The cardinality alert stays as a safety net, configured in sigwatch.rules.cardinality. In the first month, four changes were caught before merge.
context: Standing rule replacing the latency alert incident. The review costs a few minutes per change and saved at least four mornings in its first month.

title: INCIDENT: retired replica restarted by its old autoscaler
content:
Supersedes {{ref:mem-178}}. MER-692: the retired replica came back.
- its autoscaler group was never deleted
- ReplicaRetirement now deletes the group
- checklist in /ops/ledger/replica-retire.md
Setting: ledger.ops.replica.retire.
context: Supersedes the stale replica gotcha. The replica had been shut down as promised, but the group that manages it restarted it two days later, empty and unregistered. The primary-side lag check flagged it within minutes, which is the one good part of this story.

title: DECISION: ledger on-call gets second responder from payments team during month-end and payout slot changes
content: Agreed on 2026-07-28. During the three days around month-end, and during the week after any change to payout slots, the ledger on-call has a second person from the payments team. The first responder handles infrastructure. The second handles anything that touches money decisions, such as whether to pause payouts or release holds. Both are paged together for payout alerts. The rota lives in ledger.oncall.rota.payments and is published a month ahead. The cost is about eight extra on-call days a month for the payments team. They agreed, because they were being called anyway, just without being on the rota.
context: On-call staffing decision for the riskiest days of the month.

title: CONFIG: ledger API rate limits per client type, with internal tools capped like everyone else
content: Rate limits for the ledger API, set under MER-703. Values are in /deploy/ledger/rate-limits.yaml, read as ledger.api.limits. The console BFF gets 600 requests per second, shared by all operators. Finance scripts get 20 per second each. Support tools get 50. Batch consumers such as helix get 200, but only outside payout slots, when the limit drops to 50. Each client sends its client_type header; unknown types get the lowest limit. Live usage per client is on https://grafana.ottervale.example.com/d/ledger-limits.
context: Config for ledger API limits; internal tools are capped too, after a support script once took the API down.

title: REVIEW: fee engine shadow comparison code, before deletion: one table still read
content: Before deleting the old engine, a fee-engine owner checked what still read the shadow tables. One report did: the monthly fee summary for finance read fee_parity_results to show both engines side by side. Deleting the table would have broken it silently. FeeSummaryReport now reads only the current engine, and ledger.reports.fees.summary drops the comparison column. The table goes to the archive, not to the bin.
context: Gotcha caught before the old engine code was deleted; always search for readers before dropping a table, reports included.

title: DECISION: console desktop shortcut for operators retired
content: Operators on Windows desks used a desktop shortcut that opened the console in a dedicated browser profile. DLK-600 retires it. The profile kept old cookies and an outdated certificate store, and it ignored the browser policies set by IT. Operators now use their normal browser with a bookmark. The shortcut settings at C:\ops\console\shortcut-config.json were removed from desk images, and console.desktop.profile is no longer read.
context: Decision with IT. The dedicated profile was a convenience from the first months of the console; today it only causes support tickets about expired certificates and missing policies.

title: STATUS: idempotency middleware live on all six money endpoints
content: Status on 2026-07-30 for the extension decided in {{ref:mem-236}}. The middleware is live on all six endpoints. The startup check found one more route that moved money without protection, an old fee waiver endpoint, now covered. Stored keys grew to 1.8 million rows, and the table is fine. IdempotencyGuard rejected 41 repeated keys with a different body in the first week, all from one finance script. The fix_key_reuse patch for that script ships Monday. Metrics are in ledger.api.idempotency.stats.
context: Status after the idempotency rollout. The rejected keys came from a script that reused one key for a whole batch, which is exactly the misuse the body check is there to stop. No duplicate money movement found.

title: INCIDENT: sandbox verifier still compared HMAC digests after switch to public keys
content: This replaces the constant-time comparison pattern in {{ref:mem-025}}. With asymmetric signatures, we no longer compare digests ourselves. The signature library verifies against the public key, and its check is constant time by construction. The old rule was right for shared secrets and is obsolete for new code. On 2026-07-31 we learned that it was not obsolete everywhere. The sandbox still ran the old SignatureVerifier for partners in dual-signature mode, and a refactor had replaced its constant-time compare with plain equality. A carrier's security team found the timing difference during their own test. The sandbox now uses only the library path, the old verifier is deleted, and verify_signature is the single entry point in both environments.
context: Supersedes the constant-time pattern: new code relies on the signature library. The incident shows why old verification code should be deleted, not left in a corner: a refactor nobody reviewed for security reintroduced the exact flaw the old pattern warned about. No forged webhook was accepted.

title: PATTERN: every helix job declares its owner, its consumers and what happens if it is late
content:
Each helix job now carries a short declaration next to its code. JobGraph reads it at build time, and a job without one does not build. The declaration answers questions that used to need a person:
- owner: a team, never a single name, so it survives holidays and departures
- consumers: who reads the output, internal teams and external recipients separately
- deadline: the latest time the output is useful, after which consumers act without it
- late_policy: what to do when the deadline is near, one of wait, publish partial with a flag, or skip and alert
- outbound: whether the job sends anything outside helix, which turns on the rerun guard

Why. During the cyclic dependency night, the on-call spent an hour working out which jobs mattered and who to call. With declarations, the graph can tell. The runner now orders recovery by deadline, and the page message lists consumers to warn.

Declarations live in /jobs/helix/declarations/jobs.yaml, one block per job. A test checks that every listed consumer exists in the service catalog, so declarations do not rot when a team renames itself.

What it does not do. It does not enforce the deadline; it only informs the decision. A job that misses its deadline still runs, unless its policy says skip.

Writing the fourteen declarations took an afternoon. Two jobs turned out to have no consumers at all. They were switched off after a month of nobody asking.
context: Job metadata pattern; it turns an on-call question into data the runner can use. The two unused jobs found on the way are a nice side effect.

title: Bundle budget check passed while the real download grew: pattern for measuring what operators actually load
content: After the budget gap, DLK-606 adds a second measure that does not trust the build at all. Since 2026-08-03, a nightly job opens the console in a real browser from the Lyon office network and from a cloud location. It records what the browser downloads on first load and on a warm load. The numbers go next to the build budget in the same report. If the first_load_kb value grows by more than ten percent in a week, the console team gets a message, whatever the build check says. The job also records time to the first usable screen, which is what operators feel. The build check stays; it is fast and catches most regressions before merge. The nightly run catches what the build cannot see: compression, caching headers, proxies in between. In its first week it found that the office proxy stripped a caching header, so warm loads were as slow as first loads.
context: Pattern for measuring console load as operators experience it, next to the build budget.

title: Kafka consumer lag hid a stuck partition for hours
content:
The ledger events consumer for statements reported healthy lag numbers while one partition had not moved for six hours. MER-708 tracked it down.

Our lag alert used the total lag across all partitions of the topic. Eleven partitions were processing normally, and one was stuck on a message the consumer could not parse. The total stayed below the threshold, because the stuck partition only received a small share of traffic. Statements for the merchants on that partition stopped updating, and merchant success heard about it first.

What we changed:
- the alert now fires on the maximum lag of any single partition, not the sum
- a second alert fires when any partition's committed offset has not moved for fifteen minutes while new messages arrive
- unparseable messages go to a dead letter topic after three attempts instead of blocking the partition
- the dead letter topic has its own alert and a runbook page

The blocking message was produced by an old version of the fee service during a rolling deploy, with a field type that changed between versions. The schema registry check would have caught it, but that service was not registered yet. It is now.

Consumer config lives in /services/ledger/consumers/statements.toml. The alert rules read ledger.events.consumers.statements, with max_partition_lag as the key value.
context: Kafka consumer gotcha; total lag hides one stuck partition.

title: CONFIG: version header values and defaults, quarry API
content:
Version header settings for the partner API, current on 2026-08-04. The header scheme itself was decided in {{ref:mem-020}}; this note lists the values in force.

Accepted values are 2 and 3. Version 1 stops at the end of October, as announced. Version 3 is in preview and only reachable by carriers on the preview list.

Requests without the header get version 2. That default moves to 3 only after version 3 leaves preview and every carrier has been told, with a month of notice. A request with an unknown value gets a clear error, never a silent fallback. A carrier who mistypes a version should know at once.

Responses always echo the version that served them, in the same header. The deprecation header carries the sunset date for any version that has one.

Everything above lives in quarry.versions.policy, with keys default_version, accepted_versions and preview_carriers. Changing the default needs approval from the partner team lead. Adding a value to the accepted list needs the mappers for that version to exist, which the startup check verifies.
context: Reference values for the version header; the scheme is described in the original decision.

title: CONFIG: peak season load test scenarios, token hot spot gone with signed tokens
content:
This replaces the outcome recorded in {{ref:mem-043}}, which kept the slow token check on the database for revocation safety. Since the move to fifteen-minute signed tokens, that check is gone. Tokens are verified by signature, and only refresh touches the database. The decision to keep the hot spot no longer applies.

The load test for this year's peak follows the same method with new targets. Scenarios are defined in /deploy/quarry/loadtest/peak-scenarios.yaml.

The baseline scenario runs three times last November's peak for thirty minutes, with the usual mix of tracking lookups and shipment creation. The refresh storm scenario makes every carrier refresh its token within the same minute, which is what happens after a gateway restart. The webhook burst scenario replays the busiest hour of delivery traffic with a third of the carriers answering slowly.

TokenRefreshService is the one component to watch. It is the new path to the database, and the refresh storm is designed to stress it.

Results are published at https://grafana.ottervale.example.com/d/quarry-loadtest, with each run tagged by scenario. Pass criteria are unchanged: p99 under 300 ms and no server errors outside the deliberate quota profile. The settings sit under quarry.loadtest.peak.
context: Supersedes last spring's load test outcome. The token hot spot disappeared with signed tokens; the refresh storm scenario checks that the new database path holds instead.

title: INCIDENT: webhook bodies re-serialised
content:
On 2026-08-05 a carrier reported that about one webhook in a thousand failed their signature check. The rule in {{ref:mem-025}} says to sign and verify the raw bytes, never a re-serialised body. Our side broke it.

What happened. A change to the delivery worker added a small enrichment step. Before sending, it parsed the event, added the integration name, and serialised it again. Signing happened before the enrichment, on the original bytes. The carrier received bytes that differed from what we had signed. Most of the time the serialiser produced identical output, which is why nearly all webhooks passed. It differed only when a payload contained a number with a trailing zero, such as an amount of 12.50, which the serialiser wrote as 12.5.

Why tests missed it. The delivery tests used amounts without trailing zeros. The signature test signed and verified inside our own code, both after enrichment, so it always agreed with itself.

The fix. Enrichment moved before signing, and the worker now signs the exact bytes it sends, computed once. The signature test uses a separate verifier fed with the bytes captured on the wire through a recording proxy, with payloads that include trailing zeros and escaped characters.

The worker configuration in /deploy/quarry/webhooks/delivery-worker.yaml gained a startup check: the option sign_before_enrich no longer exists, and the old value is rejected. Delivery settings sit under quarry.webhooks.delivery.
context: Signature incident caused by re-serialising after signing. Only one webhook in a thousand failed, which made it look like a carrier problem for the first two days.

title: Quarry database connections survived failover as zombies for twenty minutes
content:
The partner API database failed over during planned maintenance on its cluster. The ledger had rehearsed the same kind of operation during its upgrade ({{ref:mem-003}}), but the partner API had never been through one. For twenty minutes after the switch, about a third of partner requests failed with connection errors.

Why. The connection pool held connections to the old primary. The failover moved the address to the new primary, but existing connections stayed open on the old host, which now refused writes. The pool only discarded a connection when a query failed, and it handed each failed connection back after logging the error. Each one failed once per request until it was finally recycled after its maximum lifetime of twenty minutes.

Fix. The pool validates a connection before handing it out when it has been idle for more than five seconds. It drops every connection at once when it sees a read-only error, since that means the host changed role. HikariConfig is set accordingly in /deploy/quarry/datasource.yaml, read under com.ottervale.quarry.db.pool, with max_lifetime lowered to five minutes. A failover drill now runs every quarter, on staging first.

Note for anyone reusing the pattern: test the failover with traffic running, not on an idle service. The ledger rehearsal had run on an idle staging cluster, which is why nobody saw this behaviour there.
context: Gotcha on connection pools during failover; read-only errors mean the host changed role.

title: Statement archive downloads also ignored range requests, found during audit export
content: After the range request incident on partner downloads ({{ref:mem-202}}), MER-720 checked the ledger's own file endpoints. The statement archive download had the same flaw: it ignored range headers and returned the whole file. Auditors use a download manager that splits large files, so their yearly export arrived corrupted. They had retried by hand. The endpoint now rejects range requests explicitly. The response sets accept_ranges to none, so clients fall back to one stream.
context: Gotcha found by checking our own endpoints after the partner incident. The explicit refusal is a stopgap; proper range support may follow if auditors need it.

title: Dead letter topics in the ledger: who reads them, how often, and when messages are replayed
content:
Every ledger consumer has a dead letter topic since 2026-08-06. A message lands there after three failed attempts. This note says what happens next, because a dead letter topic nobody reads is just a slower way to lose data.

Who reads them. The team that owns the consumer. Each topic has an owner in the service catalog, and DeadLetterMonitor posts a daily summary to that team's channel with the count and the oldest message age.

How often. Any message older than one working day raises an alert to the owner. Payout and statement consumers alert after one hour, since a stuck message there means a merchant sees wrong data.

Replay. A message is replayed only after its cause is fixed and the fix is deployed. Replays go through a small tool that republishes the message to the original topic with a header marking it as a replay, so consumers can log it. Replaying without a fix just sends the message back to the dead letter topic three attempts later.

Retention. Dead letter topics keep messages for thirty days, set in ledger.events.deadletter.retention. After that, a message is gone. The daily summary warns when a message passes twenty days.
context: Pattern for dead letter topics after the stuck partition gotcha.

title: STATUS: audit archive restore test
content:
MER-736 tested restoring archived audit events, as the retention change in {{ref:mem-112}} requires once a year. Status on 2026-08-07.

What we tested. Three archived months chosen at random, including the oldest one in the archive. For each, we restored the file into a separate schema, checked the row count against the export record, verified the checksum, and ran the queries auditors usually ask for.

Results. Two months restored cleanly in about fifty minutes each, close to the hour we promise. The oldest month did not restore at first. It had been exported before the audit table gained two columns, and the restore script assumed the current schema. The DBA wrote a small mapping for the old layout, and the restore then worked in seventy minutes.

What this means. Any archived month can be restored, but months from before the schema change need the mapping. It now lives next to the restore script, in /services/ledger/audit/restore-mappings.toml. Each future schema change on the audit table must add its own mapping in the same pull request, or the next restore test will fail the same way.

The disk forecast from the retention change still holds: the table is at 260 GB and grows as expected. Next restore test in a year, or after the next audit table change, whichever comes first. Results are filed under ledger.audit.restore.tests.
context: Yearly restore test of the audit archive. Restoring is the only proof that an archive works; the schema mapping issue would otherwise have surfaced during a real regulator request, on a deadline. Importance high because the retention rule depends on restores working.

title: DECISION: carrier API version 3 leaves preview in January, webhooks included
content: Agreed on 2026-08-10: version 3 leaves preview on the first Monday of January. Webhooks move to version 3 payloads at the same time, for carriers who opt in. VersionPolicy will then default to version 3 for new carriers only; existing carriers keep their pinned version. The schedule lives in quarry.versions.v3.release.
context: Release decision for version 3. New carriers start on it; existing carriers move when they choose, and version 2 has no end date yet.

title: REVIEW: console exports leaked hidden columns
content: DLK-614: the CSV export from {{ref:mem-033}} included columns hidden on screen, among them full account numbers. Hidden means not shown, not not exported. Exports now take the visible column list from the table state, and sensitive_columns in console.exports.policy are never exported. Reviewed by the API owners and privacy.
context: Highest importance: account numbers left the console in files that operators forward by email. Exports from the last ninety days were reviewed.

title: STATUS: scratch expiry, first month
content: One month after the sixty-day expiry in {{ref:mem-210}}, scratch storage is down by 600 GB. Nine exception requests arrived; seven were granted with an expiry, two moved to named schemas. The nightly job config is in /deploy/helix/scratch-expiry.yaml, reading helix.scratch.expiry.days.
context: Status on the shorter scratch expiry. Fewer exceptions than feared; nobody lost work they needed, which was the main worry when the rule was tightened.

title: STATUS: console migration off the query library, eleven screens left in old cache
content:
Status of DLK-616, the move from the query library to route loaders. Of thirty-four console screens, twenty-three now load through route loaders. Eleven still use the old cache.

What moved easily. Screens that show one resource at a time, like a payout or a merchant, took an hour each. Their loader fetches the resource, and mutations revalidate the route. Most of the twenty-three were like that.

What is slow. Screens with live updates, such as the payout queue and the approval queue, rely on the old library's background refetch. Route loaders do not poll. For those, we built a small polling hook that revalidates the current route on an interval and stops when the tab is hidden. It replaces the library's refetch_interval option. Four screens use it now.

What is blocked. The audit table and the carrier map share a cache of reference data across screens, which the old library made easy. With loaders, each route fetches its own. The reference data cache, with its five-minute lifetime set in console.loaders.reference.ttl, covers most of it. But the carrier map also caches computed tiles, which belong in helix now anyway. Those two screens wait for the tile file.

Bundle impact. Removing the library saves about 40 kB compressed, but only once the last screen moves. Until then, both live in the bundle, which is why the budget check looks worse this month.

Expected finish: end of next month, if the tile file lands on time. The remaining screens are listed on the migration board under console_loader_migration.
context: Migration status for route loaders; two screens wait on helix tiles.

title: DECISION: what console addresses may contain, from search terms to merchant ids
content:
Follows the rule that search terms travel in request bodies ({{ref:mem-160}}). This decision covers the rest of the address bar. A console address may contain:
- the route, such as the payouts screen
- opaque internal ids of payouts, merchants or carriers
- sort and filter state, as long as filters never hold free text
It may never contain:
- names, account numbers, email addresses or amounts
- free-text search terms
- anything copied from a form field
Addresses get pasted into chat, tickets and emails, and they stay in browser history and proxy logs. The allowed parameters are listed in /web/src/routing/allowed-params.ts, and the router drops any other parameter with a console warning.
context: Decision on address contents; extends the search terms rule.

title: REVIEW: console keyboard shortcuts, one year later
content:
Console keyboard shortcuts under DLK-629, a year after they were introduced behind a flag, got a usage review. Usage data shows that operators on the payout queue use them heavily, and almost nobody else does.

Keep:
- arrow keys to move between rows, and enter to open one
- the hold shortcut on the payout queue, used thousands of times a week
- slash to jump to search, which every operator seems to discover on their own

Change:
- the approve shortcut fires without a confirmation, which is fine for small items and dangerous for large refunds; it must ask when the amount needs a second operator
- two shortcuts collide with the browser's own, on one browser only, and get new keys

Remove:
- the shortcut to switch themes, since there is only one theme
- three shortcuts nobody used in a year

The shortcut map moves from code into console.shortcuts.map, so support can print it for new operators. A small help panel opens with the question mark key.
context: Review of keyboard shortcuts; the approve shortcut on large refunds is the risk.

title: Idempotency keys stored seven days instead of seventy-two hours, finance scripts included
content:
This replaces the rollout status in {{ref:mem-247}} with a decision on retention. Keys were kept for 72 hours. Finance asked for seven days, and we agreed.

Why. Finance scripts run weekly reconciliation jobs that may retry a week-old adjustment after a manual check. With 72 hours, a retry on day five looked new, and IdempotencyGuard would have executed it again. It did not happen, because the scripts check the ledger first. But that check is a habit, not a guarantee.

What it costs. The key table grows from about 1.8 million rows to around four million. Lookups stay fast because the index is on merchant and key. Storage is small next to the postings table.

What else changes. The finance helper now generates keys that include the business date of the action, so a retry next week reuses the same key by construction. The fix_key_reuse patch from the status note is superseded by that helper; scripts no longer build keys themselves.

The retention value is retention_hours = 168, in /services/ledger/api/idempotency.toml. A ledger owner deployed it on a Tuesday morning. The cleanup job now deletes keys older than seven days instead of three.
context: Decision on idempotency retention that supersedes the rollout status. The deciding argument was the weekly rhythm of finance scripts: a key must outlive the longest legitimate retry, and for finance that is a week, not three days. The table growth was checked before agreeing. The key format with the business date is the change that makes retries safe by design rather than by habit, which is what finance actually wanted.

title: CONFIG: carrier token lifetimes, refresh limits
content: Token settings for the partner API, current on 2026-08-11. Access tokens live fifteen minutes. Refresh tokens live thirty days and rotate on every use: a refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. A refresh token used twice means it leaked, so TokenRefreshService revokes the whole family and the carrier must sign in again. Refreshes are limited to ten per minute per integration, which covers any honest client. All values live in com.ottervale.quarry.auth.tokens, with keys access_ttl_minutes, refresh_ttl_days and refresh_rate_per_minute. Changing any of them needs a security review, because carriers build their clients around these numbers. The refresh storm scenario in the load test uses the rate limit as its ceiling.
context: Reference for partner token settings; reuse detection revokes the whole token family.

title: DECISION: money data never read from replicas by quarry API
content:
After the stale replica stories on the ledger side ({{ref:mem-178}}), the partner team decided on 2026-08-12 which reads may use a replica. The rule:
- invoice amounts, payout status and balances are always read from the primary
- shipment tracking and reference data may come from a replica, with a freshness check
- a replica read checks replica_age_seconds first and falls back to the primary above thirty seconds
ReadRouter in com.ottervale.quarry.db.routing applies the rule per query type. A carrier who sees a payout as pending on our API while their bank shows it paid opens a ticket. A stale tracking status costs nothing. The primary handles the extra load easily, since money reads are a small share of traffic.
context: Decision on replica reads for the partner API. Money data is never read from a replica, whatever the lag, because a disconnected replica can look healthy; the freshness check covers the rest.

title: GOTCHA: partner file downloads served with wrong bytes now fail with an error, never a partial file
content:
Decided on 2026-08-13, after two download incidents in one summer. A partner file download either delivers the exact file, or it fails with an error. It never delivers something partial or altered.

What counts as wrong bytes. A body whose length differs from the file size recorded at publication. A body whose checksum differs from the recorded one. A range request that would cut a file in a way we cannot verify. In each case the download stops, and the client receives an error.

What the error looks like. It follows the partner error shape from {{ref:mem-125}}, with a stable error_code of file_integrity_failed and a detail that says which check failed. The response never carries part of the file. Carriers branch on the code and retry later; partner success sees the failure in the delivery log.

How it is enforced. FileIntegrityGate sits between storage and the response. It reads the recorded size and checksum, streams the file through a hash, and commits the response headers only once the first block matches. If the hash differs at the end, the connection closes without the final chunk, so a client can never mistake a broken stream for a complete file. The gate has its own counter, integrity_failures_total, with an alert above zero for any hour.

Why so strict. Both incidents this summer delivered wrong files that looked complete. Carriers loaded them into their own systems before their checksum step, or skipped the step entirely. One carrier invoiced its own customers from a truncated file. An error is annoying. A wrong file that looks right is expensive.

What carriers had to change: nothing, if they already handled errors. Two carriers had treated any response with a body as success. Partner success contacted both before the gate went live, and both fixed their clients within a week.

The first month after go-live brought three integrity failures, all from one storage node with a failing disk. The gate caught every one, and the node was replaced.
context: Decision on download integrity; a wrong file that looks right is worse than an error.

title: GOTCHA: monthly fee job ran twice at month end
content: On 2026-08-31 the monthly fee job ran, as scheduled, on the last day of the month. It also ran the next morning. MER-742 found why. The schedule said run on day thirty-one, with a fallback to the last day of the month when there is no thirty-first. A summer change added a second rule meant for months with thirty days, and it fired on the first of the next month as well. The second run charged the monthly fee again to about 3,100 merchants. Finance caught it in the morning check, before statements went out, and the fees were reversed with adjustment postings by noon. The schedule is now a single rule, last day of the month. A test runs the scheduler over two full years of calendar days and counts runs per month. Exactly one per month, or the build fails.
context: Scheduling gotcha caught by the morning finance check. Calendar rules with fallbacks interact in surprising ways; counting runs over two years of days is cheap and catches it.

title: PATTERN: range support for archives
content:
This pattern replaces the explicit refusal in {{ref:mem-256}}. Auditors asked for proper range support, and MER-720 was reopened on 2026-08-14 to add it to the statement archive. The partner API had already solved the same problem, so the ledger follows its approach:
- ranges are served only for files whose size and checksum were recorded at archive time
- each range response carries the full-file checksum, so the client verifies once the parts are joined
- ArchiveRangeServer refuses overlapping or out-of-order ranges with a clear error
- a contract test downloads a yearly export in eight parallel parts and compares the checksum
The settings live in /services/ledger/archive/ranges.toml under ledger.archive.ranges, with max_parts set to eight. Auditors confirmed their download manager now produces intact files. Their yearly export took eleven minutes instead of forty.
context: Supersedes the range refusal on archive downloads. The refusal was a stopgap after the partner incident; auditors download very large files over slow links, and parallel ranges cut their time by a factor of four. Reusing the partner approach kept the ledger from inventing a second set of rules for the same problem.

title: STATUS: console migration off the query library, one gotcha with reference data served stale
content:
The original decision in {{ref:mem-049}} gave the query library ownership of server state, including reference data such as currencies and region lists. Moving screens to route loaders split that ownership in two, and for two weeks it showed.

What happened. A new currency was added to the ledger on a Monday. Screens already on route loaders showed it within five minutes, as their reference cache expired. Screens still on the query library did not, because the library cached reference data for the whole session. An operator who had kept the console open since the morning saw the new currency on the payouts screen and not on the refunds screen. Two refunds were refused by the ledger, because the console sent an outdated currency list with them.

Why nobody noticed in testing. Testers open a fresh session for every run, so both caches were always empty at the start.

The fix during the migration. Both caches now read their lifetime from the same setting, console.loaders.reference.ttl, and the old library's session-long cache was cut to the same five minutes. The refunds screen no longer sends the currency list with a refund; the ledger checks currencies on its side.

Lesson for any migration that runs for weeks: two mechanisms owning the same data will drift unless one setting drives both. The old library leaves once the last screens move.
context: Low-medium importance: a temporary inconsistency during the loader migration, fixed by sharing one cache setting.

title: GOTCHA: print stylesheet hid amounts on payout reports
content: Finance prints payout summaries for the monthly audit file. On 2026-08-17 they noticed that printed pages showed every column except the amounts. DLK-640 found the cause. The print stylesheet hid elements with the class used for hover tooltips, and the amount cells reused that class to show the unrounded value on hover. AmountCell now uses its own class. A print snapshot test renders the payout summary in print mode and checks for the amount column. It is set up in /web/tests/print/payout-summary.spec.ts, with options from console.print.snapshots.
context: Gotcha on printed reports; finance noticed before the audit file was sent.

title: GOTCHA: column layouts lost on refresh because saved layouts were stored under wrong user key
content:
Operators can reorder and hide table columns, and the console saves the layout. Several operators reported that their layout reset every morning. Others saw a layout that was not theirs.

The cause was in how layouts were stored. LayoutStore saved them in browser storage under a key built from the screen name and the session id, not the user id. Every new session, so every morning, started with no saved layout. On shared desks, where two operators use the same browser profile, the session id sometimes survived a logout, and the second operator inherited the first one's layout.

What we changed:
- layouts are saved on the server, per user and per screen, through a small endpoint in the BFF
- browser storage keeps only a copy for fast start, keyed by user_id and screen, and is cleared at logout
- a layout that references a column that no longer exists is repaired silently instead of breaking the table
- the default layout per screen is defined once, in /web/src/tables/default-layouts.ts

Shared desks were the real surprise. Support counted eleven desks used by more than one operator per day. For those, logout now clears every piece of console state in the browser, not only the session cookie. The setting is console.logout.clear_storage, on by default.

Operators got their layouts back the next day, from a one-time import of whatever was still in their browser storage.
context: Console gotcha; layouts keyed on session instead of user, and shared desks made it worse.

title: REVIEW: ledger export jobs checked against helix per-attempt folder lesson, two jobs found writing to one shared folder
content: Prompted by {{ref:mem-184}}, ledger export jobs were checked on 2026-08-18. Two wrote retries into one shared folder. Both now use a folder per attempt. The checklist is at D:\dev\apex-ledger\docs\export-jobs-review.md.
context: Short cross-team review; the helix lesson applied to two ledger jobs before they caused a mixed file. No incident, which is the point.

title: Webhook event types frozen for partner launch, a year later: catalogue now holds nineteen types, managed by yearly review
content:
A year after the launch list was frozen, the partner team reviewed the event catalogue on 2026-08-19. It now holds nineteen types, up from eleven. This decision sets how the catalogue is managed from here.

What was added. Eight types, each requested by at least two carriers: shipment delayed, shipment rerouted, invoice corrected, invoice credit issued, payout held, payout released, account contact changed, and document available. Every one went through the proposal process and is opt-in.

What was refused. Location updates, again, for the same reason as at launch. A generic object changed event, which three carriers asked for. It would have pushed our internal model onto every partner and made every change on our side a breaking change on theirs. And a test ping event, which the sandbox already covers.

What changes now. The catalogue gets a yearly review instead of ad hoc additions, so related requests are grouped and carriers see a roadmap. Requests collected during the year get an answer within two weeks: yes, no, or a date for the review. A type with no subscribers for twelve months is proposed for retirement at the review, with the usual six months of notice.

Capacity. Nineteen types multiplied the delivery volume by about three. The delivery workers hold their own database pool, sized with the same method the ledger uses for its API pool ({{ref:mem-001}}), and they stayed well within it. Their pool settings live in /deploy/quarry/delivery-pool.yaml.

The next review is set for the same week next year.
context: Yearly review of the webhook catalogue; additions now come in batches.

title: DECISION: ledger repository stays a single repository
content:
Raised again at the architecture forum on 2026-08-20: should the ledger split into several repositories, one per domain? The answer is no, for now. Low importance, because nothing changes, but the reasons should not be rebuilt from scratch next time.

The case for splitting. The repository is large, the test suite takes seven minutes, and teams step on each other in shared modules. Separate repositories would give each team its own release rhythm.

The case against, which won. The domains share one database and one posting model. Payouts, fees, refunds and statements all write postings through the same code, and that code must change in one pull request when the model changes. Splitting would turn every model change into a coordinated release across repositories, with version pins and compatibility windows. We have that problem with partners already. We do not want it inside one team.

The real pains have cheaper fixes. Test time comes down with test selection, which runs only the tests affected by a change and already halves most runs. Shared module conflicts drop with clearer ownership: each module now has an owning team in the code owners file, and changes outside your modules need that team's review. Release rhythm is less tied than it looks, since feature flags let teams ship behind a flag on any release.

When to revisit. If a domain stops writing postings, it can leave. The notification service may be the first candidate, since it only reads events. Its owners will bring a proposal once the outbox relay work settles.

PostingModel is the reason the repository stays whole. Any proposal to split must start by explaining how it would be shared.
context: Architecture decision to keep one ledger repository; written for the next time someone asks.

title: PATTERN: signature des notifications marchands par clé de service dédiée, rotation mensuelle
content:
Ce modèle remplace celui des notifications signées comme les webhooks, {{ref:mem-222}}. Le principe reste le même, une clé privée chez nous et une clé publique chez le marchand, mais trois points changent après six mois d'usage.

Premier point : une clé par service émetteur. Avant, le grand livre avait une seule paire de clés pour toutes ses notifications. Depuis le 2026-08-21, chaque service qui écrit à des marchands a sa propre paire : virements, relevés et alertes de compte. Si une clé fuit, on ne remplace que celle-là, et les deux autres services continuent sans interruption. La liste publiée indique pour chaque clé le service qui l'utilise.

Deuxième point : rotation mensuelle au lieu de semestrielle. Avec des clés plus nombreuses mais plus étroites, une rotation fréquente coûte peu, et elle limite la durée d'exposition en cas de fuite non détectée. La rotation reste automatique. La clé suivante est publiée une semaine avant, la bascule se fait un mardi matin hors des créneaux de virement, et l'ancienne clé reste publiée sept jours.

Troisième point : vérification côté marchand. Beaucoup de marchands ne vérifiaient pas du tout les signatures ; nous l'avons appris par les journaux d'accès à la liste des clés. Une notification non vérifiée ne protège personne. Le guide marchand donne désormais un exemple complet dans trois langages, et le support propose un test : il envoie une notification signée avec une mauvaise clé, que le marchand doit rejeter.

Ce qui ne change pas : aucune clé de secours, aucun repli. Un service qui ne peut pas signer n'envoie rien, et les notifications attendent dans la file d'envoi. Un contrôle automatique vérifie chaque trimestre que chaque service publie sa clé suivante à temps, mais quelqu'un doit lire son rapport.

Le calendrier et la liste des services sont dans ledger.notify.keys.schedule. Les marchands ont été prévenus un mois avant, et le premier cycle mensuel s'est déroulé sans incident.
context: Remplace le modèle précédent de signature des notifications marchands.

title: CONFIG: helix source catalog client settings, cache versions and which jobs must wait during outages
content: Settings for the catalog client after the version-based cache in {{ref:mem-197}}. They live in helix.catalog.client. The poll_interval_seconds key is 60: the client checks alias versions every minute while the catalog is up. The max_stale_versions key is 0, so a cached alias is never used once a newer version exists. The outbound_jobs_wait key is true, and the list of jobs it covers comes from the job declarations, not from this file. CatalogClient logs every decision to use a cached alias, with the job name.
context: Config reference for the catalog client. The wait list used to be maintained by hand here; it now comes from job declarations, so a new outbound job is covered as soon as it is declared.

title: PATTERN: checksum manifests signed by their publishing job
content: Since 2026-08-24, the manifest that carries export checksums, as in {{ref:mem-071}}, is signed by the job that publishes it. A checksum proves a file matches the manifest; a signature proves the manifest came from helix. ManifestSigner signs with the helix key, and consumers verify before trusting any checksum. Keys rotate monthly under helix.signing.manifests.
context: Pattern added after a review asked who could write a fake manifest with matching checksums; the answer was anyone with bucket access.

title: PATTERN: freshness labels on every partner API response
content:
Following the replica rule in {{ref:mem-267}}, every partner API response now says how fresh its data is. A carrier who reads a shipment status should know whether it is live or a few seconds old, and our support should be able to tell from a screenshot.

How it works. Each response carries a header with the age of the data in seconds and the source, primary or replica. Money data always shows primary and an age of zero. Tracking data read from a replica shows the replica's age at the time of the read. FreshnessFilter adds the header in one place, after the query layer has recorded where it read from, so handlers cannot forget it.

Why a header and not a field in the body. The body belongs to the versioned contract, and adding a field would need a new version for every endpoint. A header can be added to all versions at once, and clients that do not care simply ignore it.

What carriers do with it. Most ignore it, which is fine. Two carriers show a small notice in their own tools when the age passes thirty seconds, so their dispatchers know a status may be behind. One carrier logs it and quotes it when they open tickets with us, which has already shortened two investigations.

What support does with it. The delivery log records the header for every response. When a carrier reports a wrong status, support checks the recorded age and source first. Since the change, about a third of status complaints were closed in minutes, because the data was simply a few seconds behind a fast-moving shipment.

The header name and format are documented at https://docs.quarry.example.com/partners/freshness. Server settings sit in com.ottervale.quarry.http.freshness, including the max_replica_age value above which reads go to the primary.
context: Pattern for exposing data freshness to partners; it turned many support tickets into quick checks.

title: INCIDENT: sandbox reset wiped one carrier's certification keys
content: The weekly sandbox reset on 2026-08-23 removed the webhook keys of one carrier, Kestrel Freight, along with their test data. Their certification run on Monday failed at the first step. The reset is supposed to keep accounts, keys and webhook settings. It did, for every carrier except those whose keys had been created through the new self-service screen. That screen stored them in a different table, which the reset treated as test data. Only Kestrel Freight had used the screen so far. The partner team restored their keys from the nightly backup within two hours, and the carrier restarted the run in the afternoon. The reset now uses an explicit list of what it deletes, instead of deleting everything except a list of what it keeps. A new table is therefore safe by default until someone adds it to the deletion list on purpose.
